- Search and screening information from the K-12 AI and science education literature indicates that relevant studies include AI applications, machine learning, intelligent tutoring systems, chatbots, educational robots, automated feedback, automated scoring, learning analytics, and virtual reality, with a specific focus on K-12 science subjects, science teaching and learning, scientific argumentation, science curriculum, science education, science learning, physics, biology, chemistry, environmental science, and AISE; the search string explicitly targeted “primary education,” “elementary education,” “k-12 education,” “secondary education,” “high school,” “junior high school,” “primary school,” “secondary school,” and “middle school,” and the focus/context was “Studies focused on using AI and AI applications in K-12 science subjects teaching and learning. Studies not related to the use of AI and AI applications in K-12 science subjects teaching and learning.” [1]

- One systematic review on AI literacy in K-12 reported that the search string included TITLE-ABS-KEY with “( literacy OR education) AND ( artificial AND intelligence)” OR “AI literacy” OR “AI education,” plus “primary school,” “secondary school,” “k-12,” “middle school,” and “high school,” while excluding “computer-based learning” and “intelligent tutoring system.” The review included peer-reviewed papers on AI literacy and education at school, excluded papers where AI was limited to computer-based learning only, assessment/tutoring based on AI, college students, and K-12 programming/CS concepts as a prerequisite for learning about AI. The search in Scopus returned an initial list of 750 documents, and after title, abstract, keywords, and full-text screening, the final list was 179 documents. [2]

- The review “Pedagogical incorporation of artificial intelligence in K-12 science education: A decadal bibliometric mapping and systematic literature review (2013-2023)” states that the reviewed literature highlights “a diverse range of pedagogical approaches to incorporating AI technologies in K-12 science education,” including hands-on learning through robotics, blended pedagogical strategies, inquiry-based learning, project-based learning, and cooperative learning. It explicitly states that “Hands-on learning emerges prominently through robotics,” and that studies include robotics experiments, learning Newtonian physics through programming robot experiments, AGILEST with machine learning agents and real-time touchless hand interaction, educational chatbot systems, intelligent virtual reality for experimental chemistry education, chatbots in a 5th-grade science course, inquiry-based education using robots to improve inquiry skills and motivation, science education with ChatGPT, computational thinking and robotics in middle school science inquiry, and experiential learning systems with educational robotics to promote collaborative problem-solving skills. [3]

- The same review also states that “The reviewed literature indicates a diverse utilization of AI technologies in K-12 science education,” and identifies “robotics, chatbots, machine learning, automated scoring and feedback, and neural networks with fuzzy logic” as the key AI technologies. It says these technologies are applied to enhance learning outcomes, support student engagement, and personalize learning experiences. It further states that “Robotics involves designing, constructing, and using robots, often integrated with AI technologies, to perform tasks autonomously or interact intelligently with their environment,” and that robotics is prevalent in K-12 science education with applications in hands-on learning, cooperative learning, inquiry-based learning, and project-based learning. It says that “Seven studies highlight the effectiveness of robotics in improving scientific literacy, motivation, and inquiry skills among students,” including robotics experiments on junior high school students’ scientific literacy and educational robots affecting motivation and thermodynamic learning. [4]

- The conclusion section of the same review states that “The review of studies highlights a diverse range of pedagogical approaches to incorporating AI technologies in K-12 science education (Table 10).” It continues that “Hands-on learning and learning-by-doing approaches, especially robotics and machine learning, can significantly enhance student engagement and scientific literacy by providing experiential learning opportunities that align with real-world applications,” but that “successful implementation requires addressing challenges such as resource availability and accessibility and teacher training and literacy in these technologies.” It also states that “Inquiry-based learning and project-based learning, which promote critical thinking and problemsolving, could benefit from AI’s ability to deliver personalized learning experiences and real-time feedback,” and that “Blended learning and cooperative learning strategies, which merge traditional and digital environments, offer flexibility and inclusivity, making them suitable for diverse classroom settings.” It explicitly says “Ensuring seamless integration of AI within these strategies is crucial to enhance collaboration and interaction while maintaining pedagogical goals,” and “future implementations must consider equitable access to AI tools, particularly in under-resourced schools.” It further states that “feedback-based learning” with automated feedback promises improved student performance with timely, tailored responses. [5]

- The abstract of “Artificial Intelligence Applications in K-12 Education: A Systematic Literature Review” states that the systematic review was conducted on articles and conference papers published between 2011 and 2021 in the Web of Science and Scopus databases. It reports that “As the result of the initial search, 2075 documents were extracted and based on inclusive criteria and 210 documents were identified for further investigation.” It says AI applications were categorized into “Student performance, Teaching, Selection, and Behavior tasks, and Other,” and that “Machine Learning (ML) and Intelligent Tutoring System (ITS) were the most common approaches among AI categories.” It also states that “high school-related applications were more frequent and STEM courses were substantially targeted by AI.” [6]

- The abstract of “Systematic review of research on artificial intelligence in K-12 education (2017-2022)” states that the review searched Web of Science and six databases indexed in EBSCO host, used a PRISMA flow chart, and screened articles at the title, abstract, and full-text level. It reports themes in 66 AI studies including “AI as a predictor and indicator of academic behavior or performance, AI curriculum design, integrating AI in various subjects, evaluation of AI in education, AI to enhance learning environments and school operations, AI ethics, and the equity and safety of AI.” It also reports that AI methods were grouped into “Supervised Learning, Unsupervised Learning and Reinforcement Learning,” and AI applications were “Machine Learning (ML) model building tools, intelligent tutors, chat bot, educational games, AI robots and virtual reality devices.” It says AI applications were mostly used by teachers for “ML model demonstration, academic performance prediction and behavior prediction,” and by students for “scientific discovery learning, improving learning experience and data driven decisions.” [7]

- The review “The use of Artificial intelligence in school science: a systematic literature review” states its inclusion criteria explicitly: “The study must focus on an AI application,” “The context of the study must be in science education,” “The context of the study must be in primary or secondary education,” and “The study must perform primary or empirical research.” It says the authors defined keywords such as “artificial intelligence, adaptive learning, intelligent tutoring system, science education, primary school, and secondary school,” expanded the set from previous systematic reviews, and repeated searching and keyword adjustment until the same results were received. It says “The final search string is presented in Table 1.” It also states that studies using LEGO Mindstorms without built-in AI capabilities were excluded. Search alerts were created on ERIC, PsycInfo, Web of Science, and Scopus, and on 15 April 2022 one additional study was included, leaving the total number of included studies at 22. [8]

- The abstract of “Integrating artificial intelligence into science lessons: teachers’ experiences and views” states that the study piloted a new lesson package in science classrooms to introduce students to the idea of AI. It says the AI-integrated science lesson package was designed by the research team as “an extended activity that used the same context as an existing lesson activity.” It reports that three science teachers from different schools piloted the lesson package with small groups of students and provided feedback on the materials and implementation. The findings revealed teachers’ perceptions in terms of the connection between AI and science, challenges when implementing the AI lesson package, and recommendations on improvements. It states that teachers perceived that AI and science have similarities in developing accurate models with quality data and using simplified reasoning, and that AI and science play complementary roles when solving scientific problems. It also states that the biggest challenge was a lack of confidence in content mastery, and that the package would be challenging to get buy-in from teachers regarding curriculum adaptation and targeting the appropriate audience. The recommendations were that comprehensive AI resources be provided to teachers, and that the package can be employed for science enrichment programs after-school. [9]

- The same paper reports that the three science teachers were all in different secondary schools and had less than five years of experience teaching science in schools and had not been trained in teaching AI, but were interested in learning more about AI-integrated science lessons. It states that participants included three teachers, referred to by pseudonyms Tom, Jennifer, and Chris, and 37 students (10, 21, and 6 students, respectively). It reports a three-stage involvement: (1) an introduction session for the teachers as a PD session, (2) implementation of the AI-integrated science lesson package, and (3) a reflection session with the three teachers. It says the introduction session focused on the structure of the lesson package and included an overview of the concepts involved, including the key ideas of ML and a brief introduction on how to use the ML program, rather than a systematic elaboration of ML concepts. It states that the 3-h AI-integrated science lesson, excluding recess, was implemented after school in the three schools; the implementations were observed by the authors, audio- and video-recorded, and transcribed; field notes and student worksheets were collected; and the research team held reflection sessions with the teachers after implementation. [10]

- The abstract of “Teacher’s Perceptions of Using an Artificial Intelligence-Based Educational Tool for Scientific Writing” states that successful implementation of new instructional technologies is “closely related to the attitudes of the teachers who lead the lesson.” It says the study investigated how teachers perceived an AI-enhanced scaffolding system developed to support students’ scientific writing for STEM education. It reports that most STEM teachers positively experienced AI as “a source for superior scaffolding,” but also raised issues related to “the change in the role played by the teachers in the classroom and the transparency of the decisions made by the AI system.” It concludes that these results can be used as a foundation for future integration of AI with STEM education in schools. [11]

- The abstract of “Integrating ChatGPT into the Inquiry-Based Science Curriculum for Primary Education” states that the integration of ChatGPT into an inquiry-based science curriculum for elementary school is investigated “with an eye on increasing student involvement and learning results.” It says AI-driven tools will help teachers enable individualized learning opportunities that foster young students’ critical thinking and curiosity. It emphasizes the need for a solid basis in scientific education because it develops critical thinking and problem-solving abilities necessary to negotiate the natural world’s complexity. It also says it tackles the difficulties of using inquiry-based learning, including the pressure of standardized testing and the necessity of professional growth to provide instructors with successful approaches. It concludes that including AI in the classroom prepares students for a technologically driven future and calls for careful evaluation of ethical consequences and thorough educator training to optimize its possible value. [12]

- “Using an Artificial Intelligence Chatbot in Scientific Inquiry: Focusing on a Guided-Inquiry Activity Using Inquirybot” defines scientific inquiry as “all practices of observing, reasoning, interpreting, explaining, predicting, arguing about, and modeling scientific phenomena.” It says the study focused on guided inquiry because it is not easy to fully achieve open-ended scientific inquiry with the limited functions available in current AI chatbot technology. It explains that the study developed and adapted AI chatbots for guided-inquiry activities, meaning “small-sized inquiry activities that are partially guided by a teacher or other facilitators (the other facilitator in this study being an AI chatbot).” It says guided-inquiry activities provide students with tested procedures to arrive at a predetermined but unspecified outcome, and that they can increase interest and participation even in inquiry problems not directly designed by students. It says they are useful for elementary students to develop activities step by step. It also states that “In a guided-inquiry activity, the teacher is an active facilitator,” continuously monitoring progress, supporting groups with content or process problems, and leading discussions; teachers identify struggling groups and give appropriate help, find confusing parts, and correct them. [13]

- The same Inquirybot paper states that guided-inquiry activities are partially guided by a teacher or other facilitators, and that the AI chatbot is “the other facilitator in this study.” It emphasizes that students do not design the inquiry problems themselves; rather, the inquiry process must be led by the students and sufficiently supported by the teacher. [13]

- “AI-Infused Collaborative Inquiry in Upper Elementary School: A Game-Based Learning Approach” states that AI-infused collaborative inquiry learning incorporates “block-based programming within rich, problem-solving scenarios to support students’ development of foundational AI knowledge.” It says the approach offers significant potential for creating engaging collaborative learning experiences that integrate AI and life science. It reports that teachers will need “more immersive and comprehensive professional development focused on AI content knowledge as well as grade level appropriate activities to deploy in the classrooms.” It says AI professional development workshops should provide follow-up classroom support and easy-to-implement, grade-level and age-appropriate exemplars. It also states that balancing teacher co-design, constraints of developing AI-infused game-based learning environments, and the lack of knowledge of teachers in AI will present challenges, and that the PRIMARYAI game-based learning environment is still under active development and refinement. [14]

- A workshop report on AI in science education research states that AI is reshaping science education by transforming instructional practices, learning environments, and educators’ roles. It notes that a systematic review of 36 AI-related contributions at NARST 2024 showed AI is used as both a methodological and thematic catalyst, functioning as a “multifunctional, multimodal, and generative tool,” while raising ethical issues concerning learning goals, curriculum content, individualized feedback, teacher education, bias, and equity. It states that AI-based systems are increasingly used to support peer review through automated checks of language, data, and references or by suggesting improvements to manuscripts. It also says multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are enabling new forms of empirical inquiry and feedback scenarios that are more personalized, interactive, and accessible, supporting not only students but also teachers in developing tailored, adaptive instructional formats. [15]

- The same workshop report states that in science education research, AI intersects with curriculum and assessment, epistemic cognition, inclusion, and teacher professional development, highlighting cases where AI can support human reasoning and cases where it may introduce risks to equity or validity. It says AI is altering the conduct of research itself and raising questions about construct validity, transparency, and the ethics of algorithmic mediation. [15]

- The same workshop report states that “AI is poised to reshaping science education by transforming instructional practices, learning environments, and educators’ roles,” and that a recent systematic review spanning empirical studies from 2014 to 2023 highlighted AI’s multifaceted impact: enhancing instructional design, adapting assessments, and influencing both student and teacher experiences in science classrooms. It further says AI-driven tools in science teaching have produced measurable improvements in learning outcomes. It describes the CLAIS prototype (Collaborative Learning with AI Speakers), which positions AI as a peer within group science-learning activities. Pre-service elementary science teachers who engaged with CLAIS reported increased pedagogical and technological content knowledge and recognized changes in epistemic practices. It also says generative AI can produce physics simulations via generative models, enabling the development of virtual labs on-the-fly. [16]

- The same report says teacher attitudes toward AI in science education are generally positive, citing a study examining science teachers’ acceptance of AI with high levels of perceived self-efficacy and expectations of ease of use in AI-supported classrooms. It states that pilot interventions embedding AI directly into science curricula point to the importance of integrating AI concepts within disciplinary contexts rather than teaching AI as an abstract, standalone topic. [16]

- The same report states that “successful science teachers paired AI use with clear, inquiry-aligned objectives and embedded source verification practices, such as prompting the AI to cite its sources, provide links to referenced materials, or limit its responses to a defined set of trusted resources.” It says students were guided to enter AI conversations with focused questions, such as forming a hypothesis or interpreting a result, and exit with a preliminary claim, draft explanation, or plan for further investigation. It states that teachers integrated AI outputs into lab notebooks and CER frameworks, using feedback cycles to help students validate and revise their reasoning. It also says teachers used AI to broaden scientific representation by exploring global perspectives, case studies, and underrepresented scientists, and emphasized teaching students how to verify AI-generated content, using AI as a springboard for critical thinking rather than a source of final answers. [17]

- The same report states that science teachers used AI grading to support CER writing, lab reflections, and open-ended science explanations. It says narrative feedback was praised for helping students clarify claims and reasoning, but AI-assigned scores were often inconsistent, prompting teachers to treat the tool as a revision support rather than a summative grader. It also says AI was frequently applied to analyze students’ written arguments and that scoring issues were common, including one teacher reporting that the tool scored some students out of 20 points and others out of 10 when the assessment was worth 10 points. It states that students were confused when feedback and grades did not align. Teachers emphasized the importance of mediation—reviewing, editing, and clarifying AI feedback—to ensure alignment with content goals and student expectations. They also stressed that students must be taught to interpret AI feedback critically, understanding that the tool is a lever, not a replacement, for their own reasoning and judgment. [17]

It says AI functioned as “a third agent, an active participant that mediated feedback, supported inquiry, and extended teachers’ instructional reach while preserving human judgment and teacher authority.” It reports that over seven weeks in spring 2025, 21 in-service teachers from four Washington State public school districts and one independent school integrated four AI-powered features: Teaching Aide, Assessment & AI Grading, AI Tutor, and Student Growth Insights. More than 600 students in grades 6-12 used the platform in class at the direction of their teachers, who designed and facilitated the AI activities. Teachers were co-design partners: they planned activities, implemented them with students, and provided weekly reflections on AI’s role in classroom settings. Their feedback guided iterative improvements for Colleague AI. The research team captured data through surveys, planning and reflection forms, group meetings, one-on-one interviews, and platform usage logs. [18]

- The Teaching Aide 2 feature from the same study allows teachers to create structured student-AI conversations by adding an additional layer of prompt instruction for AI. Teachers create custom instructions for the AI on the topic it should discuss and how it should discuss it with students. All students then receive the same initial message from the AI and the conversation automatically adapts to their responses. The goal is to broaden classroom discourse, personalize learning, prompt deeper thinking, and scaffold inquiry without replacing the teacher’s voice. In the pilot, 18 teachers created 114 distinct AI-assisted in-class conversations across 21 classrooms in which up to 600 students participated, covering subjects from math to humanities. Three teachers decided not to implement the Teaching Aide tool because it did not fit with their curriculum plan. Approximately 28% of teachers reported classroom implementations with high levels of engagement, with most students participating thoughtfully in their AI-assisted conversations. Around 66% of teachers experienced mixed engagement, while only 6% reported low overall engagement. Teachers played a critical role in guiding successful implementation by modeling effective prompts, actively circulating during sessions, and consistently framing the AI as a thought partner rather than a search engine. - “The Landscape of AI in Science Education: What is Changing and How to Respond” states that platforms such as Google Teachable Machine provide opportunities for learners to manipulate variables and train algorithms for scientific inquiry, while generative AI such as GPT offers opportunities to explain graphical representations for real-world phenomena. It says AI-supported materials promote inclusivity and accessibility by adjusting to individual learning preferences, linguistic backgrounds, and cognitive needs. It states that AI assists educators and researchers in creating up-to-date learning materials, freeing curriculum designers from heavy time-consuming work. It also says AI assessment practices are shifting toward formative, performance-based, and authentic evaluation; AI has enabled automatic scoring of students’ written explanations and arguments and drawn models; AI-supported learning analytics can track how students design experiments, interpret data, and communicate scientific arguments; real-time dashboards capture patterns of misunderstanding; and longitudinal assessment models supported by AI generate comprehensive learner profiles to trace scientific reasoning over years of study. [33]

- The same paper states that the transformations in science education goals are summarized across three visions. In Vision I, AI transforms core scientific practices such as hypothesis generation, modeling, data analysis, and solution design, requiring students to develop competencies in AI-supported scientific inquiry rather than focusing solely on traditional content mastery. In Vision II, AI operates as a collaborative partner in applying science to solve authentic, real-world problems. Vision III extends science education goals further by empowering students as agents of change, where responsible and ethical engagement with AI becomes crucial for addressing socio-political, cultural, and environmental challenges. It states that these changes call for an integrative model of Science Literacy Plus, where AI literacy is interwoven with science literacy. [34]

- The same paper states that responsible practices include ensuring equitable access to AI tools, mitigating algorithmic bias, and fostering transparency, accountability, and human oversight. It says educators are encouraged to guide students in recognizing AI’s limitations, questioning whose perspectives are represented, and reflecting on broader social and environmental impacts. It also states that ethical engagement involves protecting privacy, respecting Indigenous knowledge, and promoting sustainability in the development and use of AI systems. [34]

- The same paper states that Chapter 4 emphasizes AI transforming science education goals from memorization and routine experimentation to sustained inquiry and lifelong investigation. It says AI scaffolds the inquiry cycle by supporting students as they brainstorm researchable questions, visualize and test models, analyze data, and refine explanations. It also states that partnerships among teachers, students, and designers are essential to critically examine AI outputs, refine instructional uses, and preserve student agency in investigations. Professional development and collaborative curriculum design are needed so educators can mediate AI integration while upholding inclusivity, human dignity, and democratic participation. [35]

- The same paper states that Chapter 6 says AI is reshaping teacher practice by streamlining lesson planning, formative assessment design, and classroom orchestration. It says teachers have access to automated scoring systems, intelligent dashboards, and personalized feedback mechanisms that highlight student misconceptions in real time. It also says AI can support teacher professional growth through simulations and practice-based environments where teachers can rehearse core instructional competencies, such as eliciting student thinking or facilitating scientific argumentation, in reduced-complexity contexts. It further states that ethical use demands that teachers and school systems critically interrogate how algorithms are trained, what assumptions underlie their design, and how their outputs are interpreted in relation to student learning. [36]

- The same paper states that Chapter 9 says AI is reshaping science assessment by redefining constructs, introducing new formats, and transforming classroom practices. It says traditional assessments are increasingly insufficient because generative AI can provide immediate answers to many standardized tasks, and assessment is moving toward performance-based models emphasizing authentic reasoning, complex problem-solving, collaborative inquiry, and human-AI partnerships. It says AI-resilient assessments require students to critique, refine, or extend AI-generated outputs, and that AI enables formative assessment through real-time feedback, adaptive diagnostics, and integration with classroom simulations. It says responsibly and ethically addressing these changes requires principled approaches that safeguard validity, fairness, and equity, while preserving teacher oversight through human-in-the-loop models. [37]

- “Integrating RADEC Model and AI to Enhance Science Literacy: Student Perspectives” states that AI can be utilized in various stages of the learning process to enhance students’ understanding of science. In the read stage, AI provides digital reading materials tailored to students’ levels of comprehension. During the answer stage, AI supplies evaluation questions or science exercises, automatically assesses student responses, and provides instant feedback. In the discuss stage, AI helps organize online discussions or AI-based forums where students can discuss the scientific concepts they are learning. For the explain stage, AI offers additional explanations of complex scientific concepts; for instance, AI chatbots can provide further explanations or answer student questions on specific topics. Finally, in the create stage, AI-assisted tools facilitate students in creating scientific projects or simulations based on the concepts they learn. It says AI can offer creative tools, guidance, and even assemble AI-based projects involving data processing and scientific modeling. [40]

**Fully Comprehensive Findings**

The gathered literature is heavily weighted toward reviews, conceptual papers, teacher-perspective papers, and adjacent empirical work on inquiry, argumentation, scientific reasoning, AI literacy, intelligent tutoring systems, chatbots, adaptive learning, and AI-supported feedback. Direct comparative evidence specifically in **K-12 science** for AI-powered tools versus standard or non-AI science instruction was limited in the raw material, but several sources do speak to comparative or adjacent evidence and to design/moderator differences.

The strongest directly relevant K-12 science review evidence found was the systematic review by **Heeg and Avraamidou (2023)**, which states: “ABSTRACT Artificial Intelligence is widely used across contexts and for different purposes, including the field of education. However, a review of the literature showcases that while there exist various review studies on the use of AI in education, missing remains a review focusing on science education. To address this gap, we carried out a systematic literature review between 2010 and 2021, driven by three questions: a) What types of AI applications are used in school science? b) For what teaching content are AI applications in school science used? and, c) What is the impact of AI applications on teaching and learning of school science? The studies reviewed (n=22) included nine different types of AI applications: automated assessment, automated feedback, learning analytics, adaptive learning systems, intelligent tutoring systems, multilabel text classification, chatbot, expert systems, and mind wandering detection. The majority of the AI applications are used in geoscience or physics and AI applications are used to support either knkowledge construction or skills development. In terms of the impact of AI applications, this is found across the following: learning achievement, argumentation skills, learning experience, and teaching. Missing remains an examination of learners’ and teachers’ experiences with the use of AI in school science, interdisciplinary approaches to AI implementation, as well as an examination of issues related to ethics and biases.” [1]

The same paper also provides inclusion criteria and search process details: “To be included in this review, a study must endorse the following criteria: • The study must focus on an AI application • The context of the study must be in science education • The context of the study must be in primary or secondary education • The study must perform primary or empirical research.” It further says: “The final search string is presented in Table 1.” and describes expanding keywords from prior systematic reviews, then repeating searches until the same results were received. [1]

It also states the AI applications reviewed and the kinds of outcomes:
- “The studies reviewed included nine different types of AI applications: automated assessment, automated feedback, learning analytics, adaptive learning systems, intelligent tutoring systems, multilabel text classification, chatbot, expert systems, and mind wandering detection.” [1]
- “The majority of the AI applications are used in geoscience or physics and AI applications are used to support either knkowledge construction or skills development.” [1]
- “In terms of the impact of AI applications, this is found across the following: learning achievement, argumentation skills, learning experience, and teaching.” [1]
- It further notes that “automated assessment and feedback applications were well represented, together with personalized learning systems and predictive modeling,” while less represented applications included “chatbots, multilabel text classifiers, mind wandering detection systems, and expert systems.” [1]
- It gives an example: “HASbot was developed to support students’ revision of scientific arguments in real-time when they were engaged in classroom activities.” [1]

The review also specifies that, for teaching content, “the majority of the AI applications are used in in the context of geoscience (n = 5) or physics (n = 9) lessons.” It says AI applications were used “to either teach domain-specific knowledge to students or to develop scientific argumentation skills.” It also specifically says: “The automated assessment and feedback application by Zhu et al. (2017), and further developed versions of the application by Mao et al. (2018) and Lee et al. (2019Lee et al. ( , 2021)), aimed to improve the scientific argumentation skills of students. These applications provided a curriculum during which students were asked to give multiple scientific argumentations. After submitting an argument, students received automated assessment and feedback on how to improve these arguments. Subsequently, the students were provided with an opportunity for revisions on which they would again receive a score and feedback. Overall, the automatic assessment and feedback system trained and improved the argumentation skills of students.” [1]

This same review notes a tutoring-system example relevant to comparison with standard instruction: “The intelligent tutoring system by Dolenc et al. (2015), illustrates applications focusing on knowledge transfer. This tutoring system taught the Gears subject matter, which serves as the last chapter of the Technology and Science Course in the eighth grade of an elementary school in Slovenia. By providing students with the content of this subject matter, and proposing individually adapted learning paths based on students’ cognitive abilities, students were able to master the content of this Technology and Science Course chapter.” [1]

Another key review is **Kavitha and Joshith (2024)** on pedagogical incorporation of AI in K-12 science education. It states: “The majority of studies focused on high school settings (n=10, 50%), followed by middle school (n=8, 40%) and elementary school (n=2, 10%).” It also says: “Among the methodological approaches employed, design and developmental research (Richey & Klein, 2014) emerged as the most prevalent, with eight studies adopting this methodology. Notably, this approach was particularly prominent in high school settings, with 4 out of 8 studies focusing on this educational level.” [2]

The same paper reports quasi-experimental designs among the reviewed studies: “within the experimental/quasi-experimental category (Mize & Manago, 2022), 4 out of 5 studies utilized a quasi-experimental design, which involved dividing participants into an experimental group, where AI technology (e.g., Educational Chatbot (Yen-Ting Lin & Yen-Ting Lin, 2023) was applied, and a control group without the intervention. Subsequently, pre-and post-test analyses were conducted to evaluate the impact of the intervention on the experimental group compared to the control group (Maciejewski, 2020). Additionally, four studies employed a mixed-method approach with an initial quantitative phase followed by qualitative (Ivankova et al., 2006), and two studies employed theoretical or descriptive research. Another study employed a case study research design.” [2]

The same review gives a pedagogical breakdown relevant to inquiry and AI-supported science learning: “Hands-on learning emerges prominently through robotics (Eguchi, 2017). For instance, Mayub et al. (2023) investigated how robotics experiments enhance scientific literacy among junior high school students, while Ferrarelli and Iocchi (2021) demonstrated the effectiveness of learning Newtonian physics through programming robot experiments, emphasizing their role in experiential learning and boosting student engagement (Benitti & Spolaôr, 2017). Additionally, the AGILEST approach by Zahid Iqbal and Campbell (2023) illustrates how machine learning agents and real-time touchless hand interaction facilitate active learning through learning by doing experiences, further enriching science education environments (Putu Krisna Dewi et al., 2023). Blended pedagogical strategies that integrate traditional instruction with AI technologies (Hrastinski, 2019) are evidenced by studies such as Yen-Ting Lin and Yen-Ting Lin (2023), who developed an educational chatbot system aimed at improving students’ performance in biology, and Lu et al. (2021), who implemented intelligent virtual reality for experimental chemistry education. Moreover, Deveci Topal (2021) also utilized chatbots in a 5th-grade science course, further demonstrating the integration of AI technologies to support learning objectives in science classrooms. Furthermore, inquiry-based learning emerges as another prominent pedagogical approach (Pedaste et al., 2015), as highlighted by Pedaste and Altin (2020), whose study investigated the impact of inquiry-based education using robots on learners’ inquiry skills and motivation. Similarly, Cooper (2023) explored science education with ChatGPT, emphasizing the role of generative artificial intelligence in fostering inquiry-based, student-centered learning experiences (Ali et al., 2023). Additionally, project-based learning and cooperative learning pedagogical approaches were exemplified by Fuhrmann (2021), who integrated computational thinking and robotics in middle school science inquiry, and D’Amico et al. (2020), who developed experiential learning systems with educational robotics to promote collaborative problem-solving skills.” [2]

It also reports a grade-level distribution and methodological mix: “The distribution of reviewed studies by grade levels and methodological approaches is presented in Table 9. The majority of studies focused on high school settings (n=10, 50%), followed by middle school (n=8, 40%) and elementary school (n=2, 10%).” [2]

A third important review is **Kavitha and Joshith (2024)**’s summary of pedagogical approaches and implications: “The review of studies highlights a diverse range of pedagogical approaches to incorporating AI technologies in K-12 science education (Table 10).” It explicitly identifies “inquiry-based learning,” “blended pedagogical strategies,” “project-based learning,” “cooperative learning,” “hands-on learning,” and “generative artificial intelligence” as relevant categories. [3]

The same paper also states: “Pedaste and Altin (2020), whose study investigated the impact of inquiry-based education using robots on learners’ inquiry skills and motivation.” [3]

Another source, **Van Brummelen and Lin (2020)**, provides adjacent K-12 evidence about AI tools/curricula and whether they are integrated into core science content. It states: “Many K-12 AI tools and curricula exist as standalone products or extend computer science curriculum. Two widely-used AI teaching tools are Teachable Machine [9] and Machine Learning for Kids [20], which empower learners to develop classification models without needing to program.” It also says: “In our literature review, we found one example of AI curriculum that was both integrated into a core course and designed or taught by K-12 teachers alongside researchers. This curriculum involved AI and science concepts, and was taught in Australian K-6 classrooms [17]. Although this example is insightful, much further research is needed to integrate teacher expertise and address widespread, integrated AI curriculum in K-12 classrooms [39].” [4]

The paper additionally notes that “most involve researchers rather than K-12 teachers as the instructors, and likely miss valuable expertise and feedback from professionals who have worked in the classroom,” and that some integrated examples “have not been tested in regular classrooms and teachers were not involved in the design process.” [4]

A relevant general evidence source is **Almasri (2024)**, which states that AI in science teaching and learning is increasingly popular and that machine learning has been applied to automatically evaluate scientific models in education. It says: “More specifically, machine learning, a specific artificial intelligence technology, has been applied to automatically evaluate scientific models used in the education sector. Zhai et al. (2022) employed machine learning techniques to assess the quality of these models after gathering student responses to activities. Their research demonstrates how artificial intelligence can be used to automate assessment procedures and provide students with timely and detailed feedback on their work in the area of science education.” [5]

The same paper also says that AI in science education is used for “automate assessment procedures and provide students with timely and detailed feedback,” and that “teachers can play a vital role” in AI applications in education. [5]

A closely related source is **Zhai and Crippen (2023/2026 arXiv-related snippets)**, which emphasizes the potential of AI to support scientific inquiry and assessment. One excerpt states: “For instance, platforms such as Google Teachable Machine provide opportunities for learners to manipulate variables and train algorithms for scientific inquiry (Herdliska & Zhai, 2024), while generative AI such as GPT offers opportunities to explain graphical representations for real-world phenomena (Bewersdorff et al., 2025). In addition, to mimic scientists’ authentic research, these AIsupported materials promote inclusivity and accessibility by adjusting to individual learning preferences, linguistic backgrounds, and cognitive needs, making advanced scientific exploration available to diverse populations of learners worldwide.” [6]

That same excerpt says: “Assessment practices in science education, both formative and summative, are similarly being reshaped by AI, moving away from standardized, summative testing toward formative, performance-based, and authentic evaluation (Linn & Gerard, 2024). AI has enabled automatic scoring of students’ written explanations and arguments and drawn models, significantly advancing automaticity, and extending the complexity of constructs that assessment can target (Nehm, 2024;Zhai et al., 2020). AI-supported learning analytics can track how students design experiments, interpret data, and communicate scientific arguments, thereby assessing both process and product in scientific inquiry (Pellegrino, 2024).” [6]

It also says: “real-time dashboards for teachers and learners capture patterns of misunderstanding in topics like genetics or thermodynamics, allowing for immediate intervention” and “longitudinal assessment models supported by AI generate comprehensive learner profiles, making it possible to trace the development of scientific reasoning skills across years of study.” [6]

Another directly relevant source is the **OpenAlex/Google Scholar-derived evidence on AI-assisted feedback and intelligent tutoring**, including the Tavily and Scholar snippets. The Tavily result “The Evidence Base on AI in K-12 | Executive Summary” states: “Most research on AI in education focuses on students as users of AI tools. The report reviews the current research, focusing specifically on studies that convincingly estimate causal impact, meaning studies that can tell us whether an AI tool changed outcomes for students or educators. After reviewing the full repository, we identified only 20 high-quality causal studies that rigorously examine how AI tools affect students or educators.” It also says: “Across the causal studies reviewed, evidence suggests that AI tools designed with pedagogical guardrails – such as tutoring systems that give hints or guide reasoning – show more promising outcomes than general-purpose chatbots that provide answers directly.” [7]

This same source further notes that educator-facing AI tools may reduce time spent on tasks such as lesson preparation while maintaining instructional quality. [7]

A closely related adjacent evidence snippet from **Yannier et al. (2024)** states: “We report on a randomized controlled experiment where we compare learning outcomes of children interacting with the Intelligent Science Station that has task-loop adaptivity incorporated, compared to another version that provides tasks randomly without adaptivity. Our results show that adaptivity using Bayesian Knowledge Tracing in the context of a mixed-reality system leads to better learning of scientific principles, without sacrificing enjoyment. These results demonstrate benefits of adaptivity in a mixed-reality setting to improve children’s science learning.” [8]

This is not explicitly K-12 science reasoning/inquiry relative to standard instruction, but it is strong adjacent causal evidence that AI adaptivity outperformed a non-adaptive comparator in children’s science learning. [8]

Typically, students use computer simulations to explore scientific concepts by testing hypotheses, conducting experiments, and evaluating data. Inquiry learning can improve scientific reasoning by having students ‘act like scientists’, thereby improving their learning of the content and the corresponding scientific processes.” It adds that students may struggle because they lack scientific reasoning or self-regulation, and the study tested “video modeling examples and metacognitive prompts.” [9]

(2021) educational implications**: “Designing adaptive support tools, which remind students to connect different scientific reasoning processes, based on their actions in a virtual experiment, might be also beneficial for improving scientific reasoning. Future research needs to investigate the effects of different interventions (such as video modeling examples and self-regulation instruction) on improving scientific reasoning and argumentation.” [10]

- **van der Graaf et al. (2019)**: “Inquiry-based lessons have been demonstrated to improve children’s scientific thinking (i.e. reasoning abilities and domain-specific knowledge). Although empirical evidence shows that inquiry-based learning requires instruction, research comes from two approaches that have not been bridged yet: direct instruction of scientific reasoning and teacher training of verbal support. We investigated how these two types of instruction separately or combined strengthened children’s scientific thinking by comparing four conditions: baseline, direct instruction, verbal support, and a combined approach. Effectiveness of an inquiry-based lesson series on scientific reasoning abilities, vocabulary, and domain-specific knowledge (near and far transfer) were studied among 301 fourth graders. Results showed that both approaches strengthened different components of scientific reasoning abilities, and that a combination of instructions was most effective for scientific reasoning abilities, vocabulary, and domain-specific knowledge. Domain-specific knowledge acquisition was strengthened only when both instructions were provided.” [11]

This is not AI, but it is highly relevant adjacent evidence for moderators/design differences in inquiry/scientific reasoning interventions.

- **Eymur and Çetin (2024)**: “The present study focused on the effectiveness of ADI instructional model to support students’ scientific literacy with a mixed method design… researchers investigated the implementation of this model in eighth grade students.” It then states: “Our findings suggested that ADI instructional model was more effective in increasing scientific literacy of students than structured inquiry instruction model that is more traditional laboratory instruction.” It further says experimental-group students engaged in “designing and conducting investigations, developing arguments based on claim and evidence, supporting their arguments with their peers, writing investigation reports,” and that the experimental group had “higher scores especially two dimensions of scientific literacy such as understanding the role of science… and scientific thinking and doing.” [12]

Students absolutely need to acquire the 21st century skills we discussed at the outset of this article: problem solving, communication, critical thinking, collaborative teamwork, creativity, cross-cultural interaction, and information literacy. We need to train our students how to critically analyze the results that AI tools produce.” [33]

This is not peer-reviewed evidence, but it is directly relevant to the thread’s comparative framing and the role of guardrails.

Across the gathered sources, the main recurring moderators and design differences are:

- Grade level:
  - High school dominates in some K-12 AI science reviews, with middle school and elementary less represented. [2]
  - Elementary science appears in some tutoring/adaptive systems and inquiry interventions. [1], [8], [12], [15], [18], [19]
- Methodological design:
  - Design and developmental research is common in K-12 AI science incorporation. [2]
  - Quasi-experimental and experimental/comparison-group designs appear in several studies and reviews. [2], [8], [11], [13], [15]
  - Mixed-method designs are common for studying AI-supported science or inquiry interventions. [2], [12]
  - Many AI-in-education papers remain descriptive, theoretical, or design-oriented rather than causal. [2], [5], [7]
- AI function:
  - Automated assessment / automated feedback / adaptive learning / ITS / chatbots / learning analytics are the most common functional categories. [1], [5], [6], [22], [23], [31], [32]
  - Pedagogical guardrails matter: AI that “give hints or guide reasoning” appears more promising than general-purpose chatbots that provide answers directly. [7]
- Pedagogy:
  - Inquiry-based learning, argumentation-driven inquiry, blended learning, hands-on robotics, project-based learning, and cooperative learning appear as the main science-oriented designs. [2], [3], [12], [13], [18], [19]
  - Teacher mediation and co-design are emphasized repeatedly. [4], [7], [26], [31]
- Outcomes:
  - AI-supported systems are repeatedly linked to engagement, motivation, learning performance, scientific literacy, argumentation, inquiry skills, and scientific reasoning. [1], [2], [3], [5], [6], [8], [12], [13], [14], [29], [31], [32]
  - However, direct evidence of superiority over standard instruction in K-12 science is sparse in the retrieved material; the clearest comparisons come from adjacent or partially overlapping contexts, such as adaptive mixed-reality learning, ADI versus structured inquiry, and inquiry-based approaches versus other supports. [8], [12], [13], [14]

The database and search results also surfaced several specific comparative or quasi-comparative items, though many were not purely AI-versus-standard science instruction in K-12:

- “A Comparative Analysis of AI Use in Scientific Inquiry Learning …” was surfaced in Tavily with the note: “The results indicated significant differences regarding educational placement: gifted students reported lower levels of AI-Assisted Scientific Inquiry Learning yet demonstrated higher AI literacy and greater confidence in the safe use of AI.” The snippet also names factors/constructs: “ASDAR: AI-Supported Data Analysis and Reporting, ASEDM: AI-Supported Experimental Design and Methods, ASCE: AI-Supported Conceptualization and Explanation, ASIMS: AI-Supported Information Management and Synthesis, AASILQ: AI-assisted scientific inquiry learning Questionnaire, GM: gifted male, GF: gifted female, NGM: non-gifted male, and NGF: non-gifted female.” [34]

- The Tavily result “The Evidence Base on AI in K-12 | Executive Summary” indicates that “AI tools designed with pedagogical guardrails – such as tutoring systems that give hints or guide reasoning – show more promising outcomes than general-purpose chatbots that provide answers directly.” [7]

- The arXiv result on “Transforming Science Learning Materials in the Era of Artificial Intelligence” states: “Empirical evaluations with biology lessons on cell organelles demonstrated that learners rated the system as more engaging, coherent, and helpful than simpler QA chatbots, and that many completed the entire conversational workflow. Although no significant differences in short-term test performance were observed compared to reading conditions, interaction analyses revealed that learners who engaged more deeply in conversations achieved higher learning gains, highlighting the potential of LLM-driven systems to foster adaptive, personalized science learning at scale.” [35]

- The same source also says AI-supported virtual agents “yielding medium overall effects on learning (g = 0.43) when compared to simulations without AI-supported agents.” [35]

- The arXiv/ERIC result “Resurrecting Socrates in the Age of AI” gives a quasi-experimental protocol: “approximately 80 German pre-service biology teacher students will be randomly assigned to one of two groups: an AI Socratic Tutor condition and an uninstructed chatbot control,” with “quality assessed through double-blind expert review,” but this is higher education, not K-12. [36]

- The AR/AI/robotics literature in the search results also repeatedly highlights feedback and scaffolding rather than direct content delivery:
  - “The system provides adaptive guidance by dynamically defining Sub-flowcharts for scaffolding low-performance students.” [27]
  - “The use of intelligent tutors provides the unique opportunity of personally tailored learning and feedback.” [17]
  - “Automated personalized feedback leads to considerable improvement in student learning outcomes and in the subjective evaluation of the feedback.” [37]
  - “students interacting with AI tutors showed increased cognitive engagement and better learning outcomes compared to traditional instruction” was stated in a snippet citing Holstein et al. within an engagement paper. [38]

The retrieved literature also repeatedly emphasizes limitations and cautions:
- “Missing remains an examination of learners’ and teachers’ experiences with the use of AI in school science, interdisciplinary approaches to AI implementation, as well as an examination of issues related to ethics and biases.” [1]
- “there are mixed results on the effectiveness of adaptivity based on different implementations and contexts.” [8]
- “Although ChatGPT offers many benefits, it can sometimes provide inaccurate information, necessitating human oversight in science education.” [29]
- “LLMs may produce misleading, incorrect, or educationally unproductive responses.” [39]
- “AI technologies … must be deployed in conjunction with sound pedagogy and a human touch to achieve the most significant impact.” [22]
- “teachers were not involved in the design process” is a concern for generalizability of some tools. [4]
