## Research Architecture & Open Questions

# Research Architecture & Open Questions

## Field Anchors

The contemporary research on AI-powered tools for K-12 science reasoning rests on foundational work establishing how intelligent systems can augment rather than replace teacher practice. The 2017 study "Intelligent tutors as teachers' aides: exploring teacher needs for" established that effective educational AI must be designed with explicit attention to teacher constraints, workflows, and decision-making—a principle that subsequent work has neither abandoned nor thoroughly operationalized in science-specific contexts. The TA Framework (2020) extended this by proposing systematic real-time teaching augmentation for K-12 environments, introducing the conceptual apparatus for orchestrating multiple actors (teacher, student, system) in classroom time. Three 2019 studies on classroom orchestration and teacher-student complementarity further solidified the notion that AI tools succeed only when aligned with existing pedagogical roles and designed through participatory methods that include educators. These anchors collectively establish that technical capability alone is insufficient; integration requires understanding teacher needs, classroom ecology, and the division of cognitive labor between human and machine guidance.

## Intellectual Lineage

The current run of 60 papers extends these foundations along two generational lines. The first generation (2018–2021) translated orchestration and co-design principles into prototype systems—moving from theory to proof-of-concept implementations in science classrooms, though primarily in small-scale, facilitator-intensive settings. The second generation (2022–present) has begun scaling these prototypes and exploring specific AI modalities: generative language models, adaptive prompt engineering, and simulation-based feedback. However, the lineage shows a critical narrowing: while the foundational work emphasized teacher needs and classroom ecology across diverse student populations, recent implementations cluster heavily around well-resourced schools and advanced learners, with minimal systematic investigation of how these tools perform for students with low prior science achievement, English language learners, or students in under-resourced settings. The 60 new papers appear to deepen technical sophistication (better prompting, finer-grained feedback) but have not yet circled back to re-examine teacher integration or equity outcomes that the foundational work foregrounded.

## Research Gaps

The citation structure reveals three critical absences. First, randomized controlled trials in science inquiry settings remain scarce; the field's evidence base relies heavily on qualitative case studies and small quasi-experimental designs, leaving causal claims about student reasoning gains unverified at scale. Second, underrepresented populations—English language learners, students with disabilities, and students in rural or lower-income districts—appear in anchor citations (teacher support studies) but are nearly absent from recent AI-tool implementations. Third, longitudinal outcomes beyond immediate engagement are unexplored; no papers in the run appear to track whether AI-supported inquiry translates to sustained scientific reasoning gains, transfer to novel problems, or shifts in science identity over semesters or years.

## Hypothesis Surfaces

**Hypothesis 1**: Among sixth to eighth grade ELL students engaged in inquiry-based physical science units, AI tutoring systems providing real-time, language-scaffolded feedback on hypothesis formation will increase the frequency and syntactic complexity of scientific explanations compared to standard curriculum, measured via coded transcripts in a cluster-randomized trial across 12 classrooms over one semester.

**Hypothesis 2**: Intelligent tutoring systems designed through participatory co-design with teachers serving high-poverty schools will be adopted and used with fidelity at rates 40% higher than those designed without teacher input, measured via classroom observation and log data in a matched-pair quasi-experiment.

**Hypothesis 3**: Adaptive AI prompts calibrated to individual prior achievement levels will reduce the achievement gap in post-assessment reasoning scores between high- and low-prior-achievement students, tested via item response theory analysis in a within-subjects design across three science domains.

## Research Report

### Research Questions Investigated

| Tier | Sub-question |
|------|-------------|
| Tier 1 | What counts as 'scientific reasoning' and 'inquiry skills' in K-12 science education, and how are these outcomes operationalized across grade bands and disciplines? |
| Tier 1 | Which K-12 student populations and science contexts are most relevant for studying AI-powered support for scientific reasoning and inquiry? |
| Tier 1 | What forms of AI-powered tools are being studied for science learning, and how are these distinguished from other digital or instructional supports? |
| Tier 2 | How are scientific reasoning and inquiry skills typically developed in K-12 science classrooms without AI-powered tools? |
| Tier 2 | What conventional or non-AI interventions serve as the main comparison conditions for AI tools in K-12 science learning? |
| Tier 2 | What baseline levels of scientific reasoning and inquiry performance are reported under standard science instruction, and what gaps remain? |
| Tier 3 | How are AI-powered science learning tools integrated into K-12 instruction, and what teacher roles are typically involved? |
| Tier 3 | What interaction features of AI tools are intended to support scientific reasoning and inquiry? |
| Tier 3 | What implementation conditions appear necessary for AI tools to function as designed? |
| Tier 4 | What is the comparative evidence that AI-powered tools improve K-12 students’ scientific reasoning and inquiry skills relative to standard science instruction or non-AI digital supports? |
| Tier 4 | Are effects different across grade levels, prior achievement, language background, special education status, or school context? |
| Tier 4 | Which AI-powered designs or implementation models show stronger evidence, and what tradeoffs or limitations are reported? |
| Tier 4 | When direct evidence is limited, what does adjacent research suggest about likely impacts on K-12 scientific reasoning and inquiry? |

## Defining the intervention and outcomes

The focal intervention spans several distinct tool families: intelligent tutoring systems, conversational tutors, adaptive feedback systems, AI-supported simulations, generative AI assistants, and teacher-facing analytics or orchestration tools ([1]; [4]; [9]; [46]). The research base does not treat these as interchangeable. ITS and natural-language tutors are typically structured around bounded pedagogical models, domain representations, hinting, and dialogue management, whereas newer LLM-based tools are more open-ended, generative, and variable in reliability ([42]; [9]; [46]; [24]). That distinction matters because most of the stronger positive evidence comes from structured systems, not generic chatbot use ([1]; [11]).

Scientific reasoning and inquiry are also operationalized inconsistently across studies. In the most directly relevant K-12 science studies in the pool, outcomes include science process skills, kinematics knowledge in an inquiry environment, attitude toward scientific inquiry, and preference-aligned comprehension materials rather than a consistent battery of hypothesis generation, control-of-variables reasoning, evidence evaluation, experimental design, or explanation construction ([35]; (Kim, 2015); [44]; [19]). Broader reviews of higher-order thinking in problem- and project-based learning confirm that studies often blend higher-order thinking, critical thinking, and critical-analytic thinking into overlapping constructs, which complicates synthesis for the narrower target of scientific reasoning ([18]). Reviews of eye-tracking in science education likewise show that science-learning studies often infer reasoning from attention, processing, or task performance rather than directly measuring inquiry subskills ([12]).

The populations most represented in the available science-relevant evidence are middle and high school students, especially in physics or general STEM contexts ((Kim, 2015); [35]; [44]; [49]). Elementary science is notably underrepresented in direct studies of AI-supported inquiry in this source pool. Reviews of K-12 ITS and AI-enabled STEM personalization cover elementary through high school, but the summaries provided do not specify science-specific subgroup effects by grade band ([1]; [2]). Evidence on diverse learners, language background, disability status, and prior science achievement is especially sparse for the focal domain.

## What non-AI baseline instruction and comparison conditions look like

The source pool provides only partial evidence on how scientific reasoning and inquiry are typically developed without AI. General STEM and inquiry reviews indicate that non-AI approaches include teacher-led inquiry, problem-based learning, project-based learning, scaffolding through prompts and feedback, simulations, lab work, and authentic problem solving ((Belland, 2017); (Belland, 2018); [18]; [40]). These approaches are relevant because most AI science tools are layered on top of them rather than replacing them. The baseline problem AI is meant to address is usually not the absence of inquiry pedagogy, but the difficulty of sustaining individualized support, timely feedback, and metacognitive prompting during complex inquiry tasks ((Belland, 2017); [9]; [4]).

In direct studies, comparison conditions are usually standard instruction, conventional teaching, search engines, or non-AI digital resources rather than human tutoring or carefully matched non-AI inquiry supports. In the high-school STEM quasi-experiment, the GenAI condition was compared against both a control and a search-engine condition; the GenAI-without-literacy-support group underperformed, making this one of the clearest cautionary comparisons in the source pool (QED, n=171) ([49]). In the animated pedagogical agent study, students were assigned across three conditions within an inquiry learning environment, but all learned substantially and the condition effect on kinematics knowledge was not reported as significant, indicating that the common inquiry platform may have driven most of the gain (RCT, n=61) ((Kim, 2015)). In the science-text personalization trial, the comparator was a non-personalized text condition rather than standard classroom science teaching (RCT, n=23) ([19]).

The lack of explicit baseline-performance reporting is a major limitation. Some studies provide pretest means, such as the PhET science process skill study, where mean scores increased from 29 to 80 and knowledge from 24 to 80, but because the design details are unclear and the comparator is not clearly specified, these data describe learning trajectory rather than typical performance under business-as-usual instruction ([35]). The broader literature in the pool identifies common gaps in existing instruction—insufficient personalization, limited teacher time for feedback, and uneven support for higher-order reasoning—but does not quantify baseline K-12 science inquiry performance robustly ((Belland, 2017); [37]; [31]).

## Direct K-12 science evidence

### Randomized and quasi-experimental studies in science-related settings

The middle-school GPT-4 science personalization study is one of the few directly science-themed AI trials in the pool. This study tested whether GPT-4 could personalize science texts for diverse middle-school-age learners. In a small randomized controlled trial with n=23 students, the experimental group was more likely to choose GPT-4 rewritten science paragraphs that matched their inferred preferences, with effect g=0.715 (RCT, n=23) ([19]). However, the profile-evaluation task found that 14 of 23 students selected the true profile, which was not significantly different from chance, p=.405, with effect h=0.615 (RCT, n=23) ([19]). The study therefore provides evidence that an LLM can generate differentiated science text variants aligned with inferred profiles, but not evidence that this improves scientific reasoning, comprehension, or inquiry performance.

The animated pedagogical agent study examined a science inquiry environment in high school. In this randomized controlled trial with n=61 high-school students, all students showed significant gains on the kinematics knowledge test from pretest to posttest, with d=1.10 overall, indicating that the inquiry environment itself supported learning (RCT, n=61) ((Kim, 2015)). The study also found an overall increase in self-efficacy over time, d=0.51, but the source pool summary states that the condition effect on academic outcomes was not reported as significant (RCT, n=61) ((Kim, 2015)). This is important for the present brief: adding an AI-like or agent-based layer to inquiry did not clearly outperform other versions of the same science learning environment.

The PhET science-process-skills study focused on grade-8 science learning about light and optical instruments. The source pool labels it as an RCT, but the summary describes it as a one-group pretest-posttest study. In the reported sample of n=30, science process skills increased from a mean of 29 to 80, with N-gain=0.71, and knowledge increased from 24 to 80, with N-gain=0.74 (RCT per source pool, n=30) ([35]). Because the comparison condition is not specified in the summary, this study cannot be used as strong comparative evidence for AI or AI-like simulation support relative to standard instruction, but it does indicate that simulation-supported inquiry can coincide with substantial gains in science process outcomes.

The high-school simulation-attitudes study compared a simulation-based physics condition with a control condition. In this quasi-experimental design with n=90, the intervention improved attitudes toward scientific inquiry, with post-test scores favoring the experimental group and partial η2=.748 (QED, n=90) ([44]). It also improved enjoyment of science lessons, partial η2=.785, and career interest, partial η2=.797 (QED, n=90) ([44]). This study is useful for showing that simulation-rich science learning can strengthen inquiry-related dispositions, but it is not clearly an AI intervention and it focuses on attitudes more than reasoning performance.

The high-school generative AI STEM study is the clearest direct warning sign. This quasi-experimental study included n=171 students across AP and on-level physics. The study found that generative AI without literacy support underperformed compared with control and search-engine conditions in high-school STEM learning (QED, n=171) ([49]). Survey evidence for understanding, engagement, and enjoyment was weak and non-significant, with MANOVA p=0.115 and overlapping 95% confidence intervals across groups (QED/survey, n=60) ([49]). The paper’s practical implication was not to ban AI but to pair it with AI literacy supports and clearer policies ([49]). For the present brief, that is a direct indicator that unguided GenAI use is not a reliable route to better scientific reasoning or science learning.

### What these science studies do and do not show

Taken together, the direct science studies do not establish a strong comparative case that AI-powered tools improve K-12 scientific reasoning and inquiry beyond existing instruction. One study shows personalization capability rather than learning impact ([19]). One shows an inquiry environment with overall learning gains but no clearly superior agent condition ((Kim, 2015)). One shows positive simulation-linked process-skill gains without a specified comparator ([35]). One shows favorable attitudes toward inquiry with simulations, not clearly AI ([44]). One shows that generative AI can underperform alternatives when used without scaffolding ([49]). This pattern supports a narrow interpretation: the strongest direct evidence is more consistent with “design and implementation matter enormously” than with “AI itself improves inquiry.”

## Broader experimental and meta-analytic evidence adjacent to the focal question

### Meta-analyses and systematic reviews

The most relevant broad causal synthesis is the 2025 meta-analysis of K-12 intelligent tutoring systems in the U.S. This meta-analysis directly asks whether ITS benefit K-12 students and whether effects vary by design, student characteristics, instructional features, outcome measures, and setting (meta-analysis) ([1]). The source pool summary indicates positive overall effects and heterogeneity, but it does not provide the pooled effect size, number of studies, or science-specific moderator statistics. This makes it strong for plausibility but limited for the exact research brief.

The 2025 meta-analysis of AI-enabled personalized STEM education in schools is also highly relevant because it synthesizes quantitative evidence on AI-supported personalized learning in K-12 STEM (meta-analysis) ([2]). Again, the source pool summary does not report an exact pooled effect, science-specific breakdown, or inquiry-specific moderator, so it cannot support more precise claims than that overall effects were positive and context-dependent.

The 2018 Bayesian meta-analysis of computer-based scaffolding in problem-based STEM learning is not AI-specific, but it is central for mechanism inference. It concludes that computer-based scaffolding can improve student learning in PBL STEM environments (meta-analysis) ((Belland, 2018)). The 2017 synthesis of instructional scaffolding in STEM likewise argues that authentic problem-centered instruction is effective when paired with appropriate support structures (meta-analysis) ((Belland, 2017)). For scientific inquiry, these reviews support the idea that AI’s likely value lies in scalable scaffolding—prompts, hints, feedback, decomposition of complex tasks—rather than in open-ended answer generation.

Systematic reviews of tutoring systems and AutoTutor further support this interpretation. The tutoring-systems review describes a trajectory from computer-assisted instruction to modern AI-driven ITS and considers learning and engagement benefits alongside ethics and implementation challenges ([4]). The AutoTutor review synthesizes 17 years of natural-language tutoring research and emphasizes deep reasoning questions, collaborative dialogue, and adaptive feedback as core tutoring mechanisms ([9]). Although much of this evidence is not K-12 science-specific, these are among the most directly relevant AI mechanism literatures for explanation construction and evidence-based reasoning.

Reviews of educational chatbots and LLMs provide a more cautionary complement. The educational chatbots review shows wide variation in design, deployment, and evaluation across 36 studies and does not indicate a settled effectiveness profile ([37]). The survey of LLMs for education organizes applications across student support, teacher support, and adaptive learning but is technology-centric and not outcome-specific ([46]). The umbrella review of ChatGPT and AI chatbots in education similarly synthesizes a rapidly expanding but methodologically uneven literature ([24]). These reviews collectively suggest opportunity, but not robust direct evidence for K-12 science inquiry.

### Adjacent randomized and quasi-experimental studies

The Lumilo study is important because it tests teacher-facing AI in authentic K-12 classrooms. In a randomized classroom field study with 343 middle-school students, 286 analyzed, across 18 classrooms, 8 teachers, and 4 schools or districts, students in the Glasses + Analytics condition showed greater learning gains than comparison conditions, while teachers redistributed attention toward students needing help (RCT, n=286 analyzed) ([5]). The source pool summary does not report the exact academic effect size in the excerpt provided, so it cannot be stated here. This study is outside science, but it is highly informative for inquiry-oriented classrooms where teacher orchestration and timely support are often bottlenecks.

Tutor CoPilot provides another strong adjacent model of human-AI complementarity. In a randomized controlled trial with 1,800 K-12 students and 4,136 tutoring sessions, students whose tutors had access to Tutor CoPilot were 4 percentage points more likely to pass exit tickets (RCT, n=1,800) ([11]). The intervention also changed tutor behavior: treatment tutors were more likely to use strategies associated with deeper understanding, with effects of about 2 SD on the log-odds scale for key high-quality strategies, based on 550,000+ messages (RCT, n=4,136 sessions) ([11]). No statistically significant effects were found on perceived tutor care, confidence in learning math, or session ratings (RCT, survey n=1,931–1,952) ([11]). For the present brief, this is valuable evidence that AI may improve instructional process quality more reliably than broad affective outcomes.

Evidence from ChatGPT-related meta-analysis is similarly adjacent rather than direct. The 2025 meta-analysis on ChatGPT reports effects on learning performance, learning perception, and higher-order thinking across elementary through undergraduate settings, but the source pool summary does not provide pooled statistics in the excerpt available here (meta-analysis) ([8]). This supports the possibility that LLMs can affect higher-order outcomes, yet the heterogeneity across tasks and domains means it cannot be mapped directly onto K-12 science inquiry.

Quasi-experimental studies outside science also reinforce the need for caution about dependence and transfer. The study of AI code generators for novice learners found that such tools can alter immediate task performance but raise concerns about overreliance and reduced independent understanding (QED) ([13]). The undergraduate programming QED on generative AI similarly examined programming output quality, transfer, self-efficacy, and process rather than simply final answers, highlighting that AI can change how students learn, not only what they score (QED) ([25]). These studies are not science studies, but they are directly relevant to scientific inquiry because inquiry requires independent planning, interpretation, and explanation, all of which may be vulnerable to overhelping.

## Mechanisms: how AI is supposed to support scientific reasoning and inquiry

Across the evidence base, the dominant mechanism is scaffolding. The scaffolding reviews show that learners in complex STEM tasks benefit when support helps them interpret problems, plan strategies, monitor progress, and connect evidence to explanations ((Belland, 2017); (Belland, 2018)). AutoTutor’s long-running research program operationalizes this through conversational moves: asking deep reasoning questions, eliciting student explanations, supplying hints, and maintaining dialogue until learners articulate better answers ([9]). These mechanisms map closely to the target science outcomes of evidence evaluation, explanation construction, and metacognition, even though many underlying studies are not K-12 science trials.

Tutoring-system reviews similarly emphasize adaptivity, dialogue, immediate feedback, and learner modeling as the defining features of AI-powered support ([4]; [42]). In the science-text personalization trial, the intended mechanism was differential access to explanatory science text tuned to learner preferences ([19]). In Tutor CoPilot and Lumilo, the mechanism was not direct student-AI interaction but improvement of human instructional decisions through AI guidance ([11]; [5]). That distinction is especially important for science inquiry, where teachers often need to decide when to let students struggle, when to redirect misconceptions, and how to manage lab-like activity.

Reviews of educational chatbots show that conversation can support question answering, practice, and feedback, but the review also underscores variation in whether systems are scripted, retrieval-based, or more open generative agents ([37]). Reviews of generative AI and critical thinking in EFL report similar uncertainty: LLMs may support reflection and idea generation, but they can also shortcut reasoning if students outsource core thinking steps ([21]). This concern aligns with the negative finding from the high-school STEM GenAI study and the overreliance concerns from programming studies ([49]; [13]).

Simulation and multimodal analytics research suggest a second mechanism family: AI-supported representation and monitoring. Simulation studies in science indicate that interactive representations can improve process skills and inquiry attitudes ([35]; [44]). Reviews of multimodal methods and eye-tracking in science education show growing interest in using fine-grained learner data to infer engagement, cognitive load, and inquiry behavior ([20]; [12]). However, these literatures mostly demonstrate measurement and design possibilities, not direct causal learning gains from AI adaptation.

## Implementation conditions and classroom integration

The most consistent implementation lesson is that AI works better as a structured support inside pedagogically designed activity systems than as a free-standing answer engine. The tutoring and ITS reviews repeatedly frame successful systems as integrated with curriculum, bounded tasks, and explicit learning goals ([1]; [4]; [9]). The high-school GenAI study directly supports this principle by showing weaker outcomes when generative AI was used without literacy support ([49]). The practical implication from that study was to use AI literacy programs and clearer classroom policies rather than unrestricted use.

Teacher role appears central. In Lumilo, AI improved learning by helping teachers better allocate attention in AI-supported instruction, a model of human-AI complementarity rather than automation ([5]). Tutor CoPilot likewise improved tutor practice by supplying real-time expert-like guidance to novice tutors ([11]). Reviews of AI in education also note that educators are often underrepresented in AI research design, despite their central role in implementation fidelity, ethics, and orchestration ([36]; [31]). For K-12 science inquiry, where activities often involve discussion, experimentation, and interpretation of ambiguous evidence, this teacher-mediation pattern is likely highly relevant.

Safeguards against error and overreliance are also recurrent. Reviews of ChatGPT and LLMs in education flag hallucination, bias, opacity, and inappropriate confidence as recurring risks ([24]; [46]; [31]). The RCT on AI-supported tutoring decision-making with adults shows that AI assistance improved accuracy over no-AI baselines but still underperformed AI alone, while explanations increased time per task and shifted both under-reliance and over-reliance depending on whether AI was correct (RCT, n=95) ((AI Knows Best, 2026)). Although not a K-12 science study, this is directly relevant to scientific inquiry because students and teachers using AI must decide when to trust or verify outputs. There is little direct evidence in the source pool on verification behavior in K-12 science, which remains a major gap.

Infrastructure and access are discussed more often than tested. Reviews of tutoring systems, chatbots, and LLMs note implementation challenges around device access, ethics, data privacy, and teacher readiness ([4]; [37]; [46]). However, the source pool contains little direct comparative evidence on dosage, duration, homework versus classroom use, or lab integration for science-specific AI inquiry tools.

## Heterogeneity by population, context, and design

Grade-band heterogeneity is largely unresolved for the focal question. The available direct science evidence clusters in middle and high school ([35]; (Kim, 2015); [19]; [49]). The broad K-12 meta-analyses include elementary through high school, but the source pool summary does not provide science-specific grade-band moderators ([1]; [2]). Elementary science inquiry with AI remains especially under-evidenced.

Prior achievement and learner-needs moderation are also thin. The brief asks about prior science achievement, language background, and special education status, but the source pool contains almost no direct science-specific moderator evidence on these variables. Work on assistive technology in inclusive classrooms suggests that technology-supported instruction can improve teachers’ inclusive practice, g=0.32, and that teachers observed greater learner responsiveness and confidence, but this is not a science inquiry study and does not isolate AI-powered supports (QED, n=220) ([39]). The science-text personalization study was explicitly motivated by diverse middle-school-age learners, but it did not report subgroup effects by language status, disability, or prior science achievement ([19]).

Design heterogeneity appears more consequential than learner heterogeneity in the current evidence. Structured tutoring systems, scaffolded dialogue, and teacher-facing AI supports show the strongest positive signals ([1]; [9]; [11]; [5]). Unguided or weakly guided generative AI shows the clearest negative signal in high-school STEM ([49]). Reviews of GenAI in programming, writing, and critical thinking echo this pattern: benefits are more likely when AI is constrained to feedback, revision, or bounded support tasks than when students rely on it to produce answers wholesale ([13]; [14]; [21]).

## What adjacent evidence suggests about likely impacts on scientific reasoning

Because direct science evidence is limited, adjacent research can only inform, not settle, the focal question. The most relevant adjacent evidence indicates that AI is likely to help scientific reasoning when it performs three functions: eliciting explanation, supplying adaptive feedback, and helping teachers target support. AutoTutor’s natural-language tutoring model is built precisely around explanation-centered dialogue ([9]). Tutor CoPilot shows that AI can increase tutor use of probing, explanation-oriented strategies at scale ([11]). Lumilo shows that AI can sharpen teacher noticing and attention allocation in complex classrooms ([5]). Scaffolding meta-analyses suggest these forms of support are especially valuable in ill-structured STEM tasks, which closely resemble scientific inquiry ((Belland, 2017); (Belland, 2018)).

At the same time, adjacent evidence also warns that AI may weaken durable inquiry skills if it bypasses core reasoning. The code-generator study highlights concerns that learners may complete tasks with less independent understanding ([13]). The adult RCT on tutoring decision-making shows that explanation features can increase both accuracy and misplaced reliance, depending on AI correctness ((AI Knows Best, 2026)). Reviews of LLMs in education repeatedly foreground hallucination and trust calibration as unresolved challenges ([46]; [24]). For science inquiry, where evaluating evidence and justifying claims are central, this means that any benefit from AI is conditional on students being asked to inspect, critique, and verify outputs rather than merely accept them.

The broader problem-based and project-based learning literature also matters here. Systematic review evidence indicates that higher-order, critical, and critical-analytic thinking in PBL and PjBL are shaped by how tasks are structured and assessed, not just by the medium of support ([18]). This implies that AI effects are unlikely to be uniform across science tasks. AI may be more helpful for prompting explanations, organizing evidence, or personalizing reading support than for authentic experimental design or hypothesis generation unless the tool is purpose-built for those subskills. The source pool does not contain enough direct studies to differentiate these subskills empirically.

### Synthesis and Implications

The evidence supports a restrained synthesis. First, AI-powered tools are not a single intervention class. Structured ITS, conversational tutors, teacher-facing orchestration tools, adaptive scaffolds, and open generative assistants differ substantially in mechanism and risk profile ([1]; [9]; [46]). Second, the strongest positive signals come from systems that scaffold reasoning within bounded pedagogical designs or that help humans provide better support, not from unguided student use of general-purpose GenAI ([11]; [5]; [49]). Third, the direct science evidence is too sparse and heterogeneous to conclude that AI reliably improves K-12 scientific reasoning and inquiry over standard instruction or non-AI alternatives.

For schools and practitioners, the practical implication is to treat AI as a scaffold for inquiry rather than as a substitute for inquiry. Tools are more plausibly useful when they provide prompts, hints, feedback on explanations, personalized reading support, or teacher-facing analytics tied to specific science tasks ((Belland, 2017); (Belland, 2018); [9]). Adoption should prioritize curriculum-aligned, structured uses over open-ended chatbot dependence, especially for younger learners and complex reasoning tasks ([37]; [46]). Where schools experiment with generative AI in science, they should pair it with AI literacy instruction, explicit verification norms, and teacher oversight, because the clearest direct K-12 STEM evidence shows that unsupported use can underperform conventional alternatives ([49]).

The strongest near-term opportunity may lie in human-AI complementarity. Teacher-facing and tutor-facing systems show that AI can improve the quality, timing, and distribution of instructional support without removing the educator from the loop ([5]; [11]). In science inquiry settings, this could mean helping teachers identify which students need support with evidence interpretation, which groups are stuck on variable control, or where misconceptions are emerging in real time. That use case is more strongly supported by current evidence than fully autonomous AI guidance for scientific reasoning.

### Limitations and Research Gaps

The central limitation is the scarcity of direct, high-rigor K-12 science studies. Very few RCTs or QEDs in the source pool directly test AI-powered tools for scientific reasoning or inquiry against clearly specified non-AI comparators in authentic science classrooms. Many relevant sources are broad reviews, adjacent-domain studies, or studies of science learning outcomes that do not isolate AI effects ([1]; [2]; [4]). Several experimental studies are small, short-term, or focused on proximal outcomes such as preference matching, motivation, or attitudes rather than validated inquiry subskills ([19]; (Kim, 2015)).

Comparator quality is also weak. Many studies compare AI tools against business-as-usual or loosely defined controls rather than teacher-led inquiry, non-AI digital scaffolds, or human feedback matched in intensity. Baseline reporting is limited, so the field cannot yet say much about what ordinary science instruction produces on the same measures or which gaps AI uniquely fills ([35]; [49]). Longitudinal and delayed post-test evidence is largely absent, so durable transfer of scientific reasoning after tool removal remains unresolved.

Equity evidence is especially underdeveloped. The source pool provides little direct evidence on students with disabilities, multilingual learners, low prior science achievement, or under-resourced schools in AI-supported science inquiry. Reviews frequently mention ethics, bias, and access, but few empirical studies test these as moderators ([24]; [46]; [31]). Elementary grades are underrepresented, and science domains beyond physics are sparse.

Finally, the field lacks mechanism-isolation studies. Many papers claim benefits from personalization, prompting, adaptive feedback, or dialogue, but few experimentally disentangle which of these features drives outcomes or when they backfire through overhelping or overreliance ((Belland, 2017); (Belland, 2018); [13]; (AI Knows Best, 2026)). Future research needs head-to-head K-12 science trials that compare AI scaffolds with equivalent non-AI scaffolds, report specific inquiry subskills, test transfer and delayed retention, and examine moderation by grade band, prior achievement, language background, disability status, and school context.

## Body of Evidence Maturity: EMERGING
Justification: The evidence base includes relevant meta-analyses and a small number of direct K-12 science trials, but the direct causal literature for AI-powered support of scientific reasoning and inquiry is still sparse, heterogeneous, and often indirect. Rigor is stronger in adjacent tutoring and scaffolding research than in the focal science domain, and equity, subgroup, comparator, and long-term outcome coverage remain weak.

paper_profiles.title: A meta-analysis of AI-enabled personalized STEM education in schools
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the need for quantitative evidence on the effectiveness of AI-enabled personalized STEM education in K-12 schools. Prior reviews had largely been qualitative or focused on narrower technologies, leaving unclear the overall impact of AI-supported personalized learning and the conditions under which it works best. The study therefore asks how effective AI-enabled personalized STEM education is in schools and which moderator variables explain differences in outcomes.

The authors conducted a meta-analysis following PRISMA procedures, synthesizing 99 effect sizes from 32 randomized controlled trial studies published between 2012 and 2024. The review focused on AI-enabled personalized learning interventions in school STEM subjects and coded moderators including school level, AI application type, personalized learning model, outcome type, subject area, and whether generative AI was used. The included AI applications spanned intelligent tutoring systems, personalized educational games, AR/VR, and other AI-supported tools.

The population was K-12 students across multiple school levels, including kindergarten, elementary, junior high, and senior high school, in school-based STEM learning contexts worldwide. Because this is a meta-analysis, the paper aggregates evidence across many settings rather than reporting a single intervention site or country. The focus is explicitly on student learning outcomes in school STEM education.

The main conclusion is that AI-enabled personalized STEM education produces a statistically significant small-to-medium positive effect overall compared with non-AI approaches (reported overall g = 0.455). The strongest effects were found for junior and senior high school students, AR/VR-based tools, and more learner-centered models that combine AI with classroom or collaborative pedagogies. Effects also varied by subject, with comprehensive courses showing the largest gains. By contrast, observed outcome type and generative-AI versus non-generative-AI status did not significantly moderate effects. The authors argue for evidence-based, pedagogically aligned integration of AI in K-12 STEM education.

paper_profiles.title: The role of AI assisted writing feedback in developing secondary students writing skills
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether AI-assisted writing feedback improves the writing performance of secondary-level English as a Foreign Language (EFL) students more than traditional teacher feedback alone. The authors focus on a common instructional problem in EFL writing classrooms: teachers often have limited time to provide detailed, individualized feedback, while students need frequent revision opportunities to improve grammar, vocabulary, coherence, and overall writing quality. The study also examines students’ perceptions of using an AI writing assistant as a feedback tool.

The intervention compared two feedback conditions over an 8-week period. The experimental group used Grammarly to receive immediate AI-generated feedback on drafts, including grammar, spelling, punctuation, word choice, style, sentence clarity, and coherence; after revision, the teacher also provided brief higher-order feedback. The control group followed a traditional process in which the teacher provided delayed written feedback on drafts. Both groups completed pre-test and post-test timed persuasive essays and followed the same writing curriculum with the same instructor. Writing was scored analytically across content, organization, language use, and mechanics by two independent EFL raters, and the experimental group also completed a post-study perception questionnaire.

Participants were 60 Turkish public high school students aged 15–17 enrolled in an EFL program, divided into an experimental group and a control group of 30 each. The study took place in a secondary school setting in Türkiye during regular class time, with use of the school computer lab for the AI tool. Students had little prior experience with AI-based writing tools, and parental consent was obtained because participants were minors.

The main conclusion is that AI-assisted feedback significantly improved students’ writing more than teacher-only feedback. The experimental group showed larger gains in total writing scores, especially in language use and organization, while both groups improved over time. Students also reported positive perceptions of the AI tool, including improved confidence and satisfaction with the feedback. The authors conclude that AI writing tools can effectively supplement secondary EFL writing instruction, particularly when combined with teacher guidance rather than used as a replacement for human feedback.

paper_profiles.title: How AI feedback supports lesson planning in vocational teacher education: a longitudinal intervention study using an analytical AI platform
paper_profiles.venue: Empirical Research in Vocational Education and Training
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether an analytical AI feedback system can improve lesson planning in vocational teacher education. The authors focus on a practical problem in higher education: detailed, individualized feedback on complex lesson plans is valuable for student teachers but difficult for university instructors to provide consistently and at scale. The study asks whether AI-based feedback can support or outperform human feedback on key didactic planning dimensions, and whether using such a system also influences students’ motivation, AI literacy, attitudes toward AI, digital competence, and technology self-efficacy.

The intervention centers on EDDA, an analytical AI platform that analyzes uploaded lesson plans and teaching materials using a BERT-based model trained on coded lesson plans and textbook tasks. EDDA does not generate open-ended responses like a large language model; instead, it classifies lesson plans into predefined didactic categories and returns expert-level text and visual feedback tied to established criteria. In the study, the experimental group used EDDA throughout a semester and could also consult the university instructor to discuss the AI feedback, while the control group received human feedback only. Both groups completed the same lesson-planning tasks and theoretical coursework.

The population consisted of 103 master’s students in business education in Germany, working in small groups to design 90-minute vocational lessons. The intervention spanned a semester, with students iteratively incorporating six focal dimensions or principles into the same lesson plan: sustainability, process orientation, problem orientation, action orientation, individualization, and digitalization. Outcomes included coded analyses of lesson plans as well as repeated self-report surveys on AI literacy and related meta-dimensions.

The main conclusion is that analytical AI feedback can effectively supplement traditional instructor feedback and, on some lesson-planning dimensions, match or exceed human-only feedback. The experimental group showed advantages on selected planning aspects, including some sustainability-related dimensions, social competences for sustainable development, reflexivity, and several planning features highlighted in the abstract such as action orientation, relatedness, technology use, lesson structure, and learner engagement. However, simply using the AI platform did not automatically improve AI literacy, attitudes toward AI, or motivation. The authors therefore argue that analytical AI tools are promising for feedback in teacher education, but should be embedded in a broader, human-centered instructional framework rather than treated as a standalone solution.

paper_profiles.title: Current practices and future direction of artificial intelligence in mathematics education: A systematic review
paper_profiles.venue: International Electronic Journal of Mathematics Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the need for a practical and up-to-date synthesis of how artificial intelligence is being used in mathematics education. The authors argue that prior reviews often focused on broad AI categories or research-stage systems, but gave less attention to specific, market-ready tools that educators could actually implement. The review therefore asks four main questions: how AI in mathematics education studies are distributed across educational levels, what AI tools are used and how they can be categorized, which commercialized tools are available online and what they do, and what emerging trends and future directions appear in the literature.

The study uses a systematic literature review approach. The authors searched Web of Science and Scopus for English-language journal articles published between 2019 and 2024, focused on AI in mathematics education. After screening and deduplication, 32 studies were included. The review categorizes AI tools into adaptive learning systems/intelligent tutoring systems, chatbots, augmented reality, virtual reality, learning analytics, serious games, and AI mathematics problem solvers. It also identifies named tools such as Khan Academy, Squirrel AI, ChatGPT, Bard, GeoGebra, GeoGebra AR, Photomath, Vuforia, and NeoTrieVR, and distinguishes between generative AI tools and pedagogical AI tools.

The population represented across the reviewed studies spans primary/elementary, middle/high school, university, and adult learners, with the largest share of studies at the middle/high school level, followed by university/adult and then primary levels. Because this is a review, the context is not one single intervention site but a synthesis of studies conducted across multiple countries, with especially strong representation from China, the United States, and Spain. The paper is situated in mathematics education broadly and examines both classroom-oriented and digital learning applications of AI.

The main conclusions are that AI in mathematics education is expanding rapidly and serves multiple instructional purposes, especially personalization, adaptive feedback, interactive visualization, and problem support. Chatbots were the most common category in recent studies, while AR/VR showed strong promise for engagement and conceptual understanding, especially for geometry and spatial learning. The authors conclude that commercialized pedagogical AI tools currently dominate the field, but generative AI tools are increasingly important. They also emphasize the need for more longitudinal research, stronger understanding of long-term effects and equity implications, and more work on how AI can complement rather than replace teachers.

finding.finding_summary: The review reports that adaptive learning systems and intelligent tutoring systems are among the AI approaches associated with enhanced mathematics learning and achievement in the literature reviewed. The paper references their personalized learning and adaptive feedback functions but does not provide pooled effect sizes.
finding.measure: mathematics achievement/learning outcomes

paper_profiles.title: Advancing Education through Tutoring Systems: A Systematic Literature Review
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses how tutoring systems have evolved from early computer-assisted instruction to modern AI-driven Intelligent Tutoring Systems (ITS) and Robot Tutoring Systems (RTS), and what that evolution means for learning, engagement, and ethics in education. The authors ask three main questions: which technological breakthroughs enabled personalized tutoring, how current systems use real-time adaptation to improve engagement and academic performance, and what ethical challenges have emerged alongside these technologies. The review is motivated by persistent global learning gaps and interest in AI-based tools that can personalize instruction at scale.

The study uses a PRISMA-guided systematic literature review of 86 representative studies selected from an initial pool of 340 records spanning 1972 to 2024. The authors analyze tutoring systems through a four-part framework covering artificial intelligence, system behavior, engagement, and affordances. They also conduct a latent class analysis that groups systems into three categories: computer-based ITS, robot-based verbal tutoring systems, and multimodal tutoring systems that combine verbal, visual, and physical interaction. Across the reviewed studies, key AI techniques include Bayesian Knowledge Tracing, natural language processing, and large language models.

The population context is broad rather than tied to a single sample, because this is a review of prior studies across educational settings. The included literature spans multiple learner groups, with examples and discussion prominently involving younger learners, middle school mathematics students, secondary physics learners, and some higher-education contexts. The review focuses primarily on students as end users of tutoring systems in educational environments, rather than on teachers or administrators as the main participants.

The main conclusions are that tutoring systems show strong promise for improving learning outcomes, personalization, and student engagement, but different forms have different strengths. Computer-based ITS are more scalable and cognitively adaptive, while robot-based systems are stronger for social and emotional engagement. The authors argue that hybrid systems integrating both approaches may offer the greatest educational benefit. They also conclude that important challenges remain, especially around scalability, data privacy, bias, transparency, and the still-limited cognitive adaptability of robotic systems.

paper_profiles.title: Generative artificial intelligence-supported programming education: Effects on learning performance, self-efficacy and processes
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether generative artificial intelligence (GenAI), specifically ChatGPT, improves programming education outcomes and how it shapes students’ learning processes. The authors focus on four questions: whether GenAI improves programming output quality and knowledge transfer, whether it affects programming self-efficacy, how it changes students’ programming behaviours, and how different behaviour patterns under GenAI relate to academic performance. The study responds to mixed prior findings suggesting that GenAI may improve immediate task performance but may not always support deeper learning.

The intervention was a quasi-experiment in which one group of students used a ChatGPT-based platform (ChatGPT-Next-Web using GPT-3.5-turbo) for self-directed programming learning, while a control group used other Internet resources instead of GenAI. Both groups completed the same Turtle-library programming learning tasks in a standardized computer lab setting. Measures included ratings of programming products across multiple dimensions, pre/post programming self-efficacy surveys, and fine-grained behavioural trace data captured through scripts and analysed with frequency analysis, process mining, and clustering.

Participants were 55 undergraduate Physics Education students at a public university in China. All had prior foundational Python experience but were new to the Python Turtle library. The experimental activity itself lasted 120 minutes, followed by a 40-minute post-test task completed without external resources. The study took place in university computer labs with uniform hardware, and the authors also provided the experimental group with a GenAI user guide to support interaction with the tool.

The main conclusions are that GenAI support improved short-term programming performance and increased self-efficacy, especially in self-regulation and complex programming tasks, but did not improve longer-term knowledge transfer when students later had to work without external resources. Behavioural analyses showed that GenAI-supported learners relied more on information retrieval and copying, whereas control students engaged more in independent coding and code revision. Within the GenAI group, higher-performing students used the tool more critically and interactively, showing greater epistemic agency, while lower-performing students were more likely to copy outputs directly. The authors argue that GenAI can be beneficial for programming education, but only when instructional design discourages over-reliance and supports active cognitive engagement.

paper_profiles.title: Harnessing Generative AI (GenAI) for Automated Feedback in Higher Education: A Systematic Review
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the emerging use of generative AI for automated feedback in higher education. The authors note that higher education instructors face growing pressure to provide timely, personalized, and scalable feedback, especially in online and large-enrollment courses. Prior reviews had examined automated feedback or generative AI separately, but had not focused specifically on GenAI-based feedback in higher education or on how these systems are implemented in authentic instructional settings. The review therefore asks three questions: what contexts GenAI feedback systems are used in, what their main characteristics are, and what possibilities they create for higher education.

The authors conducted a systematic review following PRISMA-style procedures and Arksey and O'Malley's framework. They searched peer-reviewed English-language journal articles published from 2019 to 2023 in Academic Search Premier and Education Source, screened 1,976 non-duplicate records, and ultimately included 10 empirical studies from Q1 or Q2 journals. The reviewed studies examined GenAI-based feedback tools such as ChatGPT, chatbots, digital tutors, and specialized writing/assessment systems. These tools were used for automated feedback in contexts including language learning, academic writing, creative thinking, and STEM courses. Across the reviewed studies, GenAI systems served purposes such as personalized learning, collaborative problem-solving, self-regulated learning, and motivation/engagement.

The population and context are higher education settings, including undergraduate and some graduate-level contexts, with both students and educators implicated in implementation. The review synthesizes studies conducted in varied instructional environments, with frequent relevance to online learning and large-scale courses. It also emphasizes instructor roles in implementation, including guiding students' use of GenAI, providing higher-level or final feedback, engineering prompts, and facilitating deeper learning beyond what automated systems can provide.

The main conclusions are that GenAI automated feedback systems show strong promise for improving educational efficiency and support in higher education. The reviewed evidence suggests these systems can reduce instructor workload, provide timely and personalized feedback, improve communication, support cognitive and emotional needs, and expand access to feedback in lower-pressure environments. At the same time, the review highlights unresolved issues such as ethical concerns, accuracy, overreliance, and the need to better define instructors' roles in AI-supported feedback ecosystems. The authors conclude that GenAI should be integrated in ways that augment rather than replace human instruction, and they call for more research as the field develops.

paper_profiles.title: Impact of AI-Blended Learning and AI-Personalized Learning on Undergraduate Biology Students' Attitude and Performance in Climate Change Education
paper_profiles.venue: Anchor University Journal of Science and Technology
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether AI-enhanced instructional approaches improve undergraduate biology students’ attitudes toward climate change and their academic performance in climate change education better than traditional classroom teaching. The study is motivated by the concern that conventional instruction may not sufficiently engage students or address diverse learning needs when teaching complex environmental topics.

The intervention compared three instructional conditions: AI-Blended Learning, AI-Personalized Learning, and Traditional Classroom Instruction. In the AI-Blended Learning condition, students used ChatGPT-3.5 alongside face-to-face teaching. In the AI-Personalized Learning condition, students relied on ChatGPT-3.5 as the primary instructional support in a fully AI-driven personalized environment. The comparison group received conventional face-to-face instruction without the AI intervention. Outcomes were measured using a Climate Change Attitude Assessment (CCAA) and a Climate Change Achievement Test (CCAT), with pretest and posttest scores analyzed using ANCOVA.

The study involved 70 300-level undergraduate biology students at Federal University Gusau in Nigeria. Students were drawn from existing classes and assigned into three groups: AI-Blended Learning (20), AI-Personalized Learning (20), and Traditional Classroom Instruction (30). The intervention lasted four weeks and covered climate change topics such as causes, impacts, mitigation strategies, and policy actions.

The main finding is that AI-Blended Learning produced substantially stronger gains in both attitude and performance than either AI-Personalized Learning or Traditional Classroom Instruction. Post hoc analyses showed that the blended approach significantly outperformed both alternatives, while AI-Personalized Learning did not significantly differ from traditional instruction on the reported comparisons. The paper concludes that integrating ChatGPT-3.5 with teacher-led classroom instruction is more effective than relying on AI alone, and recommends that higher education lecturers adopt AI-blended approaches to improve engagement and learning outcomes in environmental education.

paper_profiles.title: Studying the effect of AI Code Generators on Supporting Novice Learners in Introductory Programming
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the 2023 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether AI code generators such as OpenAI Codex help or hinder novice learners who are first learning introductory text-based programming. The authors focus on a key educational concern: although AI-generated code may improve immediate task performance, it could also create over-reliance and weaken learners’ ability to understand, modify, or retain programming knowledge. The study addresses whether novices can effectively use AI code generation, how it changes task performance, and whether prior access to such tools affects later independent coding and retention.

To study this, the researchers built a web-based Python learning environment called Coding Steps. Learners completed a three-week, 10-session remote program consisting of a Scratch-based introduction and pre-test, seven Python training sessions, and two evaluation sessions (an immediate post-test and a one-week retention test). During training, one group had access to an AI code generator powered by OpenAI Codex, while a comparison group did not. Participants worked through 45 code-authoring tasks, each followed by a code-modification task, plus multiple-choice questions on core introductory Python topics such as variables, conditionals, loops, and arrays. The system logged code edits, documentation use, errors, submissions, and AI prompt/code-generation behavior.

The population consisted of 69 novice learners aged 10-17 recruited through coding camps in two major North American cities. All reported no prior text-based programming experience, though many had experience with block-based programming environments such as Scratch. Participants were assigned to conditions using a matched-groups design based on Scratch pre-test scores to balance prior programming knowledge. The study was conducted remotely via Google Meet, with instructors available to provide support and personalized feedback during training.

The main findings were that access to Codex substantially improved performance on training-phase code-authoring tasks: learners completed more tasks, achieved higher correctness, made fewer errors, and finished faster. Importantly, prior use of the AI tool did not reduce performance on subsequent manual code-modification tasks, and learners in the Codex group performed similarly to the baseline group on the immediate post-test without access to the tool. On the one-week retention test, the Codex group showed slightly better performance, though differences were not statistically significant overall. The authors conclude that AI code generators can support novice programming learning without clear evidence of harming short-term retention, and that learners with stronger prior programming competency may benefit the most.

paper_profiles.title: Examining Faculty and Student Perceptions of Generative AI in University Courses
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how students and faculty perceive generative AI tools such as ChatGPT in higher education, with particular attention to perceived ease of use, ethical concerns, intentions to use, and views about impacts on learning. The study addresses a gap in empirical evidence about how attitudes toward generative AI differ across university roles and across student subgroups defined by gender and STEM versus non-STEM disciplines.

The study used an anonymous online survey grounded in a modified UTAUT framework and supplemented with items about perceived effects on learning competencies and ethics. The survey measured constructs such as performance expectancy, effort expectancy, social influence, hedonic motivation, habit, personal innovativeness, and behavioral intention, along with views about academic integrity, policy needs, and the frequency of generative AI use. The approach was descriptive and comparative rather than experimental.

Participants were 982 students and 76 faculty members at a single large land-grant public university in the southeastern United States during the Fall 2023 semester. The student sample included both undergraduate and other university students, and analyses compared students with faculty as well as four student subgroups: STEM male, STEM female, non-STEM male, and non-STEM female. Data were collected between December 2023 and January 2024 through voluntary online survey distribution.

The authors conclude that students and faculty were broadly similar in their attitudes toward generative AI, though students reported higher ease of use, hedonic motivation, and personal innovativeness, while faculty reported more habitual use. Both groups used generative AI at similarly low rates overall and shared concerns about negative effects on learning competencies and academic dishonesty, while also supporting the development of institutional policies. Within the student sample, male STEM students tended to express the most positive attitudes and non-STEM female students the least positive, suggesting that gender and disciplinary context shape how generative AI is received in higher education.

paper_profiles.title: Exploring Students’ Multimodal Representations of Ideas About Epistemic Reading of Scientific Texts in Generative AI Tools
paper_profiles.venue: Journal of Science Education and Technology
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how students represent their ideas about reading scientific texts generated by generative AI tools, a process the authors call GenAI-science epistemic reading. The problem addressed is that students need to draw on both their understanding of science and their understanding of GenAI in order to critically interpret AI-generated scientific information, yet existing measures in this area are often limited to Likert-scale surveys. The study asks what students’ multimodal representations of these ideas look like in terms of presentational, organisational, and orientational meanings.

The study uses a qualitative collective case study approach and develops a multimodal instrument in which students draw and write short explanations about (1) how ChatGPT/Poe generates scientific texts and (2) how they themselves read scientific texts in these tools. The authors analyze 44 students’ drawings and written responses using Lemke’s framework of presentational, organisational, and orientational meaning, and from these data they construct an analytical framework with categories such as epistemic trust, epistemic knowledge, organisational form, and representations of the nature of science and GenAI. Although the responses were collected before an explicit-reflective instructional activity that was part of a larger project, this paper focuses on the pre-instruction representations rather than testing intervention effects.

Participants were 44 Grade 8 and Grade 9 students in Hong Kong participating in extracurricular lessons. The instructional context involved a bilingual teacher who had prior online training workshops on implementing the teaching approach. Students completed the multimodal task in two classrooms before instruction, and the broader project centered on improving students’ understanding of epistemic reading of scientific texts from sources including GenAI and online media.

The main conclusion is that a multimodal approach is useful for characterising students’ ideas about GenAI-science epistemic reading in ways that standard survey instruments may miss. Students expressed a range of epistemic trust positions, including trust, critical thinking, confusion, and non-evaluation, and used different semiotic modes to express these ideas. The paper’s core contribution is an analytical framework teachers and researchers can use to diagnose and discuss students’ epistemic understanding of AI-generated scientific texts. The authors argue that such multimodal representations can serve as a richer diagnostic and instructional tool for future intervention studies on GenAI in science education.

paper_profiles.title: AI Responses to Challenging Problems and Educator Responses to AI Availability
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses how generative AI tools, specifically ChatGPT and Gemini, respond to cognitively demanding secondary mathematics tasks and what educators should do in response to increasing AI availability. The authors are concerned not only with whether GenAI can produce mathematical answers, but also with the pedagogical implications of tools that can engage in open-ended reasoning, generate explanations, and revise responses after prompting. The article situates this issue within secondary mathematics education and argues that educators should move beyond a ban-oriented stance toward instructional uses that preserve student thinking and reasoning.

The approach is a conceptual and illustrative analysis rather than an empirical intervention study. The authors posed three mathematics tasks spanning middle and high school content areas—rates and proportional reasoning, geometric proof, and quadratic interpretation—to ChatGPT 3.5, ChatGPT 4.0, and Gemini 1.0 during March–April 2024. They then analyzed the quality, strengths, and errors in the AI responses and derived two instructional strategies for educators: having students interact with GenAI to explore, clarify, and extend mathematical ideas, and having students critique AI-generated solutions and arguments. The paper includes concrete examples of prompts teachers could use to support these strategies.

The population and context are secondary mathematics education in the United States, with examples drawn from US middle school and high school mathematics curricula. However, no human participants were recruited and no classroom implementation data were collected. Instead, the article focuses on hypothetical and proposed uses of GenAI by students and educators in classroom mathematics settings.

The main conclusions are that current GenAI systems can engage with cognitively demanding mathematics tasks in ways that exceed traditional calculators or step-solving apps, but they also make substantial mathematical and logical errors. The authors therefore recommend that teachers use GenAI as a conversational and critical-thinking tool rather than as an answer engine. They argue that student learning can be supported when students are asked to interrogate, extend, and evaluate AI responses, especially in ways that preserve mathematical communication, reasoning, and proof-oriented thinking.

paper_profiles.title: Secondary school teachers’ perspectives on GenAI proliferation: generating advanced insights
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how the rapid proliferation of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is affecting secondary education, with a particular focus on academic integrity, teaching practices, assessment, and teacher support needs. The central research question asks what significant challenges and opportunities Ontario secondary school teachers perceive as GenAI becomes more common in schools. The authors position the study as addressing a gap in the literature, noting that most prior discussion has centered on postsecondary education rather than secondary schools.

The study uses a qualitative interview design grounded in invitational education as a theoretical framework. Seventeen practising Ontario secondary school teachers from five publicly funded school boards were recruited and interviewed in semi-structured sessions lasting about 60 minutes. Data were collected between November 2023 and January 2024, transcribed, member-checked, and coded in Atlas.ti. The analysis produced three main themes: generating people, generating programs, and generating policies. These themes capture teachers’ calls for professional development and expertise-building, structured and transparent school programs for GenAI integration, and clear policies to govern acceptable use, academic integrity, and institutional expectations.

The population studied was high school teachers in southern Ontario, Canada, rather than students directly. Participants represented a range of teaching experience levels and subjects, but all were secondary educators working in public school boards. The study context is school-based secondary education, though the data come from interviews rather than classroom implementation of a specific AI tool or intervention.

The paper concludes that teachers see GenAI as both a disruptive challenge and a potentially valuable educational tool, but they feel underprepared and under-supported. The authors argue that effective GenAI integration requires coordinated action across three areas: teacher capacity-building through professional development, purposeful programs and practices for assessment and instruction, and adaptable policy frameworks that support ethical and equitable use. They emphasize collaboration among teachers, administrators, policymakers, parents, and other stakeholders, and propose a train-the-trainer style model using teacher champions to support scalable GenAI integration while preserving academic integrity.

paper_profiles.title: Suitability of Chinese GenAI platforms for early childhood education: A multifaceted evaluation
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses whether currently available Chinese generative AI platforms are suitable for use in early childhood education (ECE), a context in which young children’s developmental needs, age-appropriate content, and ethical protections are especially important. The authors argue that existing AI evaluation frameworks do not adequately capture ECE-specific requirements, so they develop and apply a Chinese evaluation framework organized around three dimensions: technical performance, pedagogical adaptability, and ethical and safety considerations.

The study evaluates 10 freely accessible Chinese GenAI platforms using a mixed-methods design that combines quantitative scoring with qualitative content analysis. Platforms were assessed on multimodal support, response speed, lesson-plan generation, activity organization, personalization for different age groups, ethical compliance, content appropriateness, and algorithmic fairness. Testing was conducted under standardized hardware, network, and prompt conditions over a two-week period in February 2025, and scoring was completed through expert review and consensus. Rather than testing learning outcomes in classrooms, the study evaluates the capabilities and risks of AI tools that might be used by early childhood educators.

The context is Chinese early childhood education, especially preschool-aged children and the educators selecting tools for them. The platforms were not necessarily designed specifically for ECE, but were chosen because they are prominent, open-access Chinese GenAI systems with potential relevance to education. The paper also discusses implications for other stakeholders, including parents, developers, and policymakers concerned with AI use in early learning environments.

The main conclusions are that the proposed framework can differentiate among Chinese GenAI platforms and identify meaningful strengths and weaknesses. Doubao and iFlytek Spark showed particularly strong overall performance, with Doubao excelling broadly and Spark performing especially well in pedagogical adaptability; DeepSeek stood out for pedagogical adaptability but performed poorly technically. Across platforms, the authors conclude that improvements are still needed in multimodal support, transparency of privacy and recommendation policies, ECE-specific datasets, personalization, and ethical safeguards before GenAI can be considered fully suitable for early childhood education.

paper_profiles.title: Exploring the potential of LLM to enhance teaching plans through teaching simulation
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether large language models (LLMs) can support teachers—not students—by improving lesson planning before instruction takes place. The authors focus on a common challenge in teaching preparation: novice teachers often struggle to anticipate students’ misconceptions, learning difficulties, and the kinds of classroom interactions that reveal whether a lesson plan is effective. The study asks whether an LLM can improve teaching plans by simulating teacher–student interactions, generating teaching reflections, and then revising the original plan accordingly.

The intervention is a prompt-based workflow using GPT-4 (and, in one comparison condition, Claude 3.5 Sonnet) to enhance high school mathematics teaching plans. Starting from existing lesson plans, the model first simulates classroom dialogue involving students with varying ability levels and typical errors, then produces teaching reflections based on those simulated interactions, and finally refines the lesson plan using those reflections. The authors evaluate eight datasets of lesson plans, including LLM-generated plans, human expert-written plans, and plans written by pre-service teachers, with improvements produced through one or two rounds of LLM-based refinement. Human raters scored plans on a detailed framework covering problem chains, teaching activities, knowledge content, teaching methods, evaluation, interdisciplinarity, practical value, scope, and overall quality.

The context is high school mathematics in China. The evaluation corpus included 480 teaching plans drawn from 60 lessons across four knowledge modules: Algebra, Functions, Geometry, and Statistics. Human evaluation was carried out by mathematics teachers with teaching experience, and the paper compares baseline lesson plans against LLM-enhanced versions rather than measuring direct student learning outcomes. The workflow was implemented through web-based LLM interfaces rather than custom-coded systems, with the aim of keeping the approach accessible to ordinary teachers.

The main conclusion is that LLM-based simulation and reflection substantially improved the quality of teaching plans. In many dimensions, the refined plans matched or exceeded the quality of high-quality human-written plans, and plans originally written by pre-service teachers also improved notably after LLM enhancement. Performance varied by content area, with the strongest results in statistics and weaker performance in geometry, where visual reasoning is harder to support through text alone. Overall, the paper argues that LLMs can serve as useful pre-class rehearsal and lesson refinement tools for teachers, especially for instructional preparation, though further work is needed on challenging question design, disciplinary depth, and broader validation in authentic teaching settings.

paper_profiles.title: Reinforcing L2 reading comprehension through artificial intelligence intervention: refining engagement to foster self-regulated learning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether an artificial-intelligence-supported reading environment can improve second-language (L2) reading comprehension, learner engagement, and self-regulated learning. The study addresses a gap in the literature on AI for reading instruction, especially for language learners, by asking whether AI-enhanced classrooms can outperform conventional instruction and how learners perceive such an environment.

The intervention centered on the ReadToMe (RTM) platform, an AI-based, multi-sensory reading system that converts curricular text into text-to-speech, synchronized highlighting, pronunciation support, concept images, dictionary support, and knowledge-graph-based scaffolds. In the experimental condition, students used RTM for homework and reading practice, while the control group received conventional reading instruction and feedback from the teacher or peers. The study used a mixed-methods design with pre/post quantitative measures and follow-up semi-structured interviews.

Participants were 60 Iranian female EFL students from two intact classes at a language institute, with 30 students in the experimental group and 30 in the control group. They were upper-intermediate/C1 learners with a mean age of 21, attending in-person classes twice weekly for about 12 weeks. Both groups used the same reading textbook, and the same instructor taught both groups to reduce teacher effects. Outcomes included an objective reading comprehension test plus self-report scales for engagement and self-regulation.
