interventions.use_case: An LLM-powered tutor embedded in a staged illustration workflow provides real-time feedback, explanations, and guidance on anatomy, perspective, composition, color theory, and localized revisions for novice drawing practice.

A stagewise illustration interface adapts the drawing process through rough sketch, line art, coloring, and finishing stages, allowing branching, backtracking, and inpainting based on user progress and edits.

An interactive drawing support system delivers step-by-step instructional scaffolding through staged visual outputs and prompts, but the paper does not evaluate a formal tutoring algorithm or learning outcomes.

paper_profiles.title: Designing for human–AI complementarity in K-12 education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses how human teachers and AI tutoring systems can be designed to work together more effectively in K-12 classrooms. The central question is whether a teacher-facing AI support tool can improve student learning by helping teachers better allocate attention during AI-supported instruction, rather than leaving the AI tutor and teacher to operate independently.

The intervention studied is Lumilo, a pair of mixed-reality smart glasses that provide teachers with real-time analytics about students’ learning, metacognition, and behavior during class. The paper describes an iterative human-centered design process, including participatory co-design with teachers, replay-based prototyping, and pilot studies used to refine the system’s causal mechanisms before the main evaluation.

The main experimental study involved 343 middle school students across 18 classrooms, 8 teachers, and 4 schools/school districts in the United States. Students worked on linear equation solving with the AI tutor Lynnette over two class sessions. Classrooms were randomly assigned to three conditions: business-as-usual without glasses, glasses without analytics, and glasses with analytics. Results showed that the full Lumilo system improved student learning relative to both control conditions, with the largest benefits for lower-performing students. The authors conclude that real-time teacher-facing AI analytics can create beneficial teacher–AI complementarity in authentic classroom settings.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed randomized field study in authentic K-12 classrooms with stratified within-teacher assignment and hierarchical linear modeling, which supports causal inference. There are some design complexities and the excerpt does not report full effect-size details here, so it is strong but not perfect evidence.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The intervention produced positive learning gains in a priority K-12 population and improved teacher targeting of support, indicating meaningful but likely modest-to-moderate impact. The excerpt does not provide a numeric effect size, so the magnitude cannot be firmly classified as large.

interventions.use_case: AI-supported linear equation tutoring with Lynnette in middle school classrooms, providing individualized problem-solving practice and adaptive instructional support during class
Lumilo mixed-reality smart glasses for teacher awareness and orchestration, showing real-time analytics about student learning, metacognition, and behavior while teachers work alongside an AI tutor

finding.finding_summary: In a randomized classroom field study with 343 middle school students (286 analyzed) across 18 classrooms, 8 teachers, and 4 schools/districts, students in the Glasses + Analytics condition showed greater pre/post learning gains on linear equation solving than students in the No Glasses business-as-usual condition and the Glasses-only condition. The paper reports a positive effect of real-time analytics above and beyond minimal monitoring support, but does not provide a numeric effect size in the excerpted text.
finding.measure: 15-minute pre/post test on linear equation solving

finding.finding_summary: The study found that Lumilo changed teacher attention allocation in ways consistent with improved instructional decision-making: teachers in the Glasses + Analytics condition spent much more time with lower-pretest students than those in the other conditions. This suggests the tool supported more targeted classroom orchestration and likely reduced the tendency for higher-knowledge students to receive disproportionate benefit, though no numeric effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Teacher time allocation across students by incoming pretest score; classroom observation and hierarchical linear modeling

paper_profiles.title: When Verification Hurts: Asymmetric Effects of Multi-Agent Feedback in Logic Proof Tutoring
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates how multi-agent, LLM-based tutoring feedback performs in a structured symbolic learning domain: propositional logic proof tutoring. The core question is whether adding role specialization and verification improves step-level feedback quality, and under what conditions verification can actually hurt performance rather than help it.

The authors build a knowledge-graph-grounded benchmark from 516 unique proof states collected from interaction logs of an undergraduate discrete mathematics tutoring system at a large public U.S. university. They study three feedback pipelines: Tutor, which sees only the correct next step; Teacher, which sees the full derivation context; and Judge, which verifies Tutor feedback using full derivation access. Seven LLMs of varying capability are evaluated as both student and feedback agents across these pipelines.

Results show a strong asymmetry: verification helps when upstream feedback is error-prone, but can reduce performance when the underlying feedback is already reliable, because it over-specifies and sometimes reveals too much. The paper also identifies a shared complexity ceiling, with performance dropping sharply beyond proof-state complexity 4–5 across all models and pipelines. Human evaluation reveals systematic failure modes such as echoing student errors, validating partially correct reasoning, premature answer revelation, and verification over-specification, showing that automated accuracy metrics can overestimate pedagogical quality.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a controlled benchmark study with a sizeable dataset of 516 proof states and systematic comparisons across pipelines, but it is not a human RCT measuring learner outcomes. Evidence is primarily algorithmic/experimental with simulated student agents and expert annotations rather than direct K-12 learning impact.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports meaningful performance differences in feedback quality and post-feedback accuracy (e.g., +10–14pp for weak models, -4–6pp for strong models), but these are model-performance effects in a logic tutoring benchmark, not demonstrated student learning gains in a K-12 population. Impact for real learners is therefore unclear and indirect.

interventions.use_case: multi-agent LLM step-level tutoring for propositional logic proof solving, including a Tutor, Teacher, and Judge pipeline that generates scaffolded hints, verifies feedback, and evaluates answer leakage/justification

paper_profiles.title: AI Knows Best? The Paradox of Expertise, AI-Reliance, and Performance in Educational Tutoring Decision-Making Tasks
paper_profiles.venue: LAK 2026: 16th International Learning Analytics and Knowledge Conference
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how people evaluate the correctness of tutor praise responses when assisted by AI-generated decision support. The central question is whether human-AI collaboration improves accuracy relative to humans working alone, and how explanation style affects performance, time, and reliance on AI. The authors focus on two explanation modalities: textual reasoning and inline highlighting.

The study uses 216 tutor-response examples drawn from a tutor training system. Ground-truth labels were created by two experienced tutors and a PhD learning scientist, and a GPT-4-based model produced labels and explanations. In the user study, 95 participants were recruited: 47 professionally trained tutors and 48 Prolific participants. Participants completed a counterbalanced online experiment with five conditions: no AI, AI label only, label plus reasoning, label plus highlighting, and label plus both reasoning and highlighting. They first received a training module on effective praise and then judged 20 items per condition.

Results show that AI assistance improved human accuracy relative to no AI, but human-AI collaboration still underperformed the AI-only baseline. Novices from Prolific benefited more from AI because they tended to follow AI suggestions, while experienced tutors more often overrode correct AI advice, producing more under-reliance. Textual reasoning reduced under-reliance when the AI was correct but increased over-reliance when the AI was wrong; inline highlighting had little measurable effect. Neither explanation style improved overall accuracy, and both increased time spent. The paper concludes that explanation design in tutor-facing decision support should aim to better calibrate trust and reduce both over- and under-reliance.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed experimental study with counterbalanced within-subject conditions and clear statistical testing, but it is not a randomized field trial in K-12 classrooms and uses a simulated tutoring judgment task rather than actual instructional outcomes. The participants are mixed professionals and Prolific respondents, so ecological validity for K-12 tutoring support is limited.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The study shows statistically significant but task-specific effects, including modest accuracy gains from AI assistance and meaningful changes in reliance patterns, but it does not demonstrate student learning gains or classroom-level impact. The primary contribution is diagnostic evidence about human-AI decision support rather than direct educational impact.

interventions.use_case: LLM-generated decision support for evaluating tutor praise responses, including binary correctness labels plus textual reasoning and inline-highlight explanations shown to human tutors

finding.finding_summary: AI assistance improved human decision accuracy versus no-AI baseline, but the human-AI team still underperformed the AI-only baseline (AI accuracy=0.8; human-AI conditions significantly better than no-AI, F(1,471)=6.83, p=.009, ηp²=.014). Novices (Prolific) generally outperformed experienced tutors overall (overall accuracy 0.747 vs 0.712; t=-2.302, p=.0236), suggesting expertise did not translate into better judgment in this task.
finding.measure: Accuracy on tutoring decision-making judgments (correctly labeling tutor praise as effective/ineffective)
finding.effect_size: ηp²=.014; t-tests reported overall group difference d=0.470
finding.std_deviation: Tutor overall SD=0.088; Prolific overall SD=0.057

finding.finding_summary: AI explanations increased time spent per task. Repeated-measures ANOVA showed significant main effects for inline highlighting (F(1,57)=25.74, p<.001, ηp²=.311) and text reasoning (F(1,57)=19.12, p<.001, ηp²=.251), with a significant interaction (F(1,57)=18.26, p=.001, ηp²=.243), indicating the explanation features added processing time rather than reducing it.
finding.measure: Average time spent per task (seconds)
finding.study_size: n=95 total; time analysis after IQR filtering reported on n=58 for within-subject ANOVA
finding.std_deviation: Tutor no-label SD=3.95s; Prolific no-label SD=3.43s; other condition SDs reported in Table 2

finding.finding_summary: Text reasoning changed reliance behavior in both directions: it reduced under-reliance when AI was correct (F(1,94)=8.71, p=.004, ηp²=.085) but increased over-reliance when AI was wrong (F(1,94)=8.81, p=.004, ηp²=.086). Inline highlighting had no significant effect on either under-reliance or over-reliance, suggesting that explanation quality influenced trust calibration more than visual salience alone.
finding.measure: Over-reliance and under-reliance rates in AI-assisted tutoring judgments

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT for Good? On Opportunities and Challenges of Large Language Models for Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This position paper examines the opportunities and challenges of large language models, especially ChatGPT, for education. Rather than reporting an empirical intervention study, it synthesizes the emerging literature and argues for ways these systems could support learning and teaching while also highlighting important risks such as bias, privacy concerns, misuse, overreliance, and difficulty distinguishing machine-generated from human-generated work.

The paper discusses potential applications across educational levels, including elementary, middle, high school, university, and professional development. It describes how large language models could support learners through tutoring, feedback, question generation, summarization, and practice activities, and support educators through lesson planning, automated assessment, personalized instruction, and content creation. It also notes broader possibilities for AR/VR and other digital learning environments.

The authors conclude that large language models may become powerful educational tools if they are integrated responsibly, with human oversight, critical thinking, fact-checking, privacy safeguards, bias mitigation, and attention to equitable access. The paper mainly offers conceptual recommendations and mitigation strategies rather than evaluating any specific deployment in schools.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a position paper and literature-informed commentary, not an empirical study, RCT, or meta-analysis. It provides conceptual arguments and recommendations rather than original quantitative evidence.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper describes potentially broad educational relevance for LLMs, but it does not report effect sizes or direct outcome impacts. Its practical implications are meaningful, yet the evidence base in this paper is indirect and largely theoretical.

interventions.use_case: Position paper on ChatGPT and other large language models as educational assistants for tutoring-like interaction, including question answering, explanations, practice generation, and dialog support for learners and teachers.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that LLMs may improve student engagement, curiosity, and interaction through conversational support and personalized prompting, but it also warns that overreliance could reduce motivation and engagement with independent inquiry. No quantitative effect sizes or sample sizes are reported because this is a position paper synthesizing prior work rather than presenting a primary empirical study.
finding.measure: Engagement, curiosity, willingness to ask questions, and learner interaction (conceptual/theoretical discussion)

finding.finding_summary: The paper emphasizes potential benefits for critical thinking, problem-solving, and fact-checking when LLMs are used as tools to generate hypotheses and compare sources, but it also highlights the risk that students may become too reliant on model outputs and weaken these same skills. This is a conceptual claim without reported quantitative evidence, effect sizes, or sample sizes.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, problem-solving, and verification/corroboration practices (conceptual/theoretical discussion)

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that LLMs can reduce teacher workload by supporting lesson planning, generating quizzes and prompts, automating feedback and grading, and streamlining content creation. One cited example notes grading effort could be reduced by up to 85% in a related NLP-based feedback setting, but this position paper itself does not report a new empirical estimate.
finding.measure: Teacher time, grading effort, and content-generation productivity (conceptual/theoretical discussion)

finding.finding_summary: A major focus of the paper is governance, fairness, privacy, sustainability, and responsible deployment of LLMs in education. It argues that institutional policies, human oversight, and ethical frameworks are necessary to realize benefits and mitigate risks, but it does not present empirical institutional outcome data.
finding.measure: Policy, governance, privacy/security, fairness, and responsible implementation considerations

paper_profiles.title: Examining the Effect of Assessment Construct Characteristics on Machine Learning Scoring of Scientific Argumentation
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether characteristics of science assessment tasks are associated with the accuracy of machine-learning (ML) scoring models for scientific argumentation responses. The authors focus on a practical question in automated assessment: when short constructed responses are scored by AI, do some kinds of items produce more reliable human-machine agreement than others? They examine three internal construct features of the assessment tasks—complexity, diversity, and structure—and test how these features relate to model performance.

The study uses 17 middle school scientific argumentation tasks aligned with a validated learning progression. Students from grades 5–8 in two California school districts completed the assessments after receiving instruction in scientific argumentation. The researchers trained separate ML scoring models for each item using 361 randomly selected responses per item, with the same preprocessing and model-development procedures across tasks. Human experts had already scored the student responses, allowing comparison of machine and human scores.

Results show that ML scoring performance was generally good, but varied by item. Models performed best on simpler items that required less complex reasoning, fewer science learning dimensions, and lower levels of argumentation structure. Higher levels of complexity, diversity, and structure were each associated with lower Cohen’s kappa values, indicating reduced agreement between machine and human scores. The paper concludes that assessment construct characteristics matter for automated scoring and that higher-order, multidimensional science argumentation tasks remain more difficult for current ML scoring approaches.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed correlational study with systematic item coding and model evaluation, but it is not an intervention trial and does not estimate causal effects on student learning. Evidence is strongest for associational validity of automated scoring performance.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper shows practically meaningful machine-scoring performance for simpler science argumentation items, but no student outcome gains are demonstrated. Its impact is therefore promising for assessment operations, yet unclear for direct educational outcomes.

interventions.use_case: machine-learning automated scoring of short written scientific argumentation responses to support scoring and potential formative feedback in K-12 science assessment

finding.finding_summary: The study found that machine-scoring performance was substantial overall, with mean Cohen’s kappa = 0.60 across 17 argumentation items scored from n=361 responses per item (accuracy mean = 0.79). However, performance declined as construct demands increased: higher Complexity, Diversity, and Structure were each associated with lower human-machine agreement (Spearman’s rs = -0.752, -0.718, and -0.764, all p < .01).
finding.measure: Human-machine agreement on scoring scientific argumentation responses; Cohen’s kappa, accuracy, Spearman correlation
finding.study_size: n=361 per item; 17 items; 932 students total

finding.finding_summary: The paper does not test student learning gains directly; instead, it evaluates automated scoring of science assessment items aligned to a learning progression. Results suggest the system can score lower-complexity items well, but scoring accuracy drops for more multidimensional or higher-level argumentation tasks, limiting its readiness for broader assessment use.
finding.measure: Automated scoring accuracy for science assessment items aligned to a learning progression

finding.finding_summary: The study suggests automated scoring can efficiently evaluate constructed-response scientific argumentation at scale, reducing reliance on human scoring for large classroom assessments. While no time-savings estimate is reported, the models achieved mean accuracy of 0.79 and substantial mean kappa of 0.60, indicating practical potential for faster assessment turnaround.
finding.measure: Feasibility of machine scoring for large-scale assessment scoring
finding.study_size: n=17 items; n=361 responses per item

paper_profiles.title: Challenges and Future Directions of Big Data and Artificial Intelligence in Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a position/review article that examines the current status, opportunities, and challenges of big data and artificial intelligence (AI) in education. Rather than reporting an empirical intervention study, it synthesizes prior research and panel discussion insights to argue how AI and learning analytics are reshaping educational research, policy, and industry. The authors frame big data and AI as increasingly important for assessment, individualized learning, and precision education, while also warning that technology adoption should be guided by educational theory, psychological understanding, and careful validation.

The paper discusses broad AI-enabled approaches such as learning analytics, machine learning, intelligent tutoring systems, dashboards for teachers, and adaptive/precision education systems. These are described in general terms across educational levels, with examples drawn from K-12, higher education, and vocational learning, but no single population or site is studied empirically. The paper emphasizes that these technologies can support prediction of learning performance, identification of student needs, and real-time instructional support, especially when combined with cognitive and educational theories.

The main conclusions are that AI and big data have strong potential to improve learning and teaching, but meaningful progress requires interdisciplinary collaboration, stronger theoretical grounding, better algorithmic validation, attention to ethics and privacy, teacher education, and balanced human-machine learning. The authors argue that educational technology should not simply optimize efficiency; it should also preserve the social and human dimensions of schooling. They conclude that future work should focus on theory-based precision education and responsible adoption of AI-supported tools.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed position/review paper, but it is not an empirical study and does not test an intervention with a defined design, sample, or outcome analysis. It provides conceptual synthesis and citations rather than primary evidence.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper has broad field-level relevance and identifies important directions for AI in education, but it reports no measurable effect sizes or direct impact estimates. Its influence is conceptual and systemic rather than demonstrated student-level impact.

interventions.use_case: learning analytics and machine-learning models that predict students' academic performance, dropout risk, and learning trajectories from log data and other educational big data
AI-powered tutoring and assessment environments such as AutoTutor, Inq-ITS, and other intelligent educational systems used as examples of adaptive support for learning

finding.finding_summary: This is a position/review paper, not an empirical effectiveness study, so it does not report a direct causal effect on achievement. It argues that big data and AI in education have encouraging potential to improve students' academic performance, retention, and assessment accuracy, citing prior work on predicting academic performance and real-time science inquiry assessment rather than reporting new effect sizes.
finding.measure: Conceptual synthesis of prior literature on academic performance, retention, and assessment/prediction accuracy

finding.finding_summary: The paper highlights AI-enabled digital assessment environments for scientific inquiry as a promising direction, especially for real-time performance assessment of science inquiry skills within microworlds. However, it does not present original outcome data; instead it cites prior systems like Inq-ITS and related educational data mining work as evidence that AI can support assessment and feedback for inquiry processes.
finding.measure: Scientific inquiry skills, inquiry performance assessment, and formative assessment metrics

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that big data and AI can improve educational policy, teacher preparation, privacy governance, and academia-industry collaboration. It is a conceptual/position piece emphasizing the need for lifelong learning systems, teacher education, and data protection rather than reporting empirical policy effects.
finding.measure: Policy recommendations, teacher readiness, privacy/data governance, and academia-industry collaboration

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests that AI and learning analytics can support teachers by informing instruction in real time, improving course planning, and reducing routine workload through automated analytics and assessment. No empirical effect size is reported because the article synthesizes opportunities and challenges rather than evaluating a specific implementation.
finding.measure: Teacher instruction support, course planning, and administrative/assessment efficiency

paper_profiles.title: Promises and challenges of generative artificial intelligence for human learning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This perspective paper examines the emerging role of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in human learning and education. Rather than reporting an empirical intervention study, it synthesizes current literature to discuss where GenAI may help or hinder learning, with a focus on how these systems could support instruction, provide feedback, generate learning resources, and transform assessment.

The paper frames GenAI as a potentially powerful tool for personalized learning support, scalable content creation, timely feedback, and more authentic assessment. It uses examples such as LLM-based tutors, AI-generated instructional materials, multimodal feedback tools, and generative agents for assessment design, while also highlighting risks including hallucinations, bias, privacy concerns, unequal access, and disruption of traditional assessments. The discussion emphasizes the need for human-AI collaboration, educator expertise, and AI literacy.

Because the article is conceptual and not an intervention study, it does not involve a specific participant population, school level, or implementation context. Its main conclusion is that GenAI should be integrated into education in a human-centered, evidence-based, and methodologically rigorous way so that it augments rather than replaces human learning, critical thinking, and creativity. The authors call for more rigorous research across educational contexts to establish when and how GenAI genuinely improves learning outcomes.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a perspective/opinion article rather than an empirical study, so it does not provide original methods, sample, or outcome evaluation. It synthesizes prior literature and offers conceptual arguments only.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper argues for potentially substantial impacts of GenAI on learning, assessment, and feedback, but it reports no direct measured effects. Its influence is therefore conceptual and policy-oriented, with unclear empirical impact on K-12 outcomes.

interventions.use_case: Generative AI chatbots and LLM-powered tutors used for personalized learning support, step-by-step guidance, adaptive questioning, and conversational tutoring (e.g., Khanmigo-like systems) across subjects and languages.
GenAI systems that analyze student work and generate instant, personalized feedback on essays, programming assignments, collaborative writing, and learning analytics dashboards.
AI-generated instructional materials and learning resources, including explanations, examples, quiz questions, and multimedia content produced by GenAI for classroom use.
GenAI-enabled authentic assessment and simulated learning environments, including virtual patients, driving/professional simulations, and multimodal agent-based scenarios.
Learning analytics dashboards and process feedback systems augmented with multimodal GenAI chatbots to interpret learner data and surface progress/needs.

paper_profiles.title: Supporting Upper Elementary Students in Learning AI Concepts with Story-Driven Game-Based Learning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how to support upper elementary students in learning foundational AI concepts through a story-driven, game-based learning environment called PRIMARYAI. The authors focus on an AI planning quest embedded in a life-science narrative about declining yellow-eyed penguin populations, asking whether the game engages students and whether a Use-Modify-Create scaffolding framework helps them learn and progress through the tasks.

The intervention combined a classroom curriculum with unplugged AI activities and in-game, block-based planning tasks. Students first completed a pre-test, then participated in an unplugged AI planning lesson, collaborated on a non-game planning activity, and subsequently played the PRIMARYAI AI planning quest over two days. The study involved fourth-grade students in rural Midwestern U.S. schools; the analysis focused on 16 students from one class because networking problems prevented the other class from completing the game. Quantitative data included pre/post content tests and gameplay trace logs, and qualitative data came from approximately one hour of video recordings.

Results showed statistically significant gains on the AI planning assessment from pre-test to post-test, suggesting the game supported learning of planning concepts. Video analysis indicated students were actively engaged during gameplay, though some technical issues affected play. Trace-log analysis suggested that the Use-Modify-Create progression generally helped students move through the missions, with the earliest phases being easiest and the final create phase most challenging. The authors conclude that the scaffolding structure and narrative game format are promising for elementary AI education, while noting a need for additional hints, better support for transitions between missions, and larger-scale studies.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed classroom implementation study with mixed methods, but it is not a controlled experiment and has a small sample (n=16, with n=14 for pre/post analysis). Evidence is therefore informative but limited in causal strength.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The study reports statistically significant but modest gains on a domain-specific AI planning test and positive engagement observations, without an effect size or broader academic transfer evidence. The impact appears promising but unclear beyond this small pilot population.

interventions.use_case: story-driven game-based learning environment for upper elementary AI education, using a science inquiry narrative and a block-based AI planning quest with Use-Modify-Create scaffolding

finding.finding_summary: Students showed significant gains on an AI planning content knowledge assessment after using PRIMARYAI. On the 11-item pre/post test, scores increased from M=4.36 (SD=1.98) to M=5.43 (SD=1.87) for the matched sample (n=14), with a paired t-test showing t(13)=3.51, p<.01. The paper does not report an effect size, but the learning gain is statistically significant and specific to AI planning concepts.
finding.measure: 11-item multiple-choice AI planning content knowledge pre-test/post-test

finding.finding_summary: Qualitative video analysis indicated that students were actively engaged during gameplay, frequently verbalizing completion and persistence-related comments such as “Mission completed!” and collaborating with peers and adults. The study also reports that 8 students raised their hands when asked who had completed all missions, suggesting substantial engagement and persistence, though no standardized engagement effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Video observations of gameplay engagement; mission completion behavior

finding.finding_summary: Trace-log analysis suggests the Use-Modify-Create scaffold supported students' ability to progress through increasingly demanding AI planning tasks. Completion rates decreased across phases but remained substantial: 93.75% completed Use, 66.67% of those completed Modify, and 60% of those completed Create, indicating that many students could transfer prior understanding to more complex problem solving.
finding.measure: Mission completion/progression across Use-Modify-Create phases; gameplay trace logs

paper_profiles.title: Teacher’s Perceptions of Using an Artificial Intelligence-Based Educational Tool for Scientific Writing
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how K-12 STEM teachers perceive an artificial intelligence-enhanced scaffolding system for scientific writing. The central question is not whether the tool improves student achievement, but how teachers interpret its instructional value, its potential classroom role, and the risks or concerns associated with AI use in schooling.

The intervention studied was an AI-based scaffolding system called AISS, built using GPT-2 to generate expert-model text completions for scientific writing tasks. Teachers first reviewed readings and examples about AI in education, then interacted directly with the system in an online doctoral course. They completed an ill-structured science task about air quality, wrote an initial draft, used AISS for sentence/paragraph generation and support, and then reflected on the experience in interviews.

Participants were nine STEM teachers working in K-12 schools in the southeastern United States, most with at least 10 years of teaching experience. The study used qualitative thematic analysis of interview transcripts and log files. Teachers generally viewed the AI tool positively, especially as a source of individualized expert modeling, immediate feedback, and support for argumentation, reasoning, evidence-based writing, and higher-order thinking. At the same time, they expressed concern about reduced teacher roles, the opacity of AI decisions, and the accuracy/validity of AI-generated outputs. The authors conclude that hands-on exposure to AI can improve teacher receptiveness and that further professional development and clearer implementation guidance are needed before wider adoption.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed qualitative thematic case study with clear methods, triangulated log files and interviews, and good inter-rater reliability, but it does not estimate causal effects on learner outcomes. It provides useful evidence about feasibility and perceptions, yet credibility for impact claims is limited relative to experimental designs.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests potentially meaningful benefits for scientific writing support and reasoning, but all evidence is perceptual and no effect sizes or outcome gains are reported. Its practical impact is promising for implementation guidance, but the demonstrated student-level impact remains unclear.

interventions.use_case: AI-enhanced scaffolding for scientific writing and argumentation support, using GPT-2 text generation to provide individualized expert-model examples, sentence/paragraph completion, and immediate feedback for K-12 STEM teachers experiencing the tool as students.
Non-adaptive instructional support embedded in an online writing task where participants searched for information, drafted an essay, and revised based on system-generated prompts and reflections.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported that the AI-enhanced scaffolding system supported scientific reasoning subskills, especially argumentation, evidence selection, and justification of claims. In qualitative interviews (n=9 STEM teachers), participants consistently described the tool as helping them reason through how to connect claims with evidence and reflect on their thinking, though no quantitative learning gains were reported.
finding.measure: Teacher interview themes about argumentation, evidence-based writing, reasoning, and higher-order thinking during scientific writing

finding.finding_summary: Teachers viewed the AI system as improving scientific writing quality by modeling stronger sentence structure, paragraph sequencing, and writing organization. In the qualitative case study (n=9), participants repeatedly described the generated text as an exemplary model for writing, but the paper did not report test scores or effect sizes.
finding.measure: Teacher perceptions of scientific writing quality, sentence structure, and paragraph organization from interviews and log files

finding.finding_summary: The tool was also perceived to foster durable skills such as metacognition, self-directed learning, and problem-solving. Teachers noted that interacting with the AI prompted reflection on their own writing process and decision-making, but these claims were based on qualitative perceptions rather than measured gains.
finding.measure: Interview-coded themes on reflection, metacognition, self-directed learning, and problem-solving

finding.finding_summary: Teachers emphasized the system’s immediate feedback and rapid generation of responses as a potential efficiency advantage over typical classroom supports. However, the paper did not quantify time savings or workload reduction; the evidence is limited to perceived efficiency from interviews with n=9 teachers.
finding.measure: Teacher perceptions of immediacy, feedback speed, and ease of use

finding.finding_summary: The paper found broad teacher receptiveness to future AI integration, but also substantial concerns about teacher role displacement, transparency, accuracy, and bias. These findings suggest implementation potential alongside governance and adoption challenges, with no quantitative institutional outcome estimates reported.
finding.measure: Teacher perceptions of classroom implementation, role change, transparency, accuracy, and AI bias

paper_profiles.title: Flipped classroom improves student learning in health professions education: a meta-analysis
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether flipped classroom instruction improves student learning compared with traditional classroom instruction in health professions education. The authors note that flipped classrooms have become increasingly popular, but that the evidence for actual learning gains had not been synthesized in a meta-analysis focused on objective student performance outcomes.

The intervention studied is a flipped classroom model in which students received pre-class video-based instruction and then attended face-to-face sessions for active learning. The review was restricted to comparative studies in peer-reviewed English-language journals that used objective assessments such as exams or post-tests. The included studies covered health professions learners such as medical, pharmacy, nursing, public health, dental, chiropractic, and related students, mostly in higher education settings across several countries, with the majority from the United States.

Across 28 studies and 4,715 total participants, the meta-analysis found a small but statistically significant benefit for flipped classrooms over traditional classrooms on student learning outcomes. The effect was stronger when instructors used quizzes at the start of in-class sessions. The authors conclude that flipped classrooms can improve learner performance in health professions education, while also noting that the studies varied in design and that no long-term retention data were available.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a meta-analysis with explicit search, inclusion criteria, moderator analyses, and publication-bias checks, which gives it strong design credibility. It is still somewhat limited for the target K-12 science topic because the included studies are all health-professions higher-education studies rather than K-12 science inquiry interventions.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The pooled effect is modest but positive (SMD=0.33), which clears the threshold for meaningful impact on the studied population. However, the relevance to K-12 science reasoning is indirect, so the practical impact for the requested topic is modest rather than large.

interventions.use_case: flipped classroom instruction using pre-recorded video lectures before face-to-face sessions, with active learning in class

finding.finding_summary: This meta-analysis found that flipped classroom instruction significantly improved student learning performance compared with traditional classroom teaching across 28 comparative studies (n=4,715 total; 2,295 flipped, 2,420 traditional). The pooled effect was SMD=0.33 (95% CI 0.21–0.46, p<0.001), based on objective post-tests/exams; however, the paper does not report science-specific subskill outcomes, so this is a broader achievement proxy rather than direct K-12 scientific reasoning evidence.
finding.measure: Objective student learning performance (post-tests, exams, objective assessments)

finding.finding_summary: Across 28 comparative studies in health professions education, flipped classrooms produced better overall academic performance than traditional classrooms (SMD=0.33, 95% CI 0.21–0.46). Outcomes were course-specific achievement measures such as exams and post-tests; the evidence suggests a modest positive effect on academic learning, though it is not K-12 or science-content specific.
finding.measure: Course achievement / objective learning assessments

finding.finding_summary: Learner perceptions favored the flipped classroom, with 228 of 320 respondents (71%) preferring flipped over traditional formats across five survey studies. The paper reports improved satisfaction and engagement-related perceptions, but these are preference/survey outcomes rather than direct behavioral or long-term social-emotional measures.
finding.measure: Student preference/satisfaction surveys

paper_profiles.title: Reflection on whether Chat GPT should be banned by academia from the perspective of education and teaching
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the debate over whether ChatGPT should be banned in academia, focusing on its implications for education, teaching, and academic integrity. Rather than reporting an empirical study, it offers an opinion-based analysis of the opportunities and risks posed by generative AI in educational settings.

The paper argues that ChatGPT and similar AI tools can support learning, teaching, and educational digital transformation by enabling personalized tutoring, more efficient information retrieval, automated text generation, and new forms of student inquiry. It discusses potential uses in school and higher education contexts, including classroom support, assessment, and broader educational reform, while also acknowledging concerns about cheating, over-reliance, privacy, bias, and ethical misuse.

The discussion is framed around students, teachers, schools, universities, and education policymakers, with examples drawn largely from K-12 and higher education policy responses in multiple countries. The author concludes that outright bans are not advisable; instead, AI tools should be regulated, integrated responsibly into education, and paired with updated teaching methods, assessment practices, and governance to protect academic integrity while leveraging their benefits.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a 2023 opinion/reflection article with no original empirical study design, no comparison group, and no measured outcomes. It is peer-reviewed but does not provide methodological evidence for causal claims.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper discusses potentially important system-level and skill-related implications of ChatGPT for education, but it reports no empirical effects or effect sizes. The impact is therefore plausible but unclear rather than demonstrated.

interventions.use_case: ChatGPT as a general-purpose educational assistant for student question answering, personalized tutoring, writing support, and teacher assistance in K-12 and higher education contexts

finding.finding_summary: This is a conceptual opinion paper, not an empirical evaluation, so it does not report measured effects on outcomes. The paper argues that ChatGPT may improve educational digital transformation and efficiency, but also raises concerns about academic integrity, privacy, and governance, with no sample size or effect size reported.
finding.measure: policy and governance discussion; no empirical outcome measure

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that ChatGPT could support critical thinking, problem solving, creativity, and self-directed learning if used appropriately, but may also weaken independent thinking and judgment through over-reliance. These claims are theoretical and not backed by experimental data in the paper.
finding.measure: theoretical discussion of critical thinking, independent thinking, and problem-solving

paper_profiles.title: Pedagogy-driven Evaluation of Generative AI-powered Intelligent Tutoring Systems
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a central problem in AI-powered intelligent tutoring systems (ITSs): current evaluation practices are fragmented, subjective, and not well suited to generative AI tutors. The authors argue that common approaches such as self-reports, generic NLP metrics, and ad hoc human judgments fail to capture pedagogical quality, metacognitive support, and active learning in educational dialogues. The paper is not an intervention study; instead, it is a position/review proposing a more principled way to evaluate GenAI-powered ITSs.

The paper reviews existing evaluation traditions for ITSs, including traditional educational evaluation, NLG-based automated metrics, and pedagogy-oriented human or semi-automated approaches. It then identifies two major challenges: the diversity of evaluation pragmatics and the lack of unification in principles, metrics, and benchmarks. To address these issues, the authors propose three research directions: building unified evaluation frameworks, measuring pedagogical guidance, and measuring active learning, with suggestions such as taxonomy-driven benchmarks, factuality/relevance checks, and graph-based modeling of dialogue flow.

The context is broad AIED and educational NLP, with examples drawn from tutoring datasets and systems in STEM, language learning, and math dialogue. No original participant study is reported. The main conclusion is that progress in GenAI tutoring requires standardized, scalable, and learning-science-grounded evaluation methods that can more reliably assess pedagogical effectiveness than current practices.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a conceptual/review-and-proposal paper rather than an empirical evaluation study. It synthesizes prior work and proposes research directions, but does not report a new controlled design or original outcome data for K-12 learners.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper has potential relevance for future educational AI evaluation practice, but it does not demonstrate direct learner impact. Its influence is mainly methodological and prospective, so any educational impact is currently unclear and indirect.

interventions.use_case: Pedagogy-driven evaluation of generative AI-powered intelligent tutoring systems and educational dialogue tutors such as LearnLM and Khanmigo, focusing on how to assess response quality, pedagogical guidance, and active-learning support.
Evaluation frameworks for classical and modern intelligent tutoring systems, including dialogue-based tutoring systems and pedagogically grounded benchmarks for tutor response assessment.

paper_profiles.title: VLM@school – Evaluation of AI image understanding on German middle school knowledge
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper presents VLM@school, a new benchmark for evaluating vision-language models (VLMs) on German-language tasks that require visual reasoning combined with subject-specific background knowledge. The authors argue that existing multimodal benchmarks are often English-only, overly multiple-choice oriented, and insufficiently grounded in real educational contexts. To address this gap, they construct a dataset of more than 2,000 open-ended questions linked to 486 images drawn from middle school curricula and related educational materials across nine domains, including arts, biology, geography, history, math, music, physics, religion, and sports.

The benchmark is designed to test whether models can answer school-level questions that depend on interpreting images rather than text-only cues. The authors also include adversarial questions that are intentionally misleading and cannot be answered from the image alone, in order to test whether models can correctly abstain from answering. Thirteen open-weight VLMs are evaluated using an automated jury-style LLM judging setup. The paper reports that even the best models remain below 45% overall accuracy, with especially weak performance in domains such as music and math and very low performance on adversarial items.

The study focuses on middle school-level content from German textbooks and related materials, with questions created by native German speakers. The main conclusion is that current VLMs still struggle substantially with realistic, curriculum-based multimodal reasoning in German, and that benchmark performance on popular public datasets does not reliably predict performance on this more educationally grounded benchmark. The authors argue that this dataset provides a more meaningful testbed for real-world visual understanding and knowledge integration, especially outside English-language settings.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed benchmark/evaluation study with a clear methodology, but it is not an educational intervention study and does not use a human-controlled experimental design. The evidence is useful for validity benchmarking but has limited causal relevance to student outcomes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper has no direct K-12 learning effect size because it evaluates AI models rather than students, so educational impact is indirect. Its main value is diagnostic: it suggests current multimodal AI is not yet reliable for science inquiry support, especially for reasoning-heavy and unanswerable-item behavior.

interventions.use_case: benchmark evaluation of vision-language models on German middle school curriculum images and open-ended questions requiring visual reasoning plus subject knowledge

finding.finding_summary: The paper evaluates VLMs on science-related middle school tasks that require interpreting diagrams and combining visual evidence with background knowledge, including biology and physics items. Performance is low: the best overall model scores under 45% accuracy, and science-adjacent subskills such as explaining physics phenomena and identifying biology terms are often incorrect; exact science-domain scores reported include physics around 32.48%-47.65% depending on model and biology around 32.84%-48.53% overall across models.
finding.measure: accuracy on open-ended benchmark questions in biology and physics requiring visual reasoning and background knowledge
finding.study_size: n=486 images; n=2038 questions; 13 VLMs evaluated

finding.finding_summary: Across nine school-subject domains, the benchmark shows that current VLMs struggle substantially with non-science curricular knowledge as well. Best overall accuracy is below 45% (top model 43.26%), with domain scores varying widely; for example, history peaks at 54.36%, religion at 52.92%/52.92% depending on model, while music and math are especially difficult at about 31% and 34% best-case accuracy respectively.
finding.measure: accuracy on open-ended middle-school subject questions across arts, geography, history, music, religion, sports, and math
finding.study_size: n=486 images; n=2038 questions; 13 VLMs evaluated

finding.finding_summary: A central contribution is showing that the models often fail at higher-order reasoning behaviors such as explaining, reversing relations, and recognizing when a question is unanswerable from the image. On adversarial questions, overall accuracy drops sharply to 3.02%-32.83% depending on the model, with several models still producing confident but wrong answers instead of saying 'I don't know.'
finding.measure: accuracy on adversarial/unanswerable questions and qualitative error analysis of reasoning failures
finding.study_size: n=486 images; adversarial subset included within n=2038 questions

paper_profiles.title: Bias Amplification in Artificial Intelligence Systems
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how artificial intelligence systems can amplify existing bias in training data and thereby produce unfair outcomes at scale. Rather than focusing on long-term speculative dangers of AI, the paper argues that present-day harms are more urgent because biased datasets, opaque models, and insufficient oversight can disproportionately affect marginalized groups. The author organizes the discussion around types of bias in machine learning, including dataset, association, automation, interaction, and confirmation bias, and distinguishes representative harm from allocative harm.

The paper does not study a specific educational intervention or K-12 implementation. Instead, it presents a policy and governance argument for how public-sector institutions should respond to AI bias. Proposed approaches include stronger data standards, improved data-sharing governance, transparency requirements, and accountability mechanisms for organizations deploying AI systems. The paper also mentions discrimination-aware machine learning as a technical strategy to encode non-discrimination constraints into models.

The context is broad public-sector and commercial AI deployment, with examples drawn from hiring, advertising, facial recognition, healthcare, criminal justice, and content moderation. No participant population, school setting, or educational user group is reported. The paper concludes that bias in AI is primarily a leadership and governance problem, and that governments should help ensure datasets are diverse, interoperable, secure, and used in ways that protect privacy and equity.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an opinion/policy essay about bias in AI systems, not an empirical study of an educational intervention. It contains no experimental, correlational, or qualitative research design evaluating student outcomes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper does not report any measured educational impact, effect sizes, or K-12 science learning outcomes. Its relevance is conceptual and policy-oriented rather than evidence of impact on learners.

paper_profiles.title: Do intelligent tutoring systems benefit K-12 students? A meta-analysis and evaluation of heterogeneity of treatment effects in the U.S.
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether intelligent tutoring systems (ITS) improve learning outcomes for U.S. K-12 students, and under what conditions their effects are strongest. It is motivated by the growing use of AI-based tutoring in schools and the need to understand not just average effects, but also heterogeneity across study designs, student populations, settings, intervention features, and outcome measures.

The authors conducted a systematic search of studies published between 2011 and 2021 and identified 18 experimental studies with 77 effect sizes across 11 ITS. The review used the MUTOS framework and the What Works Clearinghouse standards to examine both internal validity and external validity. The interventions included systems such as ALEKS, MATHia, Cognitive Tutor Algebra I, SWELL, and the Intelligent Tutoring System for the Structure Strategy, with support features such as worked-out examples, hints, feedback/explanations, reading materials, and video sequences.

The meta-analysis found a small but statistically significant overall positive effect of ITS on learning outcomes for U.S. K-12 students. Effects were similar across elementary and middle school grades and across several student subgroups, but were smaller in rural settings. MetaForest results suggested that treatment features mattered most: worked-out examples, intervention duration, intervention condition, and immediate measurement were the most important moderators. The paper concludes that ITS can benefit K-12 students, especially when designed with structured supports and implemented in ways that preserve engagement and fit the classroom context.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a meta-analysis of 18 experimental studies with 77 effect sizes, using multilevel meta-regression and robust variance estimation. It directly synthesizes causal evidence and examines moderators, which makes it strong evidence by the framework.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The pooled effect is g=0.271, which meets the threshold for medium impact. Effects are positive across both mathematics and literacy outcomes, indicating meaningful general-population benefits for K-12 students.

interventions.use_case: Meta-analysis of K-12 U.S. intelligent tutoring systems delivering personalized step-by-step or sub-step-by-step instruction, hints, feedback/explanations, worked-out examples, reading materials, and related supports across academic subjects.

finding.finding_summary: Across 18 experimental studies and 77 effect sizes, ITS produced a statistically significant positive impact on U.S. K-12 students’ learning outcomes (g=0.271, SE=0.011, p=0.001). The review treated the outcome broadly as student academic achievement, with effects varying by measurement type, timing, and intervention features.
finding.measure: Student academic achievement / learning outcomes

finding.finding_summary: For mathematics outcomes, ITS had a positive effect (g=0.253, 95% CI 0.224 to 0.281, p<0.001) across 22 effect sizes. Math outcomes were smaller than reading/writing outcomes but still statistically significant, indicating benefits for math achievement in K-12 settings.
finding.measure: Mathematics achievement

finding.finding_summary: For reading and writing outcomes, ITS showed a positive effect of g=0.323 (95% CI 0.218 to 0.428, p<0.001) across 55 effect sizes. The effect was larger than for mathematics, suggesting somewhat stronger benefits for literacy-related outcomes in the included K-12 studies.
finding.measure: Reading and writing achievement

paper_profiles.title: Certifiable Artificial Intelligence Through Data Fusion
paper_profiles.venue: AAAI FSS-21: Artificial Intelligence in Government and Public Sector
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of how to certify artificial intelligence and machine learning systems for adoption, deployment, and maintenance in safety- and mission-critical settings. The authors argue that current AI practice lacks standardized processes, metrics, and performance bounds needed to judge whether a system is trustworthy, explainable, interpretable, and accountable. To address this gap, they propose a certification-oriented framework built around the Multisource AI Scorecard Table (MAST), which combines qualitative checklist items with quantitative performance measures.

The paper describes a certification process with four stages: conceptual idea, processing design, implementation test, and managed deployment. It emphasizes verification and validation, robustness testing, uncertainty analysis, and documentation of intended use through model cards and manuals. The framework is illustrated with AI-based image fusion as a notional use case, showing how performance can be bounded across conditions such as distance and image quality. The authors conclude that certifiable AI should be treated as a systems-engineering problem that integrates human, machine, data, and environmental factors rather than certifying algorithms in isolation.

Although the paper is not an educational study, it serves as a position paper about AI certification more generally. It does not include participants, schools, or K-12 populations, and it does not evaluate an intervention empirically. The main contribution is a conceptual and methodological proposal for certifying AI/ML systems, especially in human-machine teaming contexts, with image fusion used as an example of how performance bounds might support deployment decisions.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a conceptual/framework paper with a notional technical example, not an empirical K-12 study. It does not present a controlled evaluation, student sample, or causal evidence about educational outcomes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No K-12 learning impact is measured or demonstrated. The paper is about AI certification and deployment standards, so there is no direct evidence of educational effect size or student outcome improvement.

interventions.use_case: Framework for certifying AI/ML systems and image-fusion pipelines using the Multisource AI Scorecard Table (MAST), verification/validation procedures, and performance bounds; includes a notional deep-CNN and anisotropic diffusion image-fusion use case for automatic target recognition.

paper_profiles.title: From Statistical Relational to Neurosymbolic Artificial Intelligence: a Survey
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a survey of the intersection between statistical relational AI (StarAI) and neurosymbolic AI (NeSy). It asks how logical reasoning and learning are integrated across these two communities and proposes a shared conceptual framework for comparing methods. Rather than evaluating an educational intervention or empirical outcome, the paper synthesizes prior work on logic-based AI systems.

The main contribution is a taxonomy of seven dimensions common to StarAI and NeSy systems: type of inference (proof-based vs. model-based), logical syntax, semantics, learning scope, symbolic versus subsymbolic representations, relation to logic/probability/neural paradigms, and task classes. The survey uses these dimensions to position representative systems such as ProbLog, Markov Logic Networks, DeepProbLog, Logic Tensor Networks, Semantic Loss, and others, illustrating how each framework handles reasoning and learning.

The paper focuses on theoretical and methodological issues in AI, not on a specific population, instructional setting, or experimental deployment. Its main conclusion is that StarAI and NeSy are closely related and can cross-fertilize each other: proof-based approaches naturally map logical proofs to neural architectures, while model-based approaches translate logical constraints into loss functions. The survey argues that understanding these shared principles clarifies the design space for future neurosymbolic systems and highlights open challenges in scalability, interpretability, and control.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a theoretical survey paper on neurosymbolic and statistical relational AI, not an empirical study of an educational intervention. It reports no experimental design, no K-12 sample, and no learner outcomes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper does not evaluate student-facing technology in education or report any outcome effect sizes. Its contribution is conceptual taxonomy and synthesis, so there is no measurable K-12 impact to rate.

paper_profiles.title: Enterprise AI Canvas: Integrating Artificial Intelligence into Business
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper proposes the Enterprise AI Canvas, a structured framework for planning and evaluating AI projects in business settings. The author argues that organizations often struggle to integrate AI because business value, operational decision-making, organizational change, and technical machine learning considerations are usually discussed separately. The paper’s central question is how to bring business experts, data scientists, and AI specialists together to define all relevant aspects of an AI use case before implementation.

The proposed canvas has two parts. Part 1 covers the business view: value creation, success metrics, decision and optimization processes, organizational impact, sponsorship, and relevant domains. Part 2 covers the model and data view: prediction and action, features, data sources and processing, domain expertise and data quality, constraints, and evaluation and monitoring. The framework is illustrated with a supermarket replenishment example, where AI predicts future demand and optimizes order quantities under practical constraints.

The paper is not an empirical study and does not involve a student, teacher, or school-based population. Instead, it is a conceptual/design contribution for adult professional users in business and data science roles. The main conclusion is that AI initiatives are more likely to succeed when business and technical considerations are integrated early through a shared planning artifact that supports cross-functional discussion and decision-making.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a conceptual/grey-literature style framework paper about an Enterprise AI Canvas for business use-cases, not an empirical study in K-12 education. It does not evaluate a K-12 intervention, use a comparison group, or report outcome data.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No student, teacher, or school outcome is measured, so there is no evidence of educational impact. The paper is not about science inquiry supports in K-12 and contains no impact findings relevant to the retrieved topic.

paper_profiles.title: Conceptual Modeling and Artiﬁcial Intelligence: Mutual Benefits from Complementary Worlds
paper_profiles.venue: ER 2021 / CMAI'2021 (3rd International Workshop on Conceptual Modeling Meets Artificial Intelligence)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is an editorial preface for the 3rd International Workshop on Conceptual Modeling Meets Artificial Intelligence (CMAI'2021). Rather than reporting an empirical study in education, it frames the workshop theme and argues that conceptual modeling and AI can mutually benefit one another. The paper contrasts conceptual modeling’s human-interpretable, explicit, and reproducible representations with AI’s data-driven pattern discovery and black-box predictions, emphasizing complementary strengths and weaknesses.

The paper proposes a research framework that positions conceptual modeling and artificial intelligence orthogonally and defines four research categories: exaptation CMAI, CM-driven CMAI, AI-driven CMAI, and CM- & AI-driven CMAI. It briefly summarizes the invited workshop papers and maps each to this framework, illustrating how conceptual modeling can support machine learning and how AI can contribute to conceptual modeling.

The context is a software engineering / information systems research workshop held with ER 2021, not a K-12 educational intervention. No participant population, implementation setting, or outcome measures are reported. The main conclusion is conceptual and programmatic: the field needs more integrative work that combines explicit modeling with AI methods to improve comprehensibility, development, and application of AI systems.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an editorial preface and workshop overview, not an empirical study. It does not present a research design, sample, or outcome evaluation, so it does not provide evidence meeting research credibility criteria.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No student, teacher, or institutional outcomes are evaluated. The paper is conceptual and descriptive, so there is no measurable impact estimate to classify.

paper_profiles.title: Augmented Computational Design
paper_profiles.venue: Artificial Intelligence in Performance-Driven Design: Theories, Methods, and Tools Towards Sustainability
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This chapter addresses how artificial intelligence can be used in generative design, with a focus on performance-driven architectural and engineering design. The central problem is that design decisions are often numerous, discrete, and interdependent, while desired outcomes are few and high-level; the authors argue that this makes conventional direct reasoning about design space exploration difficult. They propose an “Augmented Computational Design” framework that formalizes design as a pairing of decision space and performance space and distinguishes two dual tasks: mapping many design choices to a small number of outcomes, and navigating backward from desired outcomes to valid design choices.

The proposed approach is largely theoretical and mathematical. It draws on multi-variate calculus, Jacobian approximation, singular value decomposition, and pseudo-inverse reasoning to describe how data-driven models can support both evaluation and derivation in design. The paper also situates several AI methods along a spectrum of generative design approaches, focusing on statistical AI methods such as probabilistic graphical models, Bayesian Belief Networks, and diffusion-like ideas, while contrasting them with rule-based, optimization-based, and model-driven methods.

To illustrate the framework, the chapter presents a case study from Dutch building energy modelling (NTA 8800). In that example, a surrogate Bayesian Belief Network is trained to approximate an opaque government energy-performance calculation tool using sampled simulations, sensitivity analysis, and discretization of inputs. The illustrative context is architectural and policy-oriented rather than educational, and the chapter concludes that the framework can improve explainability and make complex design-performance relationships more tractable, especially when only a few important outputs must be linked to many design variables.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a conceptual/book-chapter style methodological treatise with an illustrative case study, not a controlled empirical evaluation. The excerpt reports a workflow and claims of feasibility, but no rigorous causal design, no peer-reviewable effect estimates for learner outcomes, and no validated educational experiment.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests practical value for improving the efficiency and interpretability of complex building-energy decision support, but the impact is indirect and not quantified with effect sizes. It is relevant to institutional decision-making, yet the demonstrated gains are methodological rather than measured outcomes.

interventions.use_case: Probabilistic meta-modelling and Bayesian Belief Network (BBN) surrogate modeling for architectural/building energy performance analysis, used to approximate a Dutch government NTA 8800 calculation model from sampled input parameters and sensitivity-selected variables.

finding.finding_summary: The chapter argues that an AI-based surrogate model can make building energy performance assessment faster and more tractable than the original NTA 8800 Excel tool, which only handles one scenario at a time and is not traceable to inputs. The demonstration uses 20,000 Sobol-sampled simulations and then reduces 269 inputs to 15 influential parameters, with those 15 explaining about 90.45% to 92.30% of the final energy performance score; however, no formal effect size or validation metric values are reported in the excerpt.
finding.measure: Computational feasibility, sensitivity-reduced input dimensionality, and surrogate-model approximation quality (NRMSE, MAPE mentioned but values not reported)

finding.finding_summary: The chapter presents the AI surrogate as useful for policy analysis and building-energy governance, especially for advising on subsidy policy, building-code compliance, and energy transition planning in the Netherlands. It frames the BBN meta-model as a way to support institutional decision-making by translating a complex regulatory calculation tool into a more usable, interpretable approximation, but it does not report experimental policy effects.
finding.measure: Policy-analysis utility and governance applicability of the surrogate model

paper_profiles.title: The Future of Embodied Design for Mathematics Teaching and Learning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses how embodied cognition can inform the design of mathematics teaching and learning, with emphasis on technologies and pedagogies that connect physical action, gesture, perception, and mathematical reasoning. Rather than presenting a single intervention study, it surveys and synthesizes research programs that link embodiment to STEM learning and proposes design principles for future mathematics education.

The article organizes prior work into six related research programs: embodied design, action–cognition transduction, gesture and multimodality, graspable math, playful learning, and embodiment perspectives on teacher education. Across these programs, the authors discuss interactive tools such as the Mathematics Imagery Trainer, gesture-supported instruction, collaborative embodied activities, and AI-embedded tutoring that responds to student movement and speech. Examples are drawn largely from mathematics learning, especially ratio, probability, slope, geometry, and algebra.

The paper’s central conclusion is that conceptual learning can be supported when students first engage in meaningful sensorimotor action or gesture and then connect those actions to formal mathematical representations and language. It argues that movement can both ground mathematical ideas and actively change cognition, and that collaborative, multimodal, and AI-supported environments may extend these benefits. The authors position embodied design as a broad theory-to-practice framework for future research and educational practice rather than as an evaluation of one discrete program.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed theoretical/design-synthesis paper rather than an empirical evaluation of a K-12 intervention. It cites multiple empirical studies, but the paper itself does not provide a primary controlled study with its own outcome estimates.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The article argues for potentially meaningful instructional implications and summarizes several positive effect sizes from prior work, but the paper itself does not demonstrate direct impact from a single evaluated intervention. Its contribution is mainly conceptual and programmatic rather than evidence of measured population-level impact.

finding.finding_summary: This paper is a theoretical and design-synthesis article on embodied mathematics learning, not a direct outcome study, but it summarizes prior empirical findings relevant to mathematical reasoning. It reports that directed body movements in high school students produced greater learning gains than comparable non-body-based activities on understanding mathematical similarity (F(1,162)=56.4, p<0.05, η2=0.04), and that geometry proof performance improved with directed actions in a study of n=120 (d=0.62, p<0.05).
finding.measure: Understanding of mathematical similarity; geometry proof performance; mathematical insight and intuition in geometry

finding.finding_summary: Scientific-reasoning relevance appears indirectly through the paper’s discussion of embodied cognition and model-based reasoning, but the empirical evidence summarized is primarily mathematics-focused rather than science-specific. The article cites action-to-cognition and gesture research as potentially supporting inference making and reasoning, but does not report a direct K-12 science outcome estimate in this paper.
finding.measure: Model-based reasoning / inference making as discussed in relation to embodied cognition

finding.finding_summary: The paper synthesizes evidence that collaborative gesture and multimodal interaction can support communication, common ground, and co-construction of ideas during problem solving. Although it is not a direct intervention trial, the cited studies suggest benefits for collaboration and shared sense-making, including collaborative gesturing across multiple bodies in mathematics reasoning tasks.
finding.measure: Collaborative sense-making, common ground, and multimodal co-construction during problem solving

paper_profiles.title: Nature Experiences in Science Education in School: Review Featuring Learning Gains, Investments, and Costs in View of Embodied Cognition
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper reviews research on the use of nature experiences in science education in primary and secondary school, with a particular focus on how these experiences relate to embodied cognition. The review asks how nature experiences are used in science teaching, which natural phenomena or topics appear especially suitable, and what challenges arise when teaching science outdoors or in other natural settings.

Using a systematised search across international databases, the author screened thousands of records and retained 114 peer-reviewed studies, including 34 empirical studies that examined facilitative effects of nature experiences on science learning. The review includes studies from multiple countries and covers interventions ranging from single-day field trips to multi-week or multi-year outdoor programs. Populations were mainly pupils aged 7–16 years in elementary, middle, and high school settings.

The review finds that nature-based science experiences can support content knowledge, understanding of scientific methods, environmental attitudes, and pro-environmental behavior, with some evidence of lasting retention when activities are well designed and repeated over time. It also notes that interventions using schoolyards, school gardens, nearby parks, and citizen science can be promising because they combine authentic experience with relatively low cost. At the same time, the paper emphasizes practical burdens on teachers, the need for careful didactic planning, and the limited theoretical grounding of much existing work. Overall, the review argues that the field is promising but still underdeveloped, especially regarding clear links between teaching practice and embodied cognition theory.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed narrative/systematised review synthesizing mostly qualitative and quasi-experimental primary studies rather than a single rigorous trial or meta-analysis. The evidence base is informative but heterogeneous, with many studies lacking effect sizes, randomization, or consistent comparison groups.
