finding.finding_summary: Teachers receiving the AT professional learning package showed better implementation and dose-related gains, suggesting improved efficiency in using AT routines and classroom supports. Within the intervention arm, more sessions attended predicted higher posttest scores (b=0.05, SE=0.02, 95% CI [0.01, 0.09], p=.018), indicating a positive dose-response relationship for implementation capacity.
finding.measure: Sessions attended; implementation/teaching-efficacy posttest scores; fidelity logs

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that teachers observed learners becoming more responsive, confident, active, and motivated during lessons when visual, multimodal, and assistive supports were used. These outcomes are qualitative and classroom-based, but consistently framed as improved engagement and participation for students with hearing impairments.
finding.measure: Observed learner engagement, confidence, participation, and responsiveness

finding.finding_summary: The study links the intervention to improved access to English language lessons for students with auditory impairments, with better comprehension and participation in classroom discussion. The evidence is qualitative rather than standardized-test based, and no student-level effect size is reported.
finding.measure: English language lesson participation and comprehension; classroom responsiveness

paper_profiles.title: 3DG: A Framework for Using Generative AI for Handling Sparse Learner Performance Data From Intelligent Tutoring Systems
paper_profiles.venue: LAK’24: International Workshop on Generative AI for Learning Analytics (GenAI-LA)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of sparse learner performance data in intelligent tutoring systems (ITSs), where missing quiz scores, attempts, and other interaction records can weaken learner modeling and knowledge tracing. The authors propose 3DG (3-Dimensional tensor for Densification and Generation), a framework that combines tensor factorization for data imputation with generative models for data augmentation.

The approach represents learner-ITS interaction data as a three-dimensional tensor with dimensions for learners, questions, and attempts. The tensor is first completed using factorization-based imputation, then clustered by inferred learning patterns, and finally expanded using generative models. The paper compares GAN and GPT-4 for simulation of additional learning-performance data, using a dataset from an AutoTutor reading-comprehension lesson developed for the Center for the Study of Adult Literacy (CSAL) with 118 participants.

The main conclusion is that the framework can densify sparse performance data and generate scalable synthetic samples that preserve individual learning-pattern structure. In the reported comparisons, GAN produced more reliable and narrower distributions of simulated parameters than GPT-4, suggesting better suitability for numerical simulation of sparse ITS performance data. The paper emphasizes that this work is a methodological framework rather than an educational intervention study.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed workshop/framework paper with a clear computational method and dataset, but it is not a causal study of educational outcomes. The evidence is methodological and descriptive rather than an RCT, QED, or meta-analysis.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper shows a potentially useful data-sparsity solution for ITS analytics, but it does not demonstrate learner outcome gains with effect sizes. Its impact on education is therefore promising but currently unclear and indirect.

interventions.use_case: Methodological framework for handling sparse learner performance data collected from an AutoTutor intelligent tutoring system lesson (reading comprehension) by imputing missing responses and augmenting learner-attempt traces for modeling and simulation.
Tensor factorization and generative AI framework for simulating sparse educational performance data; compares GAN and GPT-4 as data-generation models for ITS logs.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that tensor completion via tensor factorization efficiently imputed missing values in sparse ITS performance data, reducing sparsity from 80%–85% in the AutoTutor dataset and enabling denser learner models. This is presented as improving the feasibility and scalability of analysis/modeling, but no learner achievement effect sizes were reported (n=118).
finding.measure: Data sparsity reduction / successful imputation of missing performance entries in ITS logs

finding.finding_summary: Comparing generative approaches for simulation, GAN produced more reliable synthetic learner-performance distributions than GPT-4. The paper does not report a numeric effect size, but qualitatively notes that GAN yielded a narrower and more consistent range for the latent learning-curve parameters a and b, indicating better reliability for scalable simulation.
finding.measure: Reliability/consistency of simulated parameter distributions (a, b) for synthetic learner performance data
finding.study_size: n=118 (real dataset); simulation samples up to 20,000

finding.finding_summary: The paper applies the framework to an AutoTutor reading comprehension lesson from the Center for the Study of Adult Literacy, but it evaluates data reconstruction and simulation rather than reading learning gains. Thus, it is relevant to literacy only as the modeled domain, with no direct evidence of improved reading outcomes or effect sizes reported.
finding.measure: Reading comprehension performance data used for modeling

paper_profiles.title: DeBiasMe: De-biasing Human-AI Interactions with Metacognitive AIED (AI in Education) Interventions
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of Workshop: AI Augmented Reasoning (CHI ’25)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This position paper addresses a gap in AI literacy and human-AI interaction research: most existing educational tools focus on algorithmic or dataset bias, while giving less attention to human cognitive biases such as anchoring, confirmation bias, and automation bias. The author argues that as generative AI becomes embedded in academic work, students need support not only to use AI effectively but also to critically evaluate how their own reasoning and prompting behaviors can amplify bias.

The paper proposes DeBiasMe, a metacognitive AIED intervention designed around two main design ideas: deliberate friction and bi-directional human-AI collaboration. Deliberate friction introduces intentional pauses and reflective prompts into the workflow, while the bi-directional framework targets both the input stage (prompt formulation) and output stage (interpretation of AI responses). The prototype includes a prompt refinement tool and a bias visualization map that surface possible biases and encourage reflection, explanation, and mitigation.

The population and context are university students using generative AI in academic settings. The paper reports work-in-progress and prior mixed-methods user research with university students that informed the design, but it is not an evaluative outcome study. Its main conclusion is that effective AI literacy tools should go beyond technical competencies and explicitly cultivate metacognitive awareness, bias recognition, and adaptive scaffolding for diverse user engagement patterns.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a position paper/prototype description with no controlled evaluation, no experimental design, and no inferential outcome evidence. It is peer-reviewed workshop material, but it does not meet empirical credibility criteria for K-12 intervention evidence.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The proposed intervention could plausibly affect learner metacognition and AI use, but the paper reports no measurable impact or effect sizes. Its influence is therefore theoretical and currently unclear rather than demonstrated.

interventions.use_case: Metacognitive AI literacy intervention for university students interacting with generative AI/LLMs, including prompt refinement and post-response bias interpretation to reduce human-AI biases.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that the DeBiasMe intervention is designed to improve students’ metacognitive skills, especially awareness of bias, monitoring of reasoning, and critical engagement with AI. In the illustrative prototype and prior mixed-methods user research with university students, the tool was reported to make implicit human and AI biases explicit and actionable, but no quantitative effect sizes were reported.
finding.measure: Metacognitive support needs, bias awareness, critical thinking, and reflective engagement in AI interactions (survey/interview-based formative evaluation)

finding.finding_summary: The paper positions DeBiasMe as a bridge between academic integrity policies and students’ everyday AI use, and argues it could inform policy recommendations for frictional design and AI literacy frameworks. This is a conceptual/position contribution rather than an outcomes study, so no quantitative institutional effect estimates are reported.
finding.measure: Policy and institutional implications for AI literacy, academic integrity, and responsible innovation

paper_profiles.title: Tutor CoPilot: A Human-AI Approach for Scaling Real-Time Expertise
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses whether a human-AI system can improve the quality and effectiveness of live K-12 tutoring by giving novice tutors real-time, expert-like guidance. The core problem is that novice educators often lack access to expensive expert coaching, which can limit the quality of instruction and particularly disadvantage students from under-served communities.

The intervention, Tutor CoPilot, is a language-model-based system integrated into a virtual tutoring platform. When tutors activate it during a session, it generates context-sensitive suggestions using the lesson topic, chat context, and a selected pedagogical strategy. The system was developed using a method that extracts expert reasoning from think-aloud data and adapts it for live use. Tutors could edit, regenerate, or switch strategies, so the tool functioned as a decision-support aid rather than an automated tutor.

The study was a randomized controlled trial with 900 tutors and 1,800 K-12 students in grades 3-8 from Title I schools in a large U.S. Southern school district, delivered through an in-school virtual tutoring program for mathematics. The paper finds that students whose tutors had access to Tutor CoPilot were 4 percentage points more likely to pass exit tickets, with larger gains for students working with lower-rated or less-experienced tutors. Text analysis of more than 550,000 messages suggests that treatment tutors used more high-quality pedagogical strategies, such as prompting explanation and asking guiding questions, and fewer answer-giving strategies. Tutors reported that the system was helpful but sometimes produced suggestions that were not well aligned to grade level.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a preregistered randomized controlled trial with tutor-level random assignment, a large sample, and clear outcome measures, which strongly supports causal inference. There are some relevance and implementation caveats, but the design is high quality for K-12 intervention evidence.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The main academic effect is modest but meaningful for a priority population: a 4 percentage point increase in exit-ticket mastery, with larger gains for lower-rated tutors (up to 9 points). This suggests practical promise, though the outcome is proximal and the longer-term test-score effects were not significant.

interventions.use_case: Human-AI real-time tutoring support that generates expert-like pedagogical suggestions for live K-12 math tutors during tutoring sessions, including hints, guiding questions, worked examples, and strategy selection to improve tutor responses.

finding.finding_summary: In a randomized controlled trial with 1,800 K-12 students and 4,136 tutoring sessions, students whose tutors had access to Tutor CoPilot were 4 percentage points more likely to pass their exit tickets (62% to 66%, p<0.01). Conditional on attempting the exit ticket, students were 3 percentage points more likely to pass (p<0.01), indicating improved proximal math mastery.
finding.measure: Exit ticket pass rate; exit ticket attempted; conditional exit ticket pass rate

finding.finding_summary: Student survey outcomes showed no statistically significant effects on perceived tutor care, confidence in learning math, or session ratings. Estimated treatment effects were small and mixed (e.g., -0.004 to 0.03 on 5-point survey items) and were not significant.
finding.measure: Post-session student survey responses (e.g., tutor cared about understanding, confidence learning math, preference for understanding over memorizing, session rating, tutor rating)

finding.finding_summary: Treatment tutors were more likely to use strategies associated with deeper understanding, such as prompting students to explain and asking questions to guide thinking. The paper reports these strategies were used approximately 2 standard deviations more frequently on a log-odds scale in treatment sessions, compared with control sessions.
finding.measure: NLP-classified tutoring strategy use in 550,000+ chat messages
finding.effect_size: ~2 SD on log-odds scale for key high-quality strategies

finding.finding_summary: The system was inexpensive to deploy, with an estimated annual cost of $20 per tutor based on observed usage patterns. The intervention is positioned as a scalable alternative to traditional professional development, and tutors reported that it reduced the effort needed to generate appropriate instructional language in real time.
finding.measure: Estimated annual cost per tutor; tutor-reported usability/effort
finding.study_size: n=900 tutors assigned; cost estimate based on usage

paper_profiles.title: Using Large Language Models to Assess Tutors’ Performance in Reacting to Students Making Math Errors
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of Machine Learning Research (AAAI 2024 Workshop AI4ED)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether large language models can be used to evaluate tutor performance in responding to students’ math errors. The authors focus on a tutoring skill called “Reacting to Errors,” which emphasizes praising effort, motivating students, indirectly guiding them to notice mistakes, keeping feedback immediate, and ensuring feedback is sincere and mathematically accurate. They compare GPT-3.5-Turbo and GPT-4 on their ability to score these criteria from tutor-student dialogues.

The study uses 50 real tutoring dialogues from online math tutoring sessions. The tutors were college students at a Pennsylvania university, and the tutees were middle school students in grades 6–8 from two schools. Tutoring occurred remotely through Pencil, and the dataset included dialogues from schools with low math proficiency; school-level demographics were described, but student-level demographics were not available. The authors also used GPT-4 to generate synthetic dialogues to calibrate human annotation and establish inter-rater reliability for the rubric.

Results show that both GPT models can assess several tutor-response criteria reasonably well, especially immediate and accurate feedback, but they struggle more with process-focused and indirect responses. A major limitation is that both models have difficulty identifying whether a student actually made an error; GPT-4 performs somewhat better than GPT-3.5-Turbo but also tends to infer errors from student uncertainty. The authors conclude that GPT-3.5-Turbo may be sufficient for scalable dialogue assessment, while GPT-4 offers only modest gains at substantially higher cost, and they call for larger datasets and future work on learning transfer after tutor training.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed workshop paper using a small observational corpus and human comparison, but it is not an experimental study of learning effects. The methodology is clear, yet it primarily evaluates model scoring performance rather than educational impact.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests practical scalability benefits for tutor evaluation, but it does not measure student learning gains or produce effect sizes on educational outcomes. Impact on K-12 learning is therefore indirect and currently unclear.

interventions.use_case: Using GPT-3.5-Turbo and GPT-4 to assess tutor responses in math-error tutoring dialogues, including judging whether a student made an error and whether the tutor’s response was process-focused, motivating, indirect, immediate, and accurate.

finding.finding_summary: The paper finds that LLMs can automate scoring of tutor responses in real tutoring transcripts, suggesting a scalable alternative to time-consuming human annotation. On 50 real-life dialogues, GPT-3.5-Turbo and GPT-4 both performed adequately on several criteria, with GPT-4 generally stronger; however, this is an assessment task rather than a learning outcome.
finding.measure: F1, precision, and recall for scoring tutor response criteria; accuracy in identifying whether a student made an error

paper_profiles.title: Iris: An AI-Driven Virtual Tutor For Computer Science Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of how to provide scalable, personalized support for programming learners in large computer science courses. The authors argue that general-purpose chatbots often give complete solutions and lack access to course-specific context, which makes them less suitable for educational use.

To address this, they introduce Iris, a chat-based virtual tutor integrated into the Artemis learning platform. Iris is designed to support programming exercises by using GPT-3.5-Turbo with a role-defined prompt, few-shot examples, chain-of-thought processing, context from the student’s code and exercise description, and a self-check to avoid giving full solutions. It aims to offer subtle hints, counter-questions, and calibrated assistance rather than direct answers.

The evaluation was an online survey of students enrolled in three CS1-level introductory courses at the Technical University of Munich. Only students who had sent at least ten messages to Iris were included in the analysis. The study found generally positive student perceptions: Iris was seen as understandable, helpful, engaging, and comfortable to ask without judgment. Students viewed it mainly as a complement to human tutors rather than a replacement, and they reported more confidence relying on their own skills during exams without Iris. The paper concludes that context-aware AI tutoring can be a useful supplementary tool in programming education, while also noting the need for further work on context integration, model quality, and effects on learning outcomes.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed survey-based evaluation with clear methodology, but it is observational and self-reported rather than experimental. It provides useful descriptive evidence of user perceptions, yet does not measure causal learning effects or subgroup differences.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The study suggests positive perceived support and comfort, but it reports no objective achievement gains and no effect sizes. The impact on learning outcomes is therefore promising but unclear and likely modest based on the available evidence.

interventions.use_case: chat-based virtual tutor integrated into the Artemis programming platform to provide context-aware, calibrated hints and counter-questions for CS1 programming exercises using GPT-3.5-Turbo

finding.finding_summary: Students reported broadly positive perceptions of Iris’s support and affective safety. In the survey of students who used Iris at least 10 times (n=121 respondents; 221 users engaged overall), 60% found the interactions engaging, 92% felt comfortable asking questions without worrying about being judged, and 62% felt safe asking questions they would not ask a tutor or professor.
finding.measure: Likert-scale survey on engagement, comfort, and perceived safety (Q4, Q6, Q7)

finding.finding_summary: Students generally perceived Iris as helping their understanding of programming concepts and their problem-solving process. In the survey (n=121), 50% agreed that Iris improved their understanding of programming concepts, 44% said it directly helped with exercise issues, and 43% said solving exercises would be more challenging without it.
finding.measure: Likert-scale survey on perceived conceptual understanding, helpfulness, and reliance (Q2, Q3, Q10)

finding.finding_summary: The paper evaluates perceived usefulness for computer science programming exercises rather than objective achievement. Among surveyed users (n=121), 46% agreed Iris understands queries well, 44% agreed it provides direct help, and 50% agreed it improves understanding, but substantial neutral/disagree responses remained, indicating uneven perceived effectiveness.
finding.measure: Likert-scale survey of perceived tutor effectiveness and usefulness for programming exercises (Q1, Q2, Q3)

paper_profiles.title: Generative AI and Its Impact on Personalized Intelligent Tutoring Systems
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how generative AI, especially large language models such as GPT-4, can be integrated into intelligent tutoring systems (ITS) to enable more personalized and adaptive learning. The central problem addressed is how generative AI can improve the flexibility, responsiveness, and engagement of ITS beyond traditional rule-based or static content approaches.

The paper discusses several AI-supported tutoring functions, including automated question generation, personalized feedback, and interactive dialogue systems. These capabilities are presented as ways to tailor learning materials, hints, and explanations to individual learner needs in real time. The paper also emphasizes key implementation challenges, such as maintaining pedagogical accuracy, mitigating bias, and sustaining learner engagement.

The article is conceptual rather than empirical: it synthesizes prior literature and examples of emerging applications across educational contexts, including school-level questioning, mathematics support, and language learning. Its main conclusion is that generative AI has strong potential to transform ITS into more adaptive, equitable, and engaging tools, but realizing that potential will require careful validation, bias mitigation, and ethical governance.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a narrative/report-style conceptual paper, not an empirical study. It does not report a systematic method, sample, or causal/comparative evaluation of learner outcomes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No measurable educational impact is reported. The paper argues for potential benefits of generative AI in ITS, but provides no effect sizes or outcome evidence.

interventions.use_case: Conceptual review of integrating generative AI/LLMs such as GPT-4 into intelligent tutoring systems for personalized question generation, real-time feedback, and interactive dialogue tutoring.
Personalized tutoring systems that adapt instructional content, hints, and dialogue to individual learner needs using AI-driven generation rather than fixed rule-based materials.

paper_profiles.title: CourseAssist: Pedagogically Appropriate AI Tutor for Computer Science Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the challenge of using large language models (LLMs) as tutoring tools in computer science education without encouraging overreliance, inaccurate code generation, or responses that conflict with course learning goals. The authors argue that generic LLMs such as GPT-4 are not sufficiently pedagogically aligned for student support in programming courses, and that educationally appropriate behavior should be a core evaluation criterion for AI tutors.

To address this, they introduce CourseAssist, an LLM-based tutoring system built on GPT-4 with retrieval-augmented generation, user-intent classification, and question decomposition. These mechanisms are designed to connect answers to specific course materials and to adapt responses to different kinds of student questions, with the goal of giving hints and guidance rather than direct solutions when appropriate. The system is presented as a harm-reduction approach rather than a ban on student use of LLMs.

The paper evaluates CourseAssist on 50 question-answer pairs drawn from Piazza posts in a programming languages course at a large public university. A course instructor rated generated responses on usefulness, accuracy, and pedagogical appropriateness, and CourseAssist outperformed baseline GPT-4 on all three criteria. The system was also deployed in six computer science courses at the institution, and interviews with 20 student users suggested that it improved access to course-specific help and shortened the feedback loop on programming assignments.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a small-scale poster/report with a human evaluation and interviews, not a controlled student learning study. The methodology is useful but mostly qualitative/benchmark-based rather than a rigorous causal design.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported gains are modest-to-clear for response quality and tutoring utility, but they are not direct learning gains and lack effect sizes on student achievement. Impact on real courses is promising, yet the evidence is early-stage and limited to a small evaluation set.

interventions.use_case: CourseAssist, a GPT-4-based AI tutor for computer science education that uses retrieval-augmented generation, user intent classification, and question decomposition to provide course-specific hints and answers aligned with learning objectives.

finding.finding_summary: CourseAssist outperformed baseline GPT-4 on a 50-question human evaluation from a programming languages course. Average instructor ratings were higher for usefulness (0.91 vs 0.83), accuracy (0.92 vs 0.71), and pedagogical appropriateness (1.00 vs 0.82), indicating stronger CS tutoring quality overall.
finding.measure: Instructor human ratings of usefulness, accuracy, and pedagogical appropriateness on 50 QA pairs

finding.finding_summary: Interviews with 20 student users suggested CourseAssist shortened the feedback loop on programming assignments and increased access to course-specific tutoring help. The paper reports deployment in 6 CS courses reaching over 500 students, but does not provide a quantitative effect size for efficiency.
finding.measure: Student interviews and deployment reach/usage context

paper_profiles.title: Meaningful human control: actionable properties for AI system development
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the gap between philosophical theories of meaningful human control and practical AI system design. The authors ask how humans can remain in control of AI-based systems that act autonomously, especially when those systems create responsibility gaps, opaque decision-making, or undesirable consequences. Rather than presenting an empirical study, the paper develops a design-oriented framework meant to help researchers, designers, and engineers operationalize meaningful human control.

The proposed approach identifies four actionable properties for AI systems: an explicit moral operational design domain (moral ODD), appropriate and mutually compatible human/AI representations, sufficient ability and authority for relevant humans and AI agents to control the system, and explicit links between AI actions and human decisions made with moral awareness. These properties are illustrated with two non-education case scenarios: automated vehicles and AI-based hiring. The paper also discusses concrete methods and tools that could support each property, such as ontology modeling, co-active design, shared control, explainability, and value hierarchies.

The paper is theoretical and does not involve a participant population, intervention trial, or educational setting. Its main conclusion is that meaningful human control can be made more actionable by treating it as a set of system-level design properties spanning technical, social, and organizational elements. The authors argue these properties are necessary, though not sufficient, for meaningful human control and should be complemented by broader AI ethics and transdisciplinary design practices.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a conceptual/design framework paper, not an empirical study of an educational intervention. It proposes actionable properties for meaningful human control and illustrates them with non-education case scenarios, but does not present a clear research design, sample, or outcome data.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No student, teacher, or school outcome is measured, so there is no direct educational impact to assess. The paper is relevant conceptually for AI governance, but it does not demonstrate measured impact on K-12 learning or implementation outcomes.

paper_profiles.title: AI for Open Science: A Multi-Agent Perspective for Ethically Translating Data to Knowledge
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the ethical and practical problem of how AI for Science (AI4Science) systems, especially self-driving labs and other end-to-end discovery systems, can obscure human collaboration and reduce openness in scientific knowledge translation. The authors argue that existing discussions of responsible AI have focused on security, interpretability, and deployment, but have not sufficiently considered openness as a core requirement for scientific discovery systems.

To address this, the paper proposes AI for Open Science (AI4OS), a multi-agent discovery support framing that extends AI4Science by emphasizing open exchange of data, information, knowledge, and provenance across experimenting, data-mining, and labeling agents. The framework formalizes these roles using concepts from Knowledge Discovery and Data Mining (KDD) and introduces a theoretical openness metric intended to capture how well knowledge is translated when provenance is shared across agents.

The paper is entirely theoretical and does not report an empirical study with a participant population. Its context is scientific research infrastructure and AI-driven discovery systems rather than K-12 education. The main conclusion is that openness, transparency, and provenance sharing are ethically necessary to prevent closed AI systems from concentrating benefits within a single organization and to improve the alignment of derived knowledge with ground truth.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a theoretical/position paper about AI for Open Science and knowledge translation, not an empirical evaluation of a K-12 educational intervention. It does not present a study design, participants, or measured learning outcomes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper has no direct measured impact on student outcomes or school operations. Its contribution is conceptual and ethical, so it does not provide evidence of educational effect size or implementation impact.

paper_profiles.title: Need of AI in Modern Education: in the Eyes of Explainable AI (xAI)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This book chapter argues that modern education is increasingly shaped by AI, but that the use of complex AI systems raises major concerns about transparency, interpretability, fairness, and access. The central question is not an intervention study in classrooms, but whether explainable AI methods can help surface how AI systems make decisions and whether those decisions are biased, especially when educational opportunity is linked to family socioeconomic status.

To explore this, the authors use the Adult Census Income dataset as a proxy for parental income and train an XGBoost classifier to predict whether an individual earns more than USD 50K. They then apply several explainability and debugging tools, including permutation importance, SHAP, LIME, surrogate decision trees, and FairML, to compare feature importance and inspect local and global explanations. The paper frames parental income as a key factor in children’s educational access, but the empirical work itself is on a general adult income prediction problem rather than K-12 learners.

The main conclusion is that common feature-importance methods can miss important biases that fairness-oriented tools reveal. The authors report that FairML exposes dependence on sensitive attributes such as race, nationality, and sex, suggesting that the model’s predictions encode unfair patterns. They argue that explainability alone is insufficient unless paired with fairness analysis, and they call for more transparent, accountable, and bias-aware AI systems in education policy and decision-making.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a conceptual/book-chapter style analysis with illustrative model audits, not a controlled empirical study in K-12 education. It does not evaluate a learner intervention, does not use a design capable of causal inference about educational outcomes, and relies on a non-educational Adult Census dataset.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper does not report learner impact or measurable educational gains; it focuses on model interpretability and fairness concerns. Any implications for education policy are speculative and indirect, so there is no demonstrated positive impact on K-12 outcomes.

interventions.use_case: Explainable AI / post-hoc model interpretability and fairness auditing for educational decision-making, using LIME, SHAP, permutation importance, surrogate decision trees, and FairML on an Adult Census Income dataset to reason about bias in access-related predictions.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that AI in education can improve transparency and policy decision-making, but its empirical analysis shows substantial fairness concerns in model explanations and predictions. Using Adult Census Income data, the authors report that FairML exposes dependence on sensitive attributes such as race, nationality, and sex, while SHAP and LIME do not consistently surface these biases; no effect size is reported because this is a model-auditing study rather than a learner-outcome experiment.
finding.measure: Model fairness/bias diagnostics from feature-importance and post-hoc explanation methods (FairML, SHAP, LIME, permutation importance) applied to an XGBoost classifier

paper_profiles.title: Advancing Education through Tutoring Systems: A Systematic Literature Review
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how tutoring systems have evolved and what AI, engagement, and ethical features characterize modern Intelligent Tutoring Systems (ITS) and Robot Tutoring Systems (RTS). Rather than testing a single intervention, it systematically reviews the literature on tutoring systems in education, with particular attention to how AI techniques such as Bayesian Knowledge Tracing, large language models, and robotics support personalized, adaptive learning.

Using a PRISMA-guided search, the authors screened studies from the early 1970s through 2024 and included 86 representative papers. The review organizes tutoring systems into three latent classes: computer-based ITS, verbal robot-based systems, and multimodal systems. Across these categories, the paper compares adaptability, interaction modes, feedback, appearance, scalability, and ethical concerns.

The review concludes that AI-powered tutoring systems can improve personalization, engagement, and learning outcomes, with software-based ITS generally stronger in cognitive adaptivity and robot-based systems stronger in social/emotional engagement. It also finds persistent challenges around data privacy, bias, scalability, and the limits of robotic cognitive adaptability. The authors argue for hybrid systems that combine the strengths of ITS and RTS while adopting stronger responsible-AI safeguards.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a systematic literature review with PRISMA methods and latent class analysis, so it has a clear methodology and peer-reviewed scholarly framing. However, it is not a primary causal study and does not report pooled meta-analytic effects, limiting causal credibility for K-12 impact claims.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests broadly positive effects on learning, engagement, and scalability, but it provides no quantitative overall effect size and many claims are synthesized at a high level. Its practical impact is therefore plausible but unclear in magnitude for K-12 populations.

interventions.use_case: Systematic review of classical and AI-driven intelligent tutoring systems, including adaptive tutoring based on Bayesian Knowledge Tracing, student modeling, and personalized feedback for K-12 and broader educational contexts
Systematic review of robot tutoring systems and social/embodied tutors that use gestures, verbal feedback, and physical presence to support student engagement and learning
Review of newer generative AI and chatbot-style tutoring systems that provide conversational, context-aware feedback and adaptive explanations
Review of systems that adapt difficulty, pacing, and content based on student performance without necessarily functioning as full dialogue tutors
Historical review of early computer-assisted instruction systems as predecessors to modern tutoring systems

finding.finding_summary: This is a systematic literature review of 86 studies, and it concludes that tutoring systems generally show significant advancements that enhance adaptability and learning outcomes. The paper does not report a pooled effect size, but it repeatedly characterizes ITS and RTS as improving academic performance through personalized and adaptive instruction.
finding.measure: Learning outcomes, academic achievement, and performance gains reported across included studies

finding.finding_summary: The review finds that robot-based tutoring systems consistently support student motivation, emotional engagement, and social interaction, especially through gestures, verbal encouragement, and human-like presence. No pooled effect size is reported, but the paper emphasizes that RTS can increase willingness to participate and sustain engagement in ways that purely software-based systems often do not.
finding.measure: Motivation, engagement, emotional and social interaction, willingness to participate

finding.finding_summary: The review reports that computer-based ITS mainly support cognitive engagement through adaptive feedback, but they are less effective than robot-based systems for social-emotional engagement. This is presented as a comparative pattern across studies rather than a quantified estimate.
finding.measure: Engagement and motivation observed in reviewed tutoring system studies

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that software-based tutoring systems are easier to deploy and scale than robot-based systems because they rely on existing digital infrastructure and have lower hardware requirements. This is a review-level conclusion; it does not provide a numerical estimate of productivity or cost reduction.
finding.measure: Scalability, deployment ease, and hardware requirements

finding.finding_summary: Robot-based tutoring systems are described as facing substantial scalability and deployment barriers due to the need for physical hardware, maintenance, and infrastructure. The review does not quantify the burden, but it clearly frames these systems as less operationally efficient than software-based ITS.
finding.measure: Scalability and deployment complexity

finding.finding_summary: A major finding of the review is that AI-powered tutoring systems raise persistent ethical and governance concerns, including data privacy, algorithmic bias, transparency, and equitable access. The paper notes that many studies lack robust privacy protections while also proposing mitigation strategies such as encryption, access controls, fairness-aware algorithms, and oversight committees.
finding.measure: Ethical concern classification, privacy/security practices, and responsible AI governance considerations

paper_profiles.title: GREX-PLUS Science Book v1
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a science book / mission concept document for GREX-PLUS (Galaxy Reionization EXplorer and PLanetary Universe Spectrometer), a proposed cryogenic space telescope for JAXA’s strategic L-class program. It lays out the scientific motivation for the mission, emphasizing two broad aims: extragalactic science (especially the discovery of the first galaxies, the study of cosmic reionization, early black holes, dusty AGNs, and other high-redshift populations) and galactic/planetary science (including protoplanetary disk snowlines, interstellar molecules, exoplanet and Solar System atmospheres, and small bodies).

The paper describes the proposed instrumentation: a 1.2 m telescope cooled to 50 K, a wide-field imager covering 2–8 µm, and a high-resolution spectrometer covering 10–18 µm with resolving power around 30,000. It argues that the wide-field camera would enable deep, wide-area surveys capable of finding rare bright galaxies at very high redshift, while the spectrometer would enable velocity-resolved molecular studies impossible or difficult from the ground because of atmospheric absorption.

The intended scientific context is not a human participant study but an astronomy mission design and review document. For the extragalactic program, the paper highlights surveys of early galaxies, high-redshift quasars, submillimeter galaxies, and dusty AGNs; for the planetary program, it emphasizes locating water snowlines in protoplanetary disks and studying molecular lines in planetary and interstellar environments. The main conclusion is that GREX-PLUS would fill an observational niche not covered by existing or planned facilities, producing legacy data of broad importance for astronomy and astrophysics.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a mission science book / white paper describing a proposed space telescope and its anticipated astronomy applications, not an empirical K-12 study. It contains no evaluative research design, no student outcomes, and no intervention testing.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: There is no measured educational impact on K-12 learners or institutions. The paper is unrelated to science inquiry supports in schooling and provides no evidence of effects by grade band, achievement, language background, or disability status.

paper_profiles.title: AI-Infused Collaborative Inquiry in Upper Elementary School: A Game-Based Learning Approach
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the challenge of introducing AI learning experiences into K-12 education, with a particular focus on the elementary grades where there is very limited prior work. The authors ask how to create engaging upper-elementary learning experiences that integrate AI and life science, and how to support teachers in bringing these experiences into their classrooms.

The intervention/approach is PRIMARYAI, a game-based learning environment designed for upper elementary students. It combines inquiry-based science, problem-based learning, and block-based programming so students can learn AI concepts such as classification, machine learning, perception, and semi-autonomous navigation while solving an ecology problem about declining yellow-eyed penguin populations. The game is designed for collaborative small-group work in class and is grounded in NGSS and the K-12 Computer Science Framework.

The paper also reports a co-design component with three elementary STEM coaches in the Midwestern United States. The teachers participated in semi-structured interviews about their experience, confidence, and support needs related to computer science and AI. The qualitative findings suggest that teachers see AI as important but need substantial professional development, especially around AI content knowledge, plus grade-level-appropriate materials and follow-up classroom support. The paper concludes that combining AI-infused game-based learning with teacher support may be a promising way to introduce AI into upper elementary classrooms, but the system remains in development and needs classroom evaluation.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed design/research paper with a small qualitative component (n=3 teacher interviews) and no completed student efficacy evaluation. Methodologically it is useful for understanding implementation and design, but it does not meet RCT/QED standards for impact evidence.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports no measured student impacts yet; its contributions are design-oriented and implementation-focused. Any likely impact is still speculative because the classroom studies and pre/post assessments are only planned.

interventions.use_case: Game-based collaborative inquiry environment (PRIMARYAI) for upper elementary students to learn AI concepts through life-science problem solving, including block-based programming of semi-autonomous robots and classifier-building tasks.

finding.finding_summary: This paper does not report a completed efficacy result for student science learning; instead, it presents the design of PRIMARYAI and plans future pre/post classroom studies to measure AI and life-science learning. The authors state that the environment is intended to support inquiry-based problem solving in ecology/life science, but no effect sizes or outcome data are reported.
finding.measure: Planned pre/post assessments of AI concepts, AI ethics, and life science concepts

finding.finding_summary: No quantitative engagement results are reported, but the paper explicitly proposes measuring behavioral, social, and emotional engagement in future classroom studies of PRIMARYAI. The qualitative teacher interviews suggest the design is intended to be engaging, but evidence is prospective rather than outcome-based.
finding.measure: Planned engagement coding of group work (behavioral, social, emotional engagement)
finding.study_size: n=3 teachers for qualitative needs analysis; student engagement data not yet collected

finding.finding_summary: The paper frames PRIMARYAI as supporting collaboration, problem solving, and hypothesis discussion during group inquiry, but it does not provide student outcome data. The only empirical component is a small qualitative teacher interview study (n=3) indicating that teachers want grade-appropriate, open-ended curricula and professional development to support implementation.
finding.measure: Qualitative interview themes on pedagogical support needs and collaborative inquiry design

finding.finding_summary: The teacher interview findings indicate strong perceived need for AI professional development, curriculum support, and follow-up classroom coaching to enable adoption of AI-infused inquiry lessons in elementary classrooms. This is a qualitative implementation finding rather than a student outcome, with no effect size reported.
finding.measure: Semi-structured teacher interviews on implementation supports and readiness

paper_profiles.title: Influence of AI-driven Inquiry Teaching on Learning Outcomes
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Emerging Technologies in Learning (iJET)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether AI-driven inquiry teaching is associated with improved learning outcomes in higher education. The study frames AI as a support for organizing inquiry activities rather than as the curriculum topic itself, and it breaks inquiry teaching into four components: questioning, evidence acquisition, explanation focusing, and evaluation summary. The author investigates how each component relates to students’ learning outcomes and whether students’ familiarity with AI changes those outcomes.

The intervention/approach is not an implemented classroom experiment with a treatment group; instead, it is a questionnaire-based analysis of students’ perceptions of AI-driven inquiry teaching. The questionnaire was built from prior inquiry-learning instruments and administered to civil aviation students from six universities in China. The sample included 308 valid responses from college students across multiple grades and majors, and the paper reports Cronbach’s alpha, KMO/Bartlett tests, linear regression, and ANOVA.

The study concludes that all four inquiry-teaching components are positively associated with learning outcomes, with explanation focusing showing the strongest statistical effect. It also finds that students with greater familiarity with AI report higher learning outcomes in AI-driven inquiry teaching. Overall, the paper argues that AI can support inquiry pedagogy by helping teachers organize questioning, evidence gathering, explanation, and evaluation, but the evidence is correlational and based on self-reported survey data from a civil aviation context.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed correlational survey study using a questionnaire, reliability/validity checks, and regression/ANOVA, but not an experimental or quasi-experimental design. The claims are based on self-reported perceptions rather than objective achievement measures, so causal credibility is limited.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported associations are statistically significant and positive, but the practical magnitude is unclear because the paper does not provide standard effect sizes and relies on survey data. The findings suggest modest, context-specific benefits in a college civil aviation sample rather than clearly demonstrated generalizable impact.

interventions.use_case: AI-driven inquiry teaching in a civil aviation higher-education context, structured around AI-supported questioning, evidence acquisition, explanation focusing, and evaluation summary within inquiry lessons.

finding.finding_summary: The study reports that AI-driven inquiry teaching was positively associated with learning outcomes, with the four inquiry components of questioning, evidence acquisition, explanation focusing, and evaluation summary showing estimated improvements of 10%, 5%, 1%, and 10%, respectively. The outcome was measured via a 4-item learning-outcome questionnaire in a survey of n=308 valid civil aviation students, and the overall model was significant (F(4,303)=13.061, p=0.000) with adjusted R2=0.936.
finding.measure: Learning outcome questionnaire (Likert-scale survey); regression analysis of AI-driven inquiry components

finding.finding_summary: Students' familiarity with AI was significantly related to learning outcomes, with relatively familiar students reporting higher mean scores than very unfamiliar students (4.52 ± 0.42 vs. 3.95 ± 0.86). The one-way ANOVA found a significant group effect (F=2.682, p=0.032) across five familiarity groups (n=308 valid responses), suggesting that comfort with AI may support engagement or confidence in AI-driven inquiry settings.
finding.measure: Learning outcome scores by self-reported familiarity with AI

paper_profiles.title: Supporting Upper Elementary Students in Learning AI Concepts with Story-Driven Game-Based Learning
paper_profiles.venue: AAAI-24 (Proceedings of the Thirty-Eighth AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how to support upper elementary students in learning core AI concepts through a story-driven, game-based learning environment called PRIMARYAI. The authors are interested in whether a classroom-friendly AI learning experience can engage young students, support learning of AI planning, and help students progress through a scaffolded sequence of tasks that move from using a prebuilt solution to modifying it and then creating one from scratch.

The intervention combines AI and life-science instruction around a narrative in which students investigate why penguin populations are declining on a volcanic island. In the version studied here, students worked through an AI planning quest using a block-based interface to manipulate initial states, possible actions, and goal states for a robot. The quest used a Use-Modify-Create scaffolding framework and was preceded by an unplugged AI planning activity. The study was implemented in fourth-grade classrooms in two rural Midwestern U.S. schools over three weeks, with analysis focusing on 16 students in one class whose gameplay trace data were available.

The study used both quantitative and qualitative evidence, including pre/post tests, gameplay trace logs, and video observation. Results showed significant gains on an AI planning content assessment, strong engagement during gameplay, and evidence that the scaffolded quest design helped students move through the missions. The authors conclude that story-driven game-based learning can effectively support AI learning in elementary settings, while noting that students still needed additional support when transitioning from modifying tasks to creating them independently.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed classroom implementation with pre/post testing, trace data, and qualitative observation, but it is a small uncontrolled study (n=16 analyzed for traces; n=14 for gains) without random assignment or a comparison group. The evidence is promising but primarily descriptive and exploratory.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports a modest positive learning gain on a small sample and encouraging engagement/progression outcomes, but effect magnitude is limited and not enough to establish generalizable impact. The intervention appears useful for a priority population (upper elementary AI learners), yet broader effectiveness remains unclear.

interventions.use_case: story-driven game-based learning environment for upper elementary AI education, using a science inquiry narrative about declining penguin populations and an AI planning quest with block-based interaction
Use-Modify-Create scaffolding framework embedded in the game to support progression from using a prebuilt planning task to modifying and creating AI planning solutions
unplugged introductory AI planning activities and guided classroom curriculum that supports the game-based AI lesson sequence

finding.finding_summary: Students showed significant gains on an AI planning content knowledge assessment after the unit. On the 11-item pre/post test, mean scores increased from 4.36 (SD=1.98) to 5.43 (SD=1.87) for the 14 students with complete data, with a matched-pairs t-test showing t(13)=3.51, p<.01.
finding.measure: AI planning content knowledge pre-test/post-test (11 multiple-choice items)

finding.finding_summary: The qualitative video analysis indicated strong student engagement during gameplay, with students verbalizing progress and enthusiasm (e.g., completing missions) and 8 students raising their hands when asked who had completed all missions. The paper reports active engagement but does not provide a standardized engagement effect size.
finding.measure: Classroom video observations and student behavioral engagement during gameplay

finding.finding_summary: Trace-log analyses suggested the Use-Modify-Create scaffold helped students progress through increasingly difficult AI planning tasks. Completion rates declined across phases but remained substantial: 93.75% completed Use, 66.67% of those completed Modify, and 60% of Modify completers completed Create; Mission 1 and 2 times were strongly correlated (r=0.72), indicating smoother transition after initial interface familiarity.
finding.measure: Mission completion, progression across Use-Modify-Create phases, time spent per mission, and block-move traces
finding.std_deviation: mission time SDs reported in tables but not pooled

paper_profiles.title: Gamifying education: what is known, what is believed and what remains uncertain: a critical review
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper critically reviews empirical and theoretical research on gamification in education, with the goal of separating claims supported by evidence from beliefs and hype. The authors focus on whether gamification improves motivation, engagement, participation, and learning outcomes, and whether the field has developed a systematic understanding of how to use game elements in educational contexts.

The review examines studies published between June 30, 2014 and December 31, 2015, drawing from Google Scholar, ACM Digital Library, IEEE Xplore, and ScienceDirect. It includes 51 empirical papers and 11 theoretical papers, and analyzes them by educational level, subject, learning activity, game elements, study goals, and reported outcomes. The review covers a wide range of settings, including university courses, K-12 classrooms, online learning environments, labs, exercises, discussion forums, projects, and assessments. Most studies used common game elements such as points, badges, leaderboards, and levels, often in combinations rather than in isolation.

The paper concludes that the evidence base is still fragmented and does not yet support strong claims about long-term benefits. Gamification appears to influence engagement and some learning outcomes in certain contexts, but results are mixed and often inconclusive. The authors argue that the field needs more systematic, rigorous studies that isolate the effects of specific game elements, better justify design choices, and distinguish motivational effects from general performance effects.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a critical narrative review of empirical studies, not a meta-analysis or primary experimental study. It provides structured synthesis and methodological critique, but the evidence base is heterogeneous and the review does not report pooled effect estimates.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests possible benefits for motivation and learning, but concludes that evidence is mixed and insufficient for strong claims. Its impact on K-12 practice is therefore unclear rather than demonstrably positive.

interventions.use_case: Critical review of gamification in educational contexts, i.e. adding game design elements such as points, badges, leaderboards, levels, and narrative to learning activities, courses, labs, exercises, and online environments.

finding.finding_summary: This review finds that gamification is primarily studied for motivational and engagement effects, but the empirical evidence is mixed and often inconclusive. Across 51 empirical studies, many report improved engagement, motivation, or participation, but the authors conclude there is insufficient evidence for long-term benefits and that several studies report null or uncertain findings rather than clear positive effects.
finding.measure: Motivation, engagement, participation, retention, and related learner self-reports/behavioral indicators across reviewed studies

finding.finding_summary: The review synthesizes evidence on learning outcomes across gamified educational settings and reports mixed effects on learning performance. Some reviewed studies found improved learning outcomes, retention, or performance, while others found no improvement or inconclusive effects; the paper emphasizes that the field lacks systematic evidence for consistent learning gains.
finding.measure: Learning performance, knowledge acquisition, retention, and course/test outcomes reported in the reviewed studies

paper_profiles.title: Enhancing Information Literacy through Generative AI in the Library Classroom
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This practice article examines how generative AI chatbots can be incorporated into information literacy instruction for early undergraduate students. The authors focus on the pedagogical challenge of teaching students to use AI tools ethically and critically, especially given concerns about hallucinations, lack of attribution, privacy, and overreliance on AI-generated text. Rather than evaluating a single AI system experimentally, the paper argues for aligning AI use with the ACRL Framework for Information Literacy, especially the frames Scholarship as Conversation, Research as Inquiry, and Searching as Strategic Exploration.

The intervention described is the use of Perplexity AI in two instructional designs: a credit-bearing information literacy course at Weber State University and a first-year chemical engineering classroom activity at Pennsylvania State University. In both cases, AI is used as a scaffold for early-stage research: students generate prompts, review AI-produced summaries, inspect cited sources, evaluate credibility, identify additional keywords, and refine questions. The paper also presents two adaptable classroom assignments, one for a more integrated composition-linked course and one for a single-session subject-specific class.

The population is early undergraduate students in U.S. higher education, with librarians and instructors as the primary implementers. The authors conclude that AI can support research skill development when it is used as a conversational, citation-bearing tool that complements rather than replaces human instruction. They emphasize that the pedagogical value lies in scaffolding and source evaluation, not in AI as a curriculum topic by itself. The paper is primarily a practical framework and instructional position piece, and it recommends future assessment of student outcomes and comparisons of grounded versus ungrounded AI tools.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a practice-oriented article and conceptual classroom report, not a controlled empirical study. It provides descriptive examples and instructor observations, but no rigorous quantitative design, comparison group, or reported statistical analysis.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The article describes plausible instructional benefits for early undergraduate information literacy, but it offers no measurable effect sizes and no direct evidence of generalizable impact. The likely impact is modest and unclear, based mainly on classroom implementation guidance rather than outcomes data.

interventions.use_case: Using Perplexity AI as a conversational search and research support tool in first-year library and chemical engineering classroom activities, with prompt-based inquiry, source retrieval, summarization, and follow-up questioning.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that generative AI-supported assignments improved students' information literacy skills, especially source evaluation, keyword development, and understanding scholarly conversation. The authors report instructor-observed improvements in students' research questions being scoped more appropriately and students using retrieved sources in their annotated bibliographies, but no formal quantitative effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Information literacy performance in class assignments; quality of research questions, source evaluation, and annotated bibliography use

finding.finding_summary: The assignments were designed to build critical thinking, metacognition, and iterative inquiry through prompt refinement, lateral reading, and source verification. The paper reports that students gained a better sense of the conversation around their topic and improved their ability to narrow or broaden research questions, but the evidence is descriptive rather than experimental.
finding.measure: Critical evaluation, metacognitive reflection, and research-process skills observed in classroom activities

finding.finding_summary: The paper claims that Perplexity AI replaced the initial Googling stage with more structured guidance, helping students quickly identify relevant sources and saving class time in both the credit-bearing course and one-session activity. This is presented as improved instructional efficiency and ease of classroom integration, but without measured time-savings data.
finding.measure: Perceived efficiency of research initiation and classroom workflow

paper_profiles.title: AI-based chatbots in customer service and their effects on user compliance
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether AI-based chatbots can influence user compliance in customer-service interactions, and whether anthropomorphic verbal design cues strengthen that effect. The authors frame the problem in terms of how conversational agents can successfully elicit cooperation from users, especially when the agent is the requester rather than a human employee.

The intervention is an AI-enabled chatbot designed for an online banking customer-service scenario. In a 2 x 2 randomized online experiment, the authors manipulate two factors: verbal anthropomorphic design cues (low vs. high, using identity, small talk, and empathy) and the foot-in-the-door technique (initial small request present vs. absent). Participants first interact with the chatbot to ask a banking question, and then, depending on condition, may be asked for a small feedback request before receiving the main request to complete a longer questionnaire.

The study uses adult German participants recruited online via Facebook groups. Results show that both higher anthropomorphic cues and the foot-in-the-door sequence increase compliance with the chatbot’s request. Social presence mediates the effect of anthropomorphic cues on compliance, but it does not significantly moderate the foot-in-the-door effect. The authors conclude that disembodied AI chatbots can function as persuasive social actors in customer service, and that dialog design matters for user behavior.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed randomized online experiment with a 2x2 factorial design and clear causal identification, but it is not a K-12 education study and does not directly examine learning outcomes. There are also relevance limitations for the requested education topic because the context is customer service rather than classroom or instructional use.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper shows a sizable effect on compliance behavior in a chatbot setting, but the setting is outside education and the outcome is not an academic learning measure. For K-12 education, the practical impact is therefore indirect and unclear, since it mainly informs conversational design rather than student learning gains.

interventions.use_case: AI-based customer-service chatbot for online banking, using natural language dialogue, anthropomorphic verbal cues, and compliance-oriented request prompting
IBM Watson Assistant cloud service used as the conversational AI/NLP backend enabling natural language understanding and dialogue management

finding.finding_summary: The paper evaluates whether chatbot design increases user compliance with a service-feedback request, which is an operational goal for customer-service systems. In a randomized online experiment (n=153 analyzed), anthropomorphic design cues increased compliance substantially (b=1.380, OR=3.975, p<0.01), and the foot-in-the-door technique also increased compliance (b=0.916, OR=2.499, p<0.05).
finding.measure: Binary user compliance with the chatbot’s request for service feedback (Yes/No)
finding.effect_size: OR=3.975 for anthropomorphic design cues; OR=2.499 for foot-in-the-door

finding.finding_summary: The study directly measured social presence as a mediator of compliance in chatbot interaction. Anthropomorphic design cues significantly increased social presence and indirectly increased compliance; the mediated indirect effect was 0.6485 with a 95% bias-corrected CI [0.1552, 1.2887], while the direct effect became non-significant after adding the mediator.
finding.measure: Social Presence scale and mediation effect on user compliance

paper_profiles.title: Promoting active learning with ChatGPT: A constructivist approach in Sri Lankan higher education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses how ChatGPT can be used to shift a traditional, didactic learning environment toward active, constructivist learning in a resource-constrained higher education setting. The central question is not whether ChatGPT improves test scores, but what teaching and learning strategies make it useful for promoting active learning, social interaction, contextual learning, scaffolding, and reflective thinking.

The study was conducted in a Sri Lankan university over 12 weeks with 43 undergraduate students in a project management course. The intervention combined pre-class materials, short instructor-led introductions, group discussions, ChatGPT-supported case studies, and post-class sample answers generated with ChatGPT. The instructor also guided students in using ChatGPT responsibly, including warnings about hallucinations and the need to verify information. Data came from 15 semi-structured student interviews and thematic analysis, so the study is qualitative and based primarily on learner perceptions.

The paper identifies 16 strategies across five constructivist themes and argues that ChatGPT can help educators create more interactive, learner-centered experiences without additional resources. It concludes that AI can support personalized feedback, collaboration, and reflection, while the educator’s role shifts toward collaborator and guide. The author also notes that the approach was especially feasible in a low-resource setting, though broader generalizability remains limited.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative action-research study with semi-structured interviews and thematic analysis, not a controlled efficacy design. It provides useful implementation evidence but does not meet stronger causal credibility criteria.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports clearly positive but non-quantified impacts on engagement, collaboration, and understanding in one higher-education class. Because no effect sizes or objective outcome gains are reported, the magnitude of impact is unclear.

interventions.use_case: Using ChatGPT as a virtual tutor and collaborator in a higher-education project management course to generate case studies, support group discussions, provide instant feedback, answer questions, and scaffold active learning

finding.finding_summary: Students reported that ChatGPT-supported activities increased critical thinking, collaboration, reflective thinking, and problem-solving in a 12-week action-research intervention with 43 undergraduates in Sri Lanka. The paper is qualitative and does not report standardized effect sizes, but it describes stronger engagement in group discussion, more confident participation, and improved ability to apply concepts through the AI-supported case-study and discussion activities.
finding.measure: Semi-structured interview themes about critical thinking, collaboration, reflective thinking, and problem-solving during ChatGPT-supported active learning

finding.finding_summary: The intervention was associated with higher student engagement, motivation, and confidence in participating in class and group work. Students described ChatGPT as making learning more engaging and less intimidating, but the study provides qualitative evidence only and no numeric effect size.
finding.measure: Semi-structured interview themes on engagement, motivation, confidence, and participation

finding.finding_summary: The paper focuses on project management learning in higher education and reports that ChatGPT helped students understand course concepts through contextualized case studies and immediate feedback. Evidence is based on qualitative student interviews from a 12-week intervention rather than objective achievement testing, so no effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Qualitative perceptions of understanding and application of project management concepts

paper_profiles.title: Integrating artificial intelligence into public health education and healthcare: insights from the COVID-19 and monkeypox crises for future pandemic readiness
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how the COVID-19 pandemic disrupted higher education and healthcare systems and uses those disruptions to argue for future-ready reforms in public health education, workforce training, and healthcare delivery. It is framed as a review and perspective piece rather than an empirical intervention study. The authors discuss how universities shifted to remote, synchronous, asynchronous, and hybrid teaching during the pandemic, the challenges that arose for teaching, assessment, labs, and student support, and how these experiences can inform post-pandemic educational design.

A central focus of the paper is the potential role of artificial intelligence in public health education and healthcare. The authors describe AI as a tool for epidemiological modeling, outbreak prediction, telehealth, chatbots, diagnostic support, and the creation of digital learning content, while also emphasizing ethical, equity, privacy, and governance concerns. The paper also discusses examples from multiple countries and institutions, including higher education settings in Spain, Turkey, South Korea, Morocco, Bahrain, India, and the United States, with particular attention to higher education institutions, public health education, workforce training, and healthcare delivery during COVID-19 and related outbreaks such as monkeypox.

The paper concludes that AI should be strategically integrated into public health education and healthcare systems alongside better infrastructure, training, and ethical oversight. Rather than treating AI as a standalone solution, the authors argue for systems thinking, interdisciplinary collaboration, and policy development to ensure AI supports public health goals, improves preparedness, and strengthens resilience in future health crises.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed narrative review, not an empirical evaluation with a controlled design. It synthesizes prior literature and implementation examples, but provides no original comparative data or causal evidence.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper’s proposed AI and digital-education applications suggest potentially meaningful system-level benefits, but the review does not measure actual impact sizes. Its contribution is mainly conceptual and policy-oriented, so the observed evidence for impact remains unclear to modest.

interventions.use_case: review of AI applications for public health education and healthcare, including AI-driven epidemiological modeling, AI-powered chatbots for telehealth tasks, and machine-translation/translation-infrastructure support for COVID-19 information dissemination

finding.finding_summary: This is a narrative review rather than an intervention study, so it does not report a pooled effect size. The paper argues that COVID-19 exposed major institutional weaknesses in higher education, public health education, and healthcare delivery, while also catalyzing reforms such as blended learning, telemedicine, and AI-enabled preparedness systems.
finding.measure: Narrative synthesis of institutional practices, policy responses, and reported implementation experiences across countries and sectors

finding.finding_summary: The review describes AI and related digital tools as promising for improving efficiency in public health education and healthcare, such as faster epidemiological modeling, chatbots for appointment scheduling and symptom assessment, and more scalable translation workflows for pandemic information. However, these are presented as prospective benefits and examples rather than quantified trial results.
finding.measure: Narrative descriptions of workflow support, service delivery, and communication efficiency

paper_profiles.title: Ethical Use of Technology in Digital Learning Environments: Graduate Student Perspectives
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This book-length open educational resource examines ethical issues related to technology use in digital learning environments, with chapters authored by graduate students in an ethics and technology course. The introduction describes a co-design process in which students, instructors, and other project collaborators jointly developed open Pressbooks chapters on topics including artificial intelligence, social networking, 3D printing, academic resource sharing, adaptive learning systems, STEM, assistive technologies, admissions, and fake news.

The AI-related chapter focuses specifically on ethical considerations when using artificial intelligence-based assistive technologies in education. It argues that AI tools can support personalized learning, assessment, and classroom efficiency, but only when teachers use them judiciously and with attention to privacy, informed consent, data security, transparency, and bias. The discussion emphasizes that these tools do not replace human teachers and that professional judgment remains central.

The relevant population is graduate students in a University of Calgary digital age program, though the content of the chapters ranges across K-12, higher education, and broader professional contexts. The work is primarily conceptual and reflective rather than empirical, using Farrow’s ethics framework to guide analysis. Its main conclusion is that educational technologies, including AI-based assistive tools, should be implemented with strong ethical safeguards, clear policies, and awareness of how data collection and algorithmic systems may affect learners and teachers.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a conceptual/reflective book chapter rather than an empirical study. It does not present a clear research design, comparison group, or measured outcomes, so it does not meet criteria for experimental or observational evidence tiers.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The chapter has likely educational relevance for guiding implementation and policy discussions around AI in classrooms, but it reports no direct measured impact. Any impact is indirect and theoretical rather than demonstrated through outcomes.

interventions.use_case: ethics-focused discussion of AI-based assistive technologies in education, including speech-to-text, predictive text, grading software, and personalized learning tools used by teachers and students

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT in higher education: Opportunities, challenges, and required competencies in the absence of guiding policies
paper_profiles.venue: Journal of Education and e-Learning Research
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how ChatGPT is being used in higher education and what opportunities, challenges, and user competencies are associated with its adoption in the absence of formal institutional policies. The study asks how faculty and students perceive ChatGPT, what kinds of tasks they use it for, and what risks emerge when its use is not clearly governed.

The authors conducted a qualitative case study at a federal university in the United Arab Emirates. Data came from semi-structured interviews with 10 faculty members and 10 students, plus documentation of live ChatGPT use and other participant-shared materials. Participants included undergraduate and graduate students and teachers across several colleges.
