paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed qualitative focus group study with a clear methodology, but it does not provide experimental or quasi-experimental causal evidence. It contributes credible descriptive evidence about perceived benefits and safety concerns, but only meets one of the credibility criteria for causal impact claims.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests meaningful perceived benefits in efficiency and support, but the evidence is qualitative and does not estimate effect sizes or causal impacts. Its strongest contribution is identifying risks and governance needs rather than demonstrating measurable gains in student outcomes.

interventions.use_case: GenAI chat-based learning assistant used by university ICT students for answering questions, debugging code, explaining concepts, generating prompts, and supporting research/project tasks (e.g., ChatGPT and Microsoft Copilot during in-class activities).

finding.finding_summary: Students reported that GenAI helped them understand ICT concepts, verify code, simplify assessment criteria, and troubleshoot tasks more quickly, but they also noted that its usefulness depended heavily on prompt quality and that outputs were sometimes inaccurate. The study is qualitative (n=19) and does not report effect sizes; the main academic takeaway is improved perceived support for ICT learning alongside concerns about incorrect or incomplete answers.
finding.measure: Focus group reports of perceived understanding, task completion, and academic performance in ICT subjects

finding.finding_summary: Participants said GenAI supported critical thinking, analytical reasoning, problem-solving, and communication skills, especially when they used it to refine prompts, evaluate responses, and analyze designs. At the same time, several students worried that heavy reliance could weaken independent reasoning and reduce deep engagement; no quantitative effect sizes were reported because the study used focus groups (n=19).
finding.measure: Focus group reports of critical thinking, problem-solving, communication, and analytical skills

finding.finding_summary: Students generally described positive feelings such as excitement, convenience, and improved engagement when using GenAI, but some reported lower satisfaction and reduced sense of achievement compared with solving problems independently. Because the evidence comes from qualitative focus groups (n=19), the paper reports no numeric effect size; sentiment was mostly positive but inconsistent across subjects and tasks.
finding.measure: Participant sentiment, engagement, and sense of achievement in focus groups

finding.finding_summary: A consistent finding was that GenAI saved time and streamlined problem solving, with students repeatedly describing it as efficient, user-friendly, and useful for quick troubleshooting. The study is qualitative (n=19) and does not report effect sizes, but the perceived efficiency gain was one of the strongest themes across focus groups.
finding.measure: Perceived time savings, ease of use, and troubleshooting efficiency from focus groups

finding.finding_summary: The paper strongly emphasizes institutional risks and governance issues, including accuracy, misinformation, plagiarism, privacy, bias, and over-reliance, and it proposes the GROW-AI framework to guide responsible integration. This is a qualitative study (n=19) with no effect sizes, but it provides substantive evidence for the need for policies, guidance, and oversight rather than outcome impacts in the K-12 sense.
finding.measure: Theme analysis of ethical concerns, trust, accountability, and policy/guidance needs

paper_profiles.title: Has It All Been Solved? Open NLP Research Questions Not Solved by Large Language Models
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a position-style overview that argues the rapid progress of large language models (LLMs) has not solved the full research agenda in NLP. The authors ask what research questions remain open despite LLM capabilities and compile a set of research directions that are not directly solvable by LLMs. The paper is motivated by concerns that public discourse and funding priorities are collapsing NLP into LLM development, potentially obscuring many other important areas.

The paper does not study an intervention or conduct an empirical evaluation. Instead, it presents a structured taxonomy of 14 research areas spanning fundamental, responsible, and applied NLP. These include multilinguality, reasoning, knowledge bases, language grounding, child language acquisition, non-verbal communication, ethics, interpretability, efficient NLP, NLP in online environments, healthcare, education, computational social science, and synthetic datasets. Within each area, the authors outline open problems and cite representative prior work.

The paper’s education-related discussion is especially relevant to concerns about reliability, misinformation, and overreliance: it notes that intelligent tutoring systems and educational explanation generation require human-in-the-loop checks, because LLMs still struggle with reasoning and grounding, can produce convincingly written but unverified output, and may encourage overreliance if used as a replacement for human teachers. More broadly, the paper emphasizes that LLMs can be unreliable due to hallucinations and factual inconsistencies, so they should be treated as tools to support—not replace—human expertise.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a perspective/overview paper that enumerates open research questions in NLP and LLMs rather than evaluating an educational technology intervention. It does not report an empirical design, sample, or outcome analysis relevant to K-12 evidence standards.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper provides no measured educational impact, effect sizes, or implementation results for science inquiry supports in K-12. Its relevance to the requested topic is conceptual only, mainly noting that LLMs still struggle with reasoning, grounding, hallucination, and reliability.

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT and AI Chatbots in Education: An Umbrella Review of Systematic Reviews, Scoping Reviews, and Meta-Analyses
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Education and Information Technologies
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This umbrella review examines the rapidly expanding literature on ChatGPT and related large language model (LLM)-based chatbots in education. Its central purpose is to synthesize evidence from existing systematic reviews, scoping reviews, meta-analyses, bibliometric reviews, narrative reviews, and rapid reviews in order to identify reported benefits, limitations, ethical concerns, and policy implications of these tools in educational settings.

The paper does not study a single intervention with primary participants; instead, it aggregates findings from 41 review studies published between 2023 and 2025. The reviewed literature covers a wide range of contexts, with the strongest concentration in higher education and substantial attention to medicine/health, STEM, and language learning. The review notes that chatbots are typically used for academic writing support, tutoring, feedback, exam preparation, and self-directed learning, mostly in online, blended, or hybrid settings.

The umbrella review concludes that AI chatbots can support personalized learning, learner autonomy, motivation, and some aspects of academic performance, but the evidence base is limited by short-term, exploratory studies and an overreliance on self-reported or observational outcomes. It highlights major safety and quality concerns, especially hallucinations, outdated or inaccurate information, source opacity, overreliance by students, and threats to academic integrity. The authors argue that effective educational use requires stronger policy frameworks, educator professional development, human oversight, and more rigorous longitudinal research.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an umbrella review of 41 systematic/scoping reviews and meta-analyses, so it is peer-reviewed and methodologically structured, but it does not conduct a new meta-analysis of primary studies and explicitly notes that no formal critical appraisal checklist was used. Evidence quality is therefore moderate rather than high.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports important, practice-relevant concerns and some positive effects, but most findings are synthesized qualitatively and lack pooled effect sizes. The impact on K-12 populations is therefore suggestive but unclear, especially because the underlying literature is dominated by higher education rather than school settings.

interventions.use_case: umbrella review of ChatGPT and similar LLM-based chatbots used for tutoring, Q&A, feedback, content generation, and conversational support across education

finding.finding_summary: The review reports broadly positive effects on academic writing, comprehension, and written expression, but also notes risks that AI-generated text can suppress original thinking and critical engagement. The evidence base is mostly drawn from short-term, review-level syntheses rather than new experiments, so no pooled effect size is reported.
finding.measure: writing quality, written expression, comprehension, and academic writing performance across reviewed studies

finding.finding_summary: Reviews summarized in the umbrella review suggest ChatGPT and similar tools support vocabulary acquisition, speaking practice, and general language development in EFL/ESL contexts. However, the paper emphasizes that robust long-term evidence is limited and that much of the literature is short-term and descriptive.
finding.measure: vocabulary acquisition, speaking fluency, and language development outcomes in EFL/ESL studies

finding.finding_summary: The review finds that LLM chatbots are often used in STEM and health education for problem-solving, concept explanation, and clinical reasoning, with some reviews reporting performance comparable to or better than human learners in narrow tasks such as medical licensing preparation. At the same time, it highlights weaker performance in mathematics and software testing, plus hallucinations and factual inaccuracies in science-heavy domains.
finding.measure: problem-solving, clinical reasoning, exam preparation, and domain-specific accuracy in STEM/medical contexts

finding.finding_summary: Across non-language, non-math domains, the review reports that chatbots can support content understanding, exam preparation, and task completion in areas such as medicine, engineering, law, and professional education. Benefits are described at the review level, but the paper does not provide pooled quantitative effects.
finding.measure: domain-specific learning outcomes in medicine, engineering, law, and other professional/disciplinary contexts

finding.finding_summary: The umbrella review reports increases in motivation, confidence, autonomy, and engagement when students use chatbots for self-paced support and low-stakes practice. It also notes concerns about reduced initiative, overreliance, and shallower engagement when use is unstructured.
finding.measure: motivation, engagement, learner autonomy, confidence, and self-paced participation

finding.finding_summary: The paper repeatedly identifies possible gains in critical thinking, metacognition, creativity, and self-regulated learning, especially when educators provide structured prompts and reflection tasks. It also reports negative or null-like concerns: overreliance may reduce critical thinking and produce shallow, rote use of AI responses.
finding.measure: critical thinking, metacognition, self-regulated learning, creativity, and reflective engagement

finding.finding_summary: Reviews synthesized in the paper consistently describe productivity benefits for both students and educators, including faster feedback, content generation, grading support, and reduced routine workload. The paper does not report pooled quantitative effects, but the direction of evidence is strongly favorable for efficiency-related tasks.
finding.measure: teacher workload, feedback turnaround, content generation, grading, and task efficiency

finding.finding_summary: The umbrella review highlights major institutional concerns around academic integrity, privacy, transparency, policy readiness, and governance for AI in education. It also reports a strong consensus that schools and universities need explicit policy frameworks, but the evidence base is mostly descriptive and review-based rather than outcome-evaluative.
finding.measure: policy, governance, academic integrity, privacy, institutional preparedness, and AI literacy

paper_profiles.title: Artificial Intelligence Threatens Critical Thinking in Education Systems
paper_profiles.venue: Journal of Higher Education and Science/Yükseköğretim ve Bilim Dergisi
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This review paper examines the growing use of artificial intelligence in education and argues that, alongside benefits such as personalized learning, faster assessment, and data-driven decision-making, generative AI may carry important cognitive and ethical risks. The central question is whether AI-supported learning tools can undermine students’ critical thinking by reducing active engagement with content and encouraging dependence on machine-generated outputs.

The paper does not report an empirical intervention or a participant-based experiment. Instead, it synthesizes prior research and examples on generative AI, hallucinations, bias, cognitive offloading, and academic use of large language models. The context is broad education system use, including students, teachers, and administrators, rather than a single grade band or school setting. The article highlights issues such as biased outputs, fabricated references, inaccurate information, and the tendency of AI tools to shift responsibility away from learners.

The authors conclude that AI can both support and suppress learning, but that unchecked use is likely to strengthen overreliance, weaken memory and independent problem-solving, and erode critical thinking over time. They recommend stronger AI literacy, ethical guidance, and strategies that keep AI in a supportive role rather than replacing students’ own cognitive work.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a narrative review/opinion piece rather than an empirical study, and it does not present a systematic method, original sample, or inferential analysis. It is peer-reviewed, but the evidence base is synthesized qualitatively and heavily dependent on cited secondary studies.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper argues for negative and safety-related impacts, but it reports no original effect sizes or measurable intervention impact of its own. As a result, it does not demonstrate quantifiable impact on K-12 populations within this paper.

interventions.use_case: Use of large language models and generative AI tools in student learning tasks, especially essay writing and information synthesis, where the tools reduce the amount of cognitive effort required from students.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that AI use in education weakens critical thinking, source evaluation, and independent problem-solving by encouraging cognitive offloading and overreliance. It cites recent studies showing lower critical thinking among heavier AI users and describes evidence that LLM-supported task completion reduces ownership and memory for work produced, with the effect attributed to reduced active cognitive engagement rather than a direct test in this review itself.
finding.measure: Critical thinking assessments, cognitive offloading, ownership of work, and memory recall from cited studies

finding.finding_summary: The review describes increased student laziness, passivity, and behavioral dependency as recurring consequences of AI use in education. It frames these as motivational and engagement-related harms that emerge when students delegate intellectual work to AI rather than actively participating in learning tasks.
finding.measure: Reported laziness, passivity, and behavioral dependency in cited student studies

finding.finding_summary: The paper warns that AI-generated text can be biased, inaccurate, or hallucinatory, creating risks for student writing and academic work. It highlights fabricated references and incorrect content in generative outputs, implying potential degradation of writing quality and factual reliability when students rely on these tools uncritically.
finding.measure: Accuracy and reliability of AI-generated text; fabricated references in academic writing

finding.finding_summary: The review argues that unchecked AI adoption may amplify bias, misinformation, and ethical problems at the institutional level, including unfair educational judgments and unclear authorship/accountability. It presents these risks as broader system-level threats requiring AI literacy and governance rather than a measured intervention effect.
finding.measure: Bias amplification, misinformation risk, authorship/accountability concerns, and ethical governance issues

paper_profiles.title: A Systematic Review of Research on ChatGPT in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks what recent empirical research has found about the use of ChatGPT in higher education, with particular attention to student perceptions, attitudes, perceived usefulness, user experience, and perceived risks. It synthesizes studies published between January 2023 and March 2025 and follows PRISMA procedures to identify and review the literature.

The intervention or phenomenon studied is ChatGPT use in university learning environments, including its use for brainstorming, writing support, feedback, tutoring, and self-directed learning. The review includes 20 peer-reviewed empirical studies drawn from Web of Science and Scopus, using quantitative, qualitative, and mixed-methods approaches. The populations in the included studies were university students, and some studies also considered instructor perspectives or staff reactions as part of the broader higher-education context.

Overall, the review concludes that ChatGPT is widely perceived as useful for improving efficiency, access to explanations, and academic productivity, but these benefits are accompanied by persistent concerns about reliability, hallucinated or inaccurate content, overreliance, academic integrity, and ethical ambiguity. The paper argues that educational value depends heavily on institutional policies, instructor guidance, and AI literacy. It recommends clear usage guidelines, stronger AI literacy integration, and pedagogical redesigns that encourage critical thinking and originality.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed systematic review, but it synthesizes mostly early-stage heterogeneous studies and explicitly states that it does not include a formal quality appraisal. The evidence base is largely correlational/qualitative and no meta-analytic effect estimates are reported.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The review suggests meaningful but largely qualitative and context-dependent implications for higher education practice, especially around trust, overreliance, and academic integrity. However, it reports no pooled effect sizes and does not establish a clear medium or large impact on learner outcomes.

interventions.use_case: Systematic review of ChatGPT use in higher education as a conversational AI for student support, including explanation generation, brainstorming, writing assistance, feedback, and general academic help-seeking.

finding.finding_summary: The review synthesizes 20 empirical studies and finds that ChatGPT is often perceived as helpful for academic writing, drafting, and language clarity, but also raises concerns about hallucinations, inaccurate content, and overreliance in writing tasks. No pooled effect size is reported; the evidence is based on descriptive synthesis across heterogeneous student studies (n=20 studies, with individual samples ranging from n=12 to n=695).
finding.measure: Student perceptions and reported use for writing support, drafting, and language clarity; concerns about accuracy in AI-generated text

finding.finding_summary: Across the included studies, students often reported increased confidence, motivation, and autonomy when using ChatGPT, but some studies also noted frustration, uncertainty, and reduced active participation when the tool was overused. The review does not report a pooled effect size; it summarizes qualitative and survey evidence from 20 studies.
finding.measure: Motivation, confidence, autonomy, engagement, and student experience surveys/reflections

finding.finding_summary: A central negative concern in the review is that ChatGPT may promote shallow learning and overreliance, potentially weakening critical thinking, originality, and deep engagement with course materials. The paper also notes that some studies found benefits for idea generation and prompt-based creativity, so the overall pattern is mixed rather than uniformly harmful. No pooled effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, originality, deep engagement, and problem-solving as discussed in included studies

finding.finding_summary: The review consistently reports that ChatGPT is viewed as improving academic efficiency by providing immediate explanations, 24/7 support, and faster task completion for brainstorming, summarizing, and drafting. This is a qualitative synthesis rather than an effect-size study, so no pooled estimate is reported.
finding.measure: Perceived usefulness, task efficiency, and help-seeking behavior

finding.finding_summary: The review highlights institutional concerns about academic integrity, privacy, policy ambiguity, and the need for AI literacy and usage guidelines. It also notes that contextual factors such as instructor guidance and institutional policy shape ChatGPT’s educational impact, but no quantitative institutional effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Academic integrity concerns, policy responses, AI literacy needs, and institutional guidance/policy themes

paper_profiles.title: Can Multimodal LLMs ‘See’ Science Instruction? Benchmarking Pedagogical Reasoning in K–12 Classroom Videos
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether current large language models and multimodal large language models can reliably analyze K–12 science classroom instruction from video, not just from transcripts. The authors argue that science classrooms pose a harder test than mathematics because important instructional meaning is often distributed across speech, gestures, student actions, drawings, whiteboards, and other artifacts that transcripts alone miss. To study this, they introduce SciIBI, a benchmark for Core Instructional Practice (CIP) coding in science instruction, and evaluate eight state-of-the-art LLMs/MLLMs under zero-shot, few-shot, and chain-of-thought prompting.

The benchmark contains 113 NGSS-aligned classroom clips sourced from YouTube, spanning elementary through high school science lessons, with expert consensus annotations for four CIP categories and within-practice sophistication levels. Models were evaluated on transcript-only input and on video-plus-transcript input, and they were also required to provide supporting evidence for their predictions. The study finds that all models perform modestly at best, with the strongest result reaching 53.6% accuracy, far below prior performance on math discourse benchmarks. Visual input sometimes improves performance, especially when classroom artifacts are essential, but gains are inconsistent across models and practices.

A major contribution of the paper is its evidence-based error analysis. The authors show that models often rely on surface cues such as question forms or explanation-related keywords rather than genuine pedagogical reasoning, and that good classification accuracy does not always correspond to good evidence quality. They conclude that science classroom discourse analysis remains a challenging frontier for multimodal AI and suggest an evidence-first human-AI workflow in which models retrieve candidate evidence to support expert review rather than replacing human coders.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed benchmark/evaluation study with a clear methodology, expert consensus annotation, controlled prompting comparisons, and human-rated evidence quality assessment. However, it is not an RCT or QED of a student intervention; it is primarily diagnostic/benchmarking research rather than causal impact evaluation.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper shows modest, mixed gains from visual context for model performance (+4.8 pp average across MLLMs; best +7.1 pp), but no direct educational outcome improvement for students or teachers was measured. Its practical impact is suggestive but remains limited to model benchmarking and proposed workflow support.

interventions.use_case: Benchmarking and evaluating multimodal LLMs for automated coding of K-12 science classroom video clips into Core Instructional Practices, including transcript-only vs vision+text prompting and evidence-based justification of predictions.

finding.finding_summary: This benchmark study finds that current LLMs/MLLMs show limited and inconsistent performance on science classroom pedagogical reasoning. Across eight models, zero-shot accuracy ranged from 39.1% to 53.6% on 113 clips, with the best result coming from InternVL3-78B using vision+text (53.6%, +7.1 pp over text-only), but many errors reflected surface-level shortcut use rather than genuine pedagogical understanding.
finding.measure: Accuracy and macro-F1 on 4-way Core Instructional Practice (CIP) classification; within-practice sophistication accuracy; Evidence Quality Score (EQS) ratings

finding.finding_summary: The paper does not test end-user learning gains, but it explicitly evaluates whether MLLMs could accelerate expert review of classroom video by retrieving evidence spans for human verification. The authors argue the strongest near-term utility is as an evidence-first retrieval assistant, potentially reducing the time and labor required for expert CIP coding, though no direct workload reduction was measured.
finding.measure: Evidence-based coding support / expert review assistance concept; no direct workload metric reported
finding.study_size: n=60 model outputs rated for EQS; n=113 clips total

paper_profiles.title: Breakable Machine: A K–12 Classroom Game for Transformative AI Literacy Through Spoofing and eXplainable AI (XAI)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses how to teach critical and transformative AI literacy in K–12 by helping students understand not only how AI systems work, but also how they fail. The authors argue that AI education should move beyond building models and instead include opportunities to interrogate brittleness, bias, reliability, and sociotechnical implications through hands-on experiences with failure.

To do this, the paper presents Breakable Machine, an XAI-based classroom game in which learners try to spoof an image classifier by changing their appearance or surroundings so that the model confidently misclassifies them. Students can also inspect saliency heatmaps and explore the training data to infer why the system behaves as it does. The game is designed for grades 4–9, roughly ages 10–15, and runs in a browser on students’ devices with a teacher-facing projector view and leaderboard.

The paper is non-empirical and focuses on the design and pedagogical rationale of the resource rather than outcome evaluation. Its main conclusion is that intentionally breaking AI systems can be a productive educational strategy for fostering AI literacy, data agency, ethical awareness, and a critical stance toward AI as a fallible sociotechnical system. The authors position misclassification and adversarial play as central learning opportunities, with empirical assessment of learning outcomes left for future work.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a design/resource paper describing a classroom game and its pedagogical rationale, not an empirical evaluation of outcomes. The paper explicitly states that empirical evaluation of learning outcomes is future work.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper proposes a potentially meaningful K-12 AI literacy intervention focused on reliability, misinformation, and overreliance, but it reports no measured effects. Impact is therefore conceptually promising but empirically unconfirmed.

interventions.use_case: XAI-based classroom spoofing game for K-12 students to trick an image classifier by manipulating appearance or environment, using a shared leaderboard and saliency heatmaps to support critical AI literacy and inquiry.

Browser-based classroom learning tool that guides students through structured image-classification experimentation, model probing, and reflection using the app interface, training-data view, and teacher controls.

paper_profiles.title: Designing for human–AI complementarity in K-12 education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how to design human–AI partnerships in K-12 education so that teachers and AI tutoring systems complement one another rather than working in isolation. The core problem is that AI tutors can support student practice, but teachers still play an important role in interpreting student needs, noticing contextual factors, and providing support that software cannot. The authors argue that effective human–AI systems must be designed around real classroom work practices and should be evaluated in authentic settings.

The intervention studied is Lumilo, a pair of mixed-reality smart glasses worn by teachers in AI-supported classrooms. Lumilo shows real-time analytics about students’ learning, metacognition, and behavior, plus detailed student-level information when requested. The system was developed through participatory design with teachers and iterative prototyping, including field observations, co-design sessions, replay-based enactments, and pilot studies intended to shape teacher decision-making in positive directions.

The empirical evaluation involved middle school math classrooms using an AI tutor for linear equation solving. In the final experiment, 343 middle school students across 18 classrooms, 8 teachers, and 4 schools/districts were randomly assigned to one of three conditions: no glasses, glasses without analytics, or glasses with analytics. The paper reports that Lumilo improved student learning, especially for lower-performing students, and shifted teacher attention toward students who needed help most. The authors conclude that real-time teacher-facing analytics can make AI tutoring more effective when designed as a complement to human judgment, not a replacement for it.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed in-the-wild field experiment with random assignment of classrooms to conditions and hierarchical linear modeling, which gives it relatively strong causal credibility. Some concerns remain because the paper is a case study with a modest sample and the text excerpt does not report full effect sizes for the main outcomes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported effects on linear equation learning are positive and appear meaningful, especially for lower-pretest students, but exact effect sizes are not provided in the excerpt. The impact is therefore promising and likely modest-to-moderate rather than clearly large.

interventions.use_case: AI tutor-supported linear equation solving in middle school classrooms (Lynnette), paired with teacher-facing mixed-reality awareness support to coordinate help during class

Mixed-reality smart glasses (Lumilo/HoloLens) providing real-time teacher awareness analytics about students' learning, metacognition, behavior, and remote screen monitoring in AI-supported classrooms

finding.finding_summary: In a field experiment with 343 middle school students across 18 classrooms, 8 teachers, and 4 schools/districts (analysis on n=286 after absences), students in the Glasses + Analytics condition showed greater pre/post learning gains on linear equation solving than students in the No Glasses business-as-usual condition and the Glasses-only condition. The paper reports statistically supported positive effects, especially for lower-pretest students, but does not provide a numerical effect size in the text excerpt.
finding.measure: 15-minute pre-test and post-test on linear equation solving

finding.finding_summary: The teacher-facing Lumilo system improved outcomes above and beyond a minimal monitoring-only glasses condition. This indicates that the real-time analytics, not just the wearable display or novelty of monitoring, contributed to stronger linear-equation learning gains.
finding.measure: Pre/post linear equation solving test gains

finding.finding_summary: Classroom observations and process data suggest Lumilo changed teacher attention allocation in ways consistent with improved in-the-moment decision-making: teachers spent more time with lower-pretest students and used complementary cues from the AI system plus their own observations. The paper frames this as evidence of human–AI complementarity, but the durable-skill outcome is indirect and not measured with a dedicated scale.
finding.measure: Teacher attention allocation, classroom observation, and process data on teacher-student interactions

paper_profiles.title: Learning Assistant Supported Student Outcomes (LASSO) study initial findings
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how features of Learning Assistant (LA)-supported undergraduate STEM courses are associated with student learning outcomes. The authors use pilot data from a multi-institution study to ask whether student characteristics, instructor experience, course features, and the amount of interaction with LAs predict gains on concept inventories.

The intervention/approach studied is the Learning Assistant model, in which undergraduate or course-embedded assistants support instruction in STEM classes. Data were collected from faculty surveys and student pre/post concept inventory surveys across several institutions in the LA Alliance. The sample includes physics, biology, and chemistry courses, with outcomes measured using standardized concept inventories and effect sizes based on pre/post score changes.

The study reports that average learning gains were positive overall, with larger gains associated with more student interaction with LAs, more faculty experience teaching the course with LAs, and better student-to-LA ratios. However, the findings also show gender and race-related differences in outcomes, with male students outperforming female students and some racial groups differing from White students. The authors emphasize that these are correlational findings from preliminary data and that future work is needed to disentangle causal effects and examine specific LA practices more closely.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed correlational multi-site study using hierarchical linear models, but it is not an experimental or quasi-experimental design and does not identify causal effects of a technology intervention. The evidence is useful for pattern detection and hypothesis generation, but credibility for impact claims is limited.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The study reports moderate pre-post gains in concept inventory outcomes, but these are not attributable to a specific AI/technology intervention and are highly context-dependent. It therefore suggests unclear to modest impact rather than a clearly demonstrated intervention effect.

finding.finding_summary: This correlational HLM study of LA-supported STEM courses found overall pre-post gains in concept inventories, with a grand mean effect size of d=0.845 across 3,315 usable student pre/post pairs. However, outcomes varied substantially by discipline and student subgroup, and the paper does not isolate a causal effect of the Learning Assistant model itself.
finding.measure: Pre/post concept inventory effect sizes (Cohen's d) on FMCE, BEMA, CINS, GCA, IMCA, CCI, and GCIICS
finding.study_size: n=3,315 usable pre-post pairs; 17 instructors; 13 institutions
finding.effect_size: d=0.845 overall; by inventory ranged from d=0.052 (CCI) to d=1.248 (CINS)

finding.finding_summary: Student interaction time with LAs was positively associated with learning gains, peaking for students who spent 16-30 minutes per week with LAs. Compared with the 0 min/week group (d=0.369), the 16-30 min/week group had substantially higher average effect size (d=0.873), while the 30+ min/week group showed no further increase, suggesting a possible selection effect among the most struggling students.
finding.measure: Weekly minutes of student interaction with Learning Assistants and resulting concept inventory effect sizes
finding.effect_size: d=0.873 for 16-30 min/week vs d=0.369 for 0 min/week

finding.finding_summary: The study found that students in courses with more experienced LA-using instructors had higher learning gains, with effect size increasing by 0.154 for each additional term a faculty member had taught the course with LAs. More faculty co-planning time with LAs was also associated with better performance (+0.004 effect size per additional minute/week), although this relationship was not statistically significant.
finding.measure: Instructor experience teaching with LAs; faculty meeting/co-planning time with LAs; student concept inventory effect sizes
finding.effect_size: +0.154 per additional term taught with LAs

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports institutional and classroom-level variation in LA-supported outcomes, suggesting that implementation context matters for scalability and best-practice development. At the same time, the authors identify inequitable patterns by gender and race, including lower average effect sizes for female students (d=0.485) than male students (d=0.749), indicating that the LA model did not eliminate existing disparities in these settings.
finding.measure: Student concept inventory effect sizes disaggregated by gender and race; course/institution context features
finding.study_size: n=3,315 usable pre-post pairs; 17 instructors; 13 institutions
finding.effect_size: Female d=0.485 vs male d=0.749; white d=0.619 vs Asian d=0.557 and other d=0.509

paper_profiles.title: Taming Silent Failures: A Framework for Verifiable AI Reliability
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of silent failures in AI-enabled safety-critical systems: cases where a model produces confident but incorrect outputs without an explicit crash, error, or warning. The authors argue that conventional pre-deployment testing and white-box verification are insufficient for complex deep neural networks operating in open-world conditions, especially under distribution shift, sensor faults, occlusion, and other environmental stressors.

To address this, the paper proposes the Formal Assurance and Monitoring Environment (FAME), a two-phase framework that combines offline formal specification and synthesis with online runtime monitoring and mitigation. Safety requirements are expressed in Signal Temporal Logic and converted into lightweight monitors that observe AI inputs and outputs at runtime, detect violations, and trigger fail-safe, fail-operational, or fail-degraded responses. The framework also includes a feedback loop that logs violations for retraining and specification refinement.

The paper’s empirical demonstration uses a YOLOv4 pedestrian-detection system in the CARLA simulator for an autonomous driving perception task. Across nominal and challenging driving scenarios, the authors report that the monitor detected most silent failures while producing no false positives in nominal conditions. The main conclusion is that verifiable runtime assurance can provide a practical safety net around opaque AI components, and that this approach may support certification-oriented safety processes such as ISO 26262 and ISO/PAS 8800. The paper is not an education study and does not involve K-12 learners or teachers.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a framework and proof-of-concept engineering paper, not a K-12 educational intervention study. It reports a single simulated autonomous-vehicle case study rather than a rigorous educational evaluation, so it does not meet criteria for educational evidence quality tiers beyond descriptive/technical demonstration.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: There is no direct educational outcome or K-12 impact reported. The paper’s results concern detection of silent failures in a simulated perception system, not learner achievement, engagement, or institutional outcomes in education.

interventions.use_case: runtime assurance / formal verification framework for monitoring AI-powered perception outputs, synthesizing safety monitors from STL specifications to detect silent failures, misinformation-like wrong outputs, and overreliance risks in safety-critical systems

paper_profiles.title: GOD model: Privacy Preserved AI School for Personal Assistant
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper proposes the Guardian of Data (GOD) model, a privacy-preserving framework for evaluating and improving personal AI assistants on-device. The core problem it addresses is the tension between personalization and privacy: proactive assistants need sensitive user data to anticipate needs, but collecting and using such data raises concerns about trust, autonomy, and unauthorized disclosure.

The proposed approach runs inside a Trusted Execution Environment (TEE) and generates curriculum-based evaluation tasks that range from simple factual retrieval to more complex cross-domain and proactive recommendation problems. It also introduces data connectors for secure verification, a scoring function based on coverage, quality, and freshness, and anti-gaming safeguards such as identity checks, cross-verification, and fraud penalties.

The paper is not an empirical study with human participants; it is a systems/framework paper focused on on-device personal AI rather than K-12 education. Its main conclusion is that a secure, curriculum-based, privacy-preserving evaluation and training loop can help personal assistants become more proactive while keeping raw user data on device and reducing the risks of fraud, misuse, and loss of trust.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a preprint / framework proposal with conceptual architecture, equations, and illustrative examples, not a peer-reviewed empirical study. It does not report a credible experimental design, comparator, or validated K-12 outcome evidence.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No K-12 learning or student outcome impact is demonstrated. The paper is about privacy-preserving evaluation of personal AI assistants, with no empirical effect sizes on educational populations or science inquiry outcomes.

interventions.use_case: A privacy-preserving on-device personal AI assistant that uses a TEE-based 'AI school' framework to evaluate and improve proactive recommendations from private user data (email, calendar, receipts, social media) using curriculum-based queries, imitation learning, and reinforcement learning.

Trusted Execution Environment (TEE)-based secure evaluation and grading infrastructure for on-device AI, including data connectors, anti-gaming safeguards, and privacy-preserving verification of user data.

paper_profiles.title: The Quest for Reliable Metrics of Responsible AI
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of how to evaluate responsible AI systems reliably, with a particular focus on fairness metrics used in recommender systems. The authors argue that although many metrics exist, their robustness, interpretability, and mathematical validity are often insufficiently examined, which can make metric scores misleading or unstable.

Rather than studying a classroom, school, or K-12 intervention, the paper synthesizes prior work on fairness evaluation in recommender systems and extends those lessons to AI in science (AIS). The approach is conceptual and reflective: the authors review prior analyses of metric limitations, describe issues such as invalid mathematical operations, unknown or unreachable score ranges, low sensitivity, and redundancy, and then propose corrected metrics and new evaluation approaches.

The paper offers practical guidelines for designing reliable metrics of responsible AI, including questions to ask about validity, range, sensitivity, and redundancy. Its main conclusion is that metric development itself must be treated as a core part of responsible AI, because evaluation scores can be unreliable or overstate fairness if metric limitations are ignored. The guidelines are intended to generalize beyond recommender systems to AIS and other AI applications.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a theoretical/reflection paper and guidelines piece, not an empirical study of an educational intervention. It does not present a controlled design, participant data, or causal evaluation relevant to K-12 efficacy criteria.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper has indirect impact by improving how AI systems may be evaluated and governed, but it does not measure learner outcomes. Its relevance is mainly conceptual and methodological, so any practical impact is unclear and modest.

interventions.use_case: Methodological analysis of fairness and responsible-AI evaluation metrics for AI systems, with examples drawn from recommender systems and broader AI-in-science contexts rather than a student-facing educational tool.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that reliable evaluation metrics are necessary for responsible AI governance and policy, especially in high-stakes AI-in-science contexts. It does not report an experimental effect size; instead, it provides guidelines and conceptual evidence that flawed metrics can mislead policy and evaluation practice.
finding.measure: Robustness/reliability of fairness evaluation metrics; interpretability and validity of metric scores

finding.finding_summary: The paper proposes corrected metrics and new evaluation approaches that are intended to make responsible-AI assessment easier and more usable in practice. It reports that some existing metrics can crash, have unreachable ranges, or be redundant, implying that better metric design can improve the efficiency and reliability of evaluation workflows.
finding.measure: Metric computability, score-range interpretability, sensitivity, redundancy

paper_profiles.title: Inverted Classroom an der Hochschule Karlsruhe - ein nicht quantisierter Flip
paper_profiles.venue: Das Inverted Classroom Model: Begleitband zur ersten deutschen ICM-Konferenz
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper discusses the introduction and early evaluation of the Inverted Classroom Model (ICM) at Hochschule Karlsruhe as part of the SKATING project. The central problem is how to improve teaching and reduce student difficulties in engineering-oriented higher education, especially issues related to heterogeneous prior knowledge, limited semester-long studying, and high dropout risk. The authors frame ICM as a potentially useful response because it shifts content delivery outside class and uses class time for guided practice, interaction, and deeper learning.

The approach studied is not a single standardized intervention but a set of pilot implementations of ICM variants, ranging from minimally inverted lecture summaries to partially or fully inverted topics in mathematics. The paper emphasizes careful adaptation to course, instructor, and student needs, and it outlines an evaluation strategy combining student surveys, classroom observation, usage statistics, and course outcomes. In the described pilot, an upper-level engineering mathematics course at Hochschule Karlsruhe was partly inverted using recorded video materials made available through ILIAS and YouTube, with in-class time used for problem solving and discussion.

The authors conclude that ICM can be implemented in a flexible, staged way and may support student engagement, self-paced learning, and richer in-class interaction. However, they stress that success depends on fit with local conditions, student cooperation, and careful evaluation of both intended and unintended effects such as increased workload, technical problems, and differential benefits across learners. The paper is primarily a methodological and reflective report on early implementation rather than a results paper with definitive outcome findings.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative/pilot report with descriptive process evaluation, student feedback, and planned follow-up comparisons, not a controlled experiment. It is peer-reviewed conference/book chapter style academic work, but the evidence base is low on causal credibility.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports promising but unquantified benefits and mainly discusses implementation feasibility and student engagement. Because no effect sizes are reported and the scope is a small pilot, the impact is modest and unclear for broader generalization.

interventions.use_case: inverted classroom implementation using recorded lecture summaries, short instructional videos, forum support, and online materials for K-12/tertiary-style blended learning support

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports a pilot inverted-classroom implementation in higher mathematics (Höhere Mathematik 3) with about 20 students, but provides no numerical effect size. The author describes improved engagement with the topic Differentialgleichungssysteme and plans to compare future exam results against prior years, indicating a positive but still preliminary academic signal rather than a quantified impact.
finding.measure: student understanding/participation in higher mathematics topic sessions; planned comparison of exam results

finding.finding_summary: The article emphasizes increased student motivation, curiosity, and a 'flow' experience as key success criteria, and reports mostly positive student feedback during the pilot. Students noted concerns about missing opportunities to ask questions and possible extra time burden, but the overall reception of the method was favorable.
finding.measure: student feedback, perceived motivation/curiosity, satisfaction surveys, informal responses

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that the inverted classroom supports active problem solving, peer work, and more interaction in class, and observes large in-class phases of guided self-study and partner problem solving. No numerical effect size is reported, but the intended and observed emphasis is on collaboration and self-regulated preparation.
finding.measure: observed collaboration/partner work, self-study behavior, participation in discussion

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports clear implementation and preparation costs: about 1 hour of production time per recording, plus roughly 30 minutes of teacher setup and 30 minutes of organization per session when the professor self-recorded the material. At the same time, it suggests that once materials are created, later semesters may require less effort, so the overall workload effect is mixed and context-dependent.
finding.measure: teacher preparation time, production time, organizational workload

finding.finding_summary: The paper frames the inverted classroom as a potentially scalable reform strategy for improving persistence and making engineering study more feasible, especially at applied universities with heterogeneous entrants. This is a conceptual and pilot-level institutional argument rather than a quantified outcome, but it is clearly positioned as supporting broader teaching reform and study success.
finding.measure: institutional adoption potential, perceived fit for study reform and dropout reduction

paper_profiles.title: Trust and Reliance on AI in Education: AI Literacy and Need for Cognition as Moderators
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how students’ trust in an AI assistant relates to their reliance on AI-generated recommendations during problem-solving, with a particular focus on whether trust is associated with appropriate reliance versus overreliance. The authors frame the problem around the growing use of generative AI in education and the risk that students may accept fluent but incorrect outputs without sufficient evaluation. They ask whether higher trust predicts better calibrated use of AI support, or whether it instead corresponds to weaker discrimination between correct and misleading advice.

To study this, the researchers ran a single-session laboratory experiment with 432 undergraduate students enrolled in computing-related courses at the University of Florida. Participants solved 14 Python output-prediction problems while interacting with an AI chatbot that provided a mix of accurate and intentionally misleading recommendations and explanations. The design used a Wizard-of-Oz approach for the initial responses, with OpenAI API handling follow-up questions. Participants completed pre- and post-task surveys measuring AI literacy, need for cognition, programming self-efficacy, programming literacy, and post-task trust in the assistant.

Results showed that higher trust was associated with lower appropriate reliance, meaning students with greater trust were less likely to accept correct AI advice and reject incorrect advice in a calibrated way. Overreliance on misleading suggestions was common, while underreliance was rare. The trust–reliance relationship was nonlinear but did not reverse within the observed range. AI literacy and need for cognition moderated the association, such that these characteristics were linked to more selective reliance at lower levels of trust, but the negative relationship between trust and appropriate reliance became stronger as trust increased. The authors conclude that educational AI tools should include instructional and system supports that prompt verification and reflective evaluation, such as cognitive forcing functions and justification prompts.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed experimental study with a sizable sample and randomized ordering of tasks, but it is not an RCT of an educational intervention in the usual sense and relies on a lab-based Wizard-of-Oz setup plus self-report moderators. It provides credible correlational/experimental evidence about trust and reliance, but not full causal evidence for a learning intervention.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The findings indicate a meaningful negative relationship between trust and appropriate reliance (R2 = .173; r = -0.42) in a programming-learning context, but the study does not test an educational intervention that improves K-12 outcomes. Impact is therefore informative for design and safety, yet the direct educational effect is indirect and the population is higher education rather than K-12.

interventions.use_case: AI chatbot assistant used during programming output-prediction tasks, providing recommendations and explanations with a mix of accurate and intentionally misleading suggestions; follow-up Q&A used OpenAI gpt-3.5-turbo-0125 in a Wizard-of-Oz setup.

finding.finding_summary: Higher post-task trust was associated with lower appropriate reliance on the AI assistant during Python problem-solving. In the main model, trust negatively predicted appropriate reliance (b = -3.65, SE = 0.39, t(430) = -9.48, p < .001, R2 = .173), indicating less selective acceptance/rejection of AI recommendations as trust increased. The outcome reflects metacognitive judgment and critical evaluation rather than task accuracy alone.
finding.measure: Appropriate reliance on AI recommendations during 14 Python output-prediction problems

finding.finding_summary: Task accuracy was also negatively associated with trust in the AI assistant. Students completed the programming task with mean accuracy of 61.21% (SD = 10.93), and higher trust predicted lower accuracy (r = -0.38, p < .001), consistent with greater acceptance of misleading recommendations in this setting.
finding.measure: Programming task accuracy on 14 Python output-prediction problems

finding.finding_summary: Moderation analyses showed that AI literacy and need for cognition significantly moderated the trust–appropriate reliance relationship, while programming self-efficacy and programming literacy did not. The trust × AI literacy interaction was negative (b = -1.03, p = .014) and the trust × need for cognition interaction was also negative (b = -0.99, p = .040), suggesting these traits supported more selective reliance mainly when trust was lower.
finding.measure: Interaction effects in regression models predicting appropriate reliance from trust and learner characteristics
finding.effect_size: AI literacy interaction b = -1.03; Need for cognition interaction b = -0.99

paper_profiles.title: Beyond Misinformation: A Conceptual Framework for Studying AI Hallucinations in (Science) Communication
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of how to conceptualize and study AI hallucinations as a distinct source of misinformation, rather than treating them only as technical errors. The author argues that generative AI systems, especially large language models, can produce false but plausible outputs without human intent, creating challenges for existing misinformation frameworks that were built around human actors and intentional deception.

The paper proposes a conceptual framework grounded in a supply-and-demand model and the idea of distributed agency. On the supply side, it distinguishes hallucinations from human misinformation by tracing their origins to probabilistic text generation, limitations in training data, and weaknesses in gatekeeping and alignment. On the demand side, it outlines how users, groups, and institutions may perceive, share, and respond to hallucinated content across macro, meso, and micro levels, including issues of trust, credibility, digital literacy, and group reinforcement.

The paper is not an empirical study of K-12 learners or educators; it is a theoretical and research-agenda piece focused on communication scholarship and science communication more broadly. Its main conclusion is that AI hallucinations should be treated as a separate category of misinformation with distinct production mechanisms and social consequences, and that future research should examine their emergence, spread, and effects on audiences, institutions, and information ecosystems.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a conceptual/framework essay rather than an empirical study. It does not present a study design, sample, or measured outcomes, so it provides no direct evidence to evaluate under the K-12 evidence framework.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper has no demonstrated intervention effect on learners or institutions because it is theoretical only. Its contribution is to define a research agenda around AI hallucinations, misinformation, and safety, not to report impact findings.

paper_profiles.title: Disagreement as a way to study misinformation and its effects
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a conceptual problem in misinformation research: the common definition of misinformation is too narrow to explain the broader social, political, and psychological outcomes often attributed to it, such as polarization, distrust, and vaccine hesitancy. The authors argue that these outcomes are better studied through the lens of disagreement—conflicting beliefs, attitudes, values, and epistemologies between communities—rather than by focusing only on false or misleading content.

The paper does not test an intervention in a K-12 or education setting. Instead, it proposes a theoretical framework and compares it with prevailing misinformation concepts. The authors argue that disagreement better captures the factors that shape misinformation-related harms, allows more neutral and automatable measurement, and can help identify more effective intervention strategies. They also re-evaluate several existing misinformation interventions through this lens and show how disagreement can guide new strategies, including for vaccine hesitancy and ideological polarization.

Empirically, the paper includes longitudinal analyses of disagreement in text data: letters to the editor of The New York Times from 1950–2022 and vaccine-related tweets on Twitter. These analyses suggest disagreement has increased since 2006 and show that disagreement measures correlate with existing misinformation-related indicators. The broader conclusion is that disagreement is a more useful framework for studying misinformation effects, though the authors emphasize that their empirical findings are preliminary and meant as demonstrations rather than benchmarks.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a conceptual/theoretical review article with illustrative quantitative analyses, not an intervention study in K-12 education. It does not evaluate a pedagogical technology or AI system in a way that would support causal or quasi-experimental evidence grading.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper has no direct measured impact on student learning or educational practice in K-12 science inquiry. Its contribution is mainly conceptual, proposing disagreement as a framework for misinformation research rather than demonstrating educational outcomes.

paper_profiles.title: New Kid in the Classroom: Exploring Student Perceptions of AI Coding Assistants
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This exploratory paper asks how undergraduate novice programmers perceive AI coding assistants when using them in an authentic programming assessment. The central concern is whether AI support helps students learn and solve problems or instead encourages overreliance and weak transfer when support is removed.

The study examined a two-part exam in an introductory object-oriented programming course. In the first part, 20 undergraduate students at the District University of Bogota could use AI code assistants such as ChatGPT, Perplexity, Grok, or DeepSeek while completing a Java programming task. In the second part, one week later, they had to extend their solution without any AI assistance. Afterward, students completed an anonymous survey with Likert-scale and open-ended questions, and the author analyzed the responses descriptively and thematically.

Results show that students generally viewed AI as useful for speed, debugging, and initial conceptual support, but their confidence and performance dropped when they had to work unaided. Qualitative responses suggested that many students could understand or adapt AI-generated code only partially, and some acknowledged dependence on the tool. The paper concludes that AI assistants can support programming education, but they should be integrated as scaffolds rather than substitutes for independent problem solving, because overreliance may hinder knowledge transfer and deeper learning.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a small exploratory qualitative/mixed-methods case study with n=20 and no randomization or causal identification. It provides useful descriptive evidence, but credibility is limited by self-report, single-course context, and lack of objective learning outcome measures.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests meaningful but unclear impact: students perceived speed/efficiency gains, yet also reported overreliance and weak knowledge transfer. Because the evidence is descriptive and effect sizes are not tied to learning gains, the overall educational impact is modest and uncertain.

interventions.use_case: student use of AI coding assistants (e.g., ChatGPT, Perplexity, Grok, DeepSeek) to generate, explain, debug, and adapt Java code during an introductory programming exam

finding.finding_summary: This exploratory case study found that AI assistants were perceived as helpful for grasping code concepts and boosting confidence during the first programming task, but many students struggled when asked to work without AI in the second task, suggesting limited transfer and possible overreliance. In the open-ended responses, students frequently reported partial understanding, difficulty with syntax/debugging, and concern that AI reduced independent problem-solving, although some said it supported conceptual scaffolding and code adaptation. No experimental effect size was reported; the study reported descriptive means such as perceived faster solving (M=3.65/5) and moderate overall AI use (M=3.15/5), plus a Spearman correlation between perceived AI use and faster solving (ρ=0.64, p=0.002).
finding.measure: Student perceptions of understanding, confidence, transfer to unaided problem-solving, and reported difficulty with independent coding tasks after AI use
finding.effect_size: ρ=0.64 (perceived AI usage vs perceived faster solving)
finding.std_deviation: σ=0.88 (overall AI usage), σ=1.12 (perceived conceptual understanding)

finding.finding_summary: Students strongly perceived AI as improving programming efficiency, especially by speeding up problem solving and debugging. The quantitative survey showed the highest rating for faster solving (M=3.65/5), and a Spearman correlation indicated that heavier AI use was associated with stronger perceived speed gains (ρ=0.64, p=0.002). However, this efficiency benefit coexisted with concerns about shallow understanding and later dependence when AI was removed.
finding.measure: Likert-scale perceptions of faster solving, AI usage, and open-ended comments about speed/debugging
finding.std_deviation: σ=0.88 (overall AI usage); M=3.65/5 for perceived speed gains

paper_profiles.title: Enhancing secondary school students' attitudes toward physics by using computer simulations
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Data and Network Science
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether computer simulations can improve secondary school students’ attitudes toward physics, particularly attitudes toward scientific inquiry, enjoyment of science lessons, and interest in science-related careers. The authors frame the study as a response to concerns about negative attitudes toward physics and the need for more interactive science instruction.

The intervention used PhET interactive simulations of Newton’s Second Law of Motion in an eleventh-grade physics unit. Students in the experimental group completed simulation-based inquiry activities, while the control group received conventional face-to-face instruction and hands-on experiments. The study used a pre-test/post-test quasi-experimental design with 90 Grade 11 students from two public schools in Al Ain, United Arab Emirates, and measured attitudes using selected TOSRA scales.

Results showed statistically significant post-test differences favoring the simulation group on all three attitude dimensions: attitudes toward scientific inquiry, enjoyment of science lessons, and career interest in physics/science. The authors also reported large effect sizes and gender-related differences, with the simulation-based approach benefiting both male and female students. They conclude that computer simulations can meaningfully strengthen students’ attitudes toward physics and recommend wider integration of simulations into physics teaching, along with teacher training and further longitudinal research.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a quasi-experimental pre-test/post-test control-group study with 90 secondary students and appropriate comparison groups, giving it moderate credibility. It is not randomized and relies on attitude outcomes rather than direct achievement, so it does not meet blue-tier standards.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported group effects are very large (e.g., t=22.76; partial η² values around .75-.80 across key subscales), indicating substantial impact on the measured attitude outcomes. The intervention targets a priority K-12 science population and shows strong positive effects.

interventions.use_case: PhET interactive computer simulation used as an inquiry tool to teach Newton’s Second Law of Motion in 11th-grade physics, replacing conventional face-to-face instruction and hands-on lab work with simulation-based virtual experiments.

finding.finding_summary: The study found statistically significant improvements in students’ attitudes toward science-related learning after the PhET simulation intervention. On the full TOSRA-related attitude measure, the experimental group (n=45) outperformed the control group (n=45) at post-test, t(88)=22.76, p=.000, with much higher mean scores (EG M=4.17, SD=.18 vs CG M=2.68, SD=.39).
finding.measure: TOSRA attitude scales, including attitudes toward scientific inquiry, enjoyment of science lessons, and career interest in science/physics

finding.finding_summary: The simulation-based group showed significant gains on the TOSRA Attitudes toward Scientific Inquiry scale. Post-test scores favored the experimental group (M=4.01, SD=.34) over the control group (M=2.49, SD=.54), with t(88)=15.819, p=.000 and a large multivariate group effect (partial η²=.748 for ASI in the group comparison).
finding.measure: TOSRA Attitudes toward Scientific Inquiry (ASI) scale

finding.finding_summary: The intervention improved students’ enjoyment of science lessons. The experimental group scored much higher than the control group on ESL post-test means (EG M=4.24, SD=.33 vs CG M=2.72, SD=.48), with t(88)=17.169, p=.000 and a large group effect in the MANOVA/ANOVA results (partial η²=.785).
finding.measure: TOSRA Enjoyment of Science Lessons (ESL) scale

finding.finding_summary: The PhET-based condition also improved career interest in physics/science. Post-test CIS scores favored the experimental group (EG M=4.26, SD=.29) over the control group (CG M=2.85, SD=.43), with t(88)=18.067, p=.000 and a large group effect (partial η²=.797).
finding.measure: TOSRA Career Interest in Science/Physics (CIS) scale

paper_profiles.title: Students’ Acquisition of Science Process Skills in Chemistry through Computer Simulations and Animations in Secondary Schools in Tanzania
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Learning, Teaching and Educational Research
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether computer simulations and animations improve secondary school students’ acquisition of integrated science process skills in chemistry compared with conventional instructional materials. The problem addressed is the persistent weakness in science process skills in Tanzanian secondary schools, attributed to teacher-centered instruction, limited laboratory resources, and low access to ICT-supported inquiry learning.

The study used a quasi-experimental pretest-posttest comparison with mixed methods. Four public secondary schools in the Dodoma and Singida regions of Tanzania participated, involving 320 level-three chemistry students and 20 chemistry teachers. The treatment group learned chemical kinetics, equilibrium, and energetics using computer simulations and animations (from Yenka Chemistry and PhET), while the control group used conventional materials such as textbooks, diagrams, pictures, models, and laboratory materials. Both groups were taught through a 5E inquiry-based approach, and student focus group discussions provided qualitative data.

Results showed no significant pretest differences between groups, but the treatment group outperformed the control group on the posttest science process skills measure. The authors conclude that computer simulations and animations support students’ inquiry, help them visualize abstract chemistry concepts, and improve skills such as hypothesizing, identifying variables, planning experiments, interpreting data, and drawing conclusions. They recommend wider use of simulations and animations in Tanzanian secondary school chemistry.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a quasi-experimental pre/post study with control and treatment groups, plus qualitative triangulation. It is not randomized, but it does provide a reasonably designed comparison with baseline equivalence and clear outcome measures.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The study reports a sizable positive post-test difference on science process skills, with treatment-group gains well above control performance. Because the outcome is a priority K-12 science reasoning skill and the difference is substantial, the impact is best rated green rather than yellow.

interventions.use_case: computer simulations and animations used in secondary school chemistry lessons on chemical kinetics, equilibrium, and energetics to support inquiry-based science process skill development

finding.finding_summary: Students exposed to computer simulations and animations scored substantially higher on the integrated science process skills test than those taught with conventional materials. Post-test means were 65.79 (SD=13.45) for the treatment group versus 48.03 (SD=11.72) for the control group, with a statistically significant between-group difference (p=0.000).
finding.measure: 25-item integrated science process skills test covering hypothesis formation, identifying variables, operationally defining, planning experiments, interpreting data, and drawing conclusions
finding.std_deviation: treatment post-test SD=13.45; control post-test SD=11.72

paper_profiles.title: Affect in Peer Group Learning During Virtual Science Inquiry: Insights From Self-Reports and Video Observations
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates how affect is expressed and experienced during collaborative science inquiry in a computer-based virtual learning environment, and whether affect is related to group performance. The authors ask whether students’ positive and negative emotions differ across phases of inquiry, whether affect differs by group outcome, and how self-reported affect compares with observed affect from video coding.

The intervention/context is a web-based virtual science inquiry environment called Virtual Baltic Sea Explorer (ViBSE). High school students worked in small peer groups on an interdisciplinary science task involving hypotheses, planning, experimentation in a virtual laboratory, analysis, and preparing a group presentation. Students completed repeated self-report affect scales after each working session, and researchers coded affective behavior from video segments using a multimethod approach.

The study included six carefully selected intact groups of three students each (18 students total) from a larger sample of 39 groups in Finnish high schools. The paper finds that positive affect was dominant overall in both self-reports and observations across all phases, though experimentation elicited relatively more negative affect. Differences between high-, average-, and low-performing groups were visible, especially in self-reports, but the authors report no clear effect of affect on group outcome. Observations generally showed lower-intensity affect than self-reports and revealed some negative affect that students did not report, underscoring the value of combining methods when studying collaborative science learning.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed qualitative/multimethod observational study, not an RCT or QED. It provides rich descriptive evidence but does not meet higher-credibility causal criteria for intervention effects.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports no measurable positive impact of the virtual inquiry environment on outcome and includes no effect size. Findings are informative for design and affect in collaborative science learning, but the impact on learner outcomes is unclear and likely modest at best.

interventions.use_case: web-based virtual science inquiry environment (Virtual Baltic Sea Explorer) with simulation-based laboratory tasks for high school students investigating pH effects on copepods in the Baltic Sea food chain

finding.finding_summary: This study did not test an instructional improvement in science reasoning; instead, it examined whether affect related to group outcome during virtual science inquiry. Across six groups (n=18 focal students; 39 groups in the broader class), no effect of affect on group outcome was found, despite differences in presentation quality across high, average, and low groups.
finding.measure: quality of final group presentation in a virtual science inquiry task (research plan, hypotheses, understanding, presentation structure, conclusions, scientific language)
finding.study_size: n=18 focal students (6 groups); broader class n=120, 39 groups

finding.finding_summary: Positive affect was prevalent across self-reports and observations, but the Experimentation phase showed more negative affect than the other phases in self-reports (e.g., 33% negative vs. 12% in Planning and 10% in Conclusions). Across groups, high-performing groups were more consistently positive, while low-performing groups showed more negative affect; however, the study concluded that affect did not predict group outcome overall.
finding.measure: self-reported affect scale and video-coded observed affect (valence and arousal/intensity) across planning, experimentation, and conclusions phases

finding.finding_summary: The paper closely examined collaborative interaction and within-group consistency in affect during joint science inquiry. High-performing groups showed more consistent positive affect and smoother collaboration, whereas the average and low groups showed more ambivalence, confusion, and unequal participation; no numeric effect size was reported.
finding.measure: video-observed interaction quality, within-group affect consistency, and participation patterns during collaborative inquiry

paper_profiles.title: Applying Science Learning PhET Simulation to Improve Process Skill and Knowledge Aspect of Junior High School Student
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether using PhET simulation in science learning can improve junior high school students’ science process skills and knowledge about light and optical instruments. The authors frame the problem as students’ low engagement and weak learning outcomes in conventional science lessons, especially for abstract topics that are difficult to understand through text or lecture alone.

The intervention was a science lesson supported by the PhET simulation program, which the authors describe as functioning like a virtual laboratory. The study used a one-group pretest-posttest pre-experimental design with 30 eighth-grade students at SMPN 1 Ngoro, Indonesia. Data were collected through tests, observations, and student questionnaires; the paper reports pretest and posttest scores, N-gain, observed student activity, and student responses.

Results showed gains in both science process skills and knowledge, with high N-gain values reported for both outcomes. Student activity during learning was described as high, and student responses were largely positive.
