The authors conclude that PhET-assisted science learning can improve students’ process skills and knowledge aspects, while noting that careful preparation and time management are important for effective implementation.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a small pre-experimental one-group pretest-posttest study with no comparison group, so internal validity is limited. It is peer-reviewed, but the design provides only low-to-moderate credibility evidence for causal claims.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported gains are large (N-gain 0.71 and 0.74) on a priority K-12 science topic, suggesting potentially meaningful impact. However, the lack of a control group and the small sample make the real-world impact uncertain.

interventions.use_case: PhET simulation-supported science learning for junior high school students on light and optical instruments, using virtual simulation as a classroom/virtual lab substitute to support inquiry and concept building.

finding.finding_summary: In a one-group pretest-posttest study with 30 grade-8 students, PhET-supported science learning increased science process skills from a pretest mean of 29 to a posttest mean of 80. The paper reports an N-gain of 0.71 (high criterion), with improvements across problem formulation, hypothesis formulation, data analysis, communication, and concluding.
finding.measure: Science process skills test / process skills assessment

finding.finding_summary: The same PhET intervention improved students' knowledge of light and optical instruments from a pretest mean of 24 to a posttest mean of 80 in the 30-student sample. The study reports an N-gain of 0.74 (high criterion), indicating substantial gains on cognitive knowledge indicators such as laws of reflection, image formation, and optical devices.
finding.measure: Knowledge test on light and optical instruments

finding.finding_summary: Student engagement/activity during PhET-based learning was described as high, with the highest observed activity being experiment/observation (18.3%) and low irrelevant behavior (3%). Students also reported a very positive response to the learning process (83%), with response items ranging from 77% to 90%.
finding.measure: Classroom activity observation and student response questionnaire

paper_profiles.title: On the Modular Isomorphism Problem for groups of class 3 and obelisks
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the Modular Isomorphism Problem (MIP) for finite p-groups: whether an isomorphism of modular group algebras kG and kH implies an isomorphism of the underlying groups G and H. The authors develop algebraic and group-theoretic techniques using the small group algebra, Jennings theory, and invariants derived from the lower central series and related quotients.

The paper proves new positive results for several families of p-groups, especially groups of nilpotency class 3 and certain 2-generated groups. It shows that, under specific structural conditions, the small group algebra determines the group up to isomorphism, and it also establishes invariance results for members of the lower central series for 2-generated class-3 groups with central exponent-p third commutator subgroup. The work further analyzes p-obelisks and exhibits an example of non-isomorphic groups with isomorphic small group algebras, showing limits of previously used strategies.

The setting is entirely mathematical and computational, focused on abstract finite p-groups and their modular group algebras rather than human participants or educational contexts. The main conclusion is that the small group algebra and related invariants resolve additional cases of the MIP, while also clarifying where existing methods fail.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This paper is a pure mathematics research article on the modular isomorphism problem for finite p-groups and modular group algebras. It does not study any educational technology intervention, K-12 population, or learning outcome.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: There is no educational intervention, implementation, or learner outcome in this paper, so it has no direct impact on K-12 science inquiry or AI-supported education.

paper_profiles.title: Data Preservation in High-Energy Physics
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of how to preserve and reuse data from high-energy physics experiments after the original collaborations and detector operations have ended. It argues that these datasets are scientifically valuable because they are often unique, costly to reproduce, and potentially useful for new theoretical work, cross-experiment combinations, re-analyses with improved methods, and educational outreach. The document is an intermediate report from an international study group convened in 2008–2009 to examine the state of data preservation in high-energy physics.

The paper does not study an educational intervention or AI-supported science inquiry in K-12. Instead, it lays out preservation models ranging from enhanced documentation only, to simplified data formats, to preserving analysis software, to full preservation of reconstruction and simulation software together with raw/basic data. It also discusses the infrastructure, funding, governance, validation, and archival expertise needed to sustain preserved data over time, including the proposed role of a data archivist and the potential use of virtualisation.

The context is the international high-energy physics community, including large collaborations, computing centres, laboratories, and funding agencies. The paper concludes that urgent action is needed because many experiments are nearing or past their end dates, and that full preservation of analysis capability is recommended when feasible. It proposes a global governance structure, the International Data Preservation Forum, to coordinate policy, standards, and access to preserved data.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a grey-literature/consensus report on data preservation policy in high-energy physics, not an empirical K-12 study. It contains no comparison group, no measured educational outcomes, and no causal identification.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper has no direct impact on K-12 science learning outcomes or AI-supported inquiry. Its relevance is only indirect and institutional, focused on HEP archival governance rather than educational effects.

finding.finding_summary: This is a policy/report-style study on high-energy physics data preservation, not an educational intervention experiment. It argues that long-term preservation can improve future scientific opportunities, reuse, and outreach, but it presents no experimental effect estimates or student-level outcome data.
finding.measure: Policy, governance, and data preservation framework recommendations for HEP institutions

paper_profiles.title: On Laminar Groups, Tits Alternatives, and Convergence Group Actions on S2
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a purely theoretical mathematics article about groups of circle homeomorphisms that preserve laminations. The central problem is to understand the structure of pseudo-fibered groups, a class of laminar groups motivated by actions arising from fibered 3-manifolds and pseudo-Anosov dynamics. The authors ask what dynamical and algebraic properties follow from the existence of two invariant, very full, loose laminations with distinct endpoints.

The paper develops several results about these groups. First, it proves a Tits alternative for torsion-free pseudo-fibered groups: every subgroup either contains a non-abelian free subgroup or is virtually abelian. The proof is based on dynamical analysis of periodic points and fixed-point configurations of hyperbolic and pseudo-Anosov-like elements, together with ping-pong and Hölder’s theorem. Second, for purely hyperbolic pseudo-fibered groups, it proves that the group acts on the 2-sphere as a convergence group via a Cannon-Thurston type quotient construction.

The context is abstract group actions on S1 and S2, not an educational setting. The paper provides examples from free products of finite cyclic groups and relates its results to 3-manifold groups, Fuchsian groups, and conjectures about hyperbolic 3-manifold groups. Its main conclusions are structural and conjectural, with no empirical data, participants, or intervention study.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This paper is a mathematics article on group actions, laminations, and convergence groups, not an education study. It contains no empirical evaluation, no K-12 participants, and no AI or instructional technology intervention.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: There is no educational outcome or intervention impact to assess. The paper has no direct relevance to K-12 learning effects or educational implementation outcomes.

paper_profiles.title: 3 Questions on Cut Groups
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a theoretical mathematics article about finite group theory, not an education study. It investigates three open questions about cut groups, also called inverse semi-rational groups, and their structural properties.

The first question asks whether the degrees of the fields generated by character table entries are uniformly bounded across all cut groups. The paper notes known positive results for solvable cut groups and for quasi-simple or almost simple groups, while also contrasting these with related classes where the answer is negative.

The second question concerns whether Sylow 3-subgroups of cut groups are themselves cut. The paper reviews partial positive results from prior work for several classes of groups, including solvable, Frobenius, odd-order, and quasi/simple groups. The third question asks whether certain normal p-subgroups in solvable cut groups have exponent dividing p for p in {5,7}. The paper mainly synthesizes existing results and poses open problems; it does not report an intervention, participants, or empirical outcomes.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a pure mathematics/theory paper on cut groups and character tables, with no educational technology intervention, no K-12 context, and no empirical study design. It is not evidence about AI-supported science inquiry or student outcomes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: There is no educational or learner impact reported, and no intervention effects are evaluated. The paper has no direct relevance to K-12 learning outcomes or technology implementation.

paper_profiles.title: On partial Π-property of subgroups of finite groups
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper studies a group-theoretic property called partial Π-property for subgroups of finite groups. The authors define the new property as a weakening of the previously known Π-property and show, via examples, that the converse implication does not hold. The work is not an empirical study in education or AI; instead, it develops abstract finite group theory results and proves a series of theorems and propositions about subgroup embedding conditions and their consequences for group structure.

The main results give sufficient conditions under which normal p-subgroups, Sylow subgroups, or certain cyclic/maximal subgroups must lie in hypercentral or p-hypercentral parts of the group, leading to conclusions such as p-nilpotence, p-supersolvability, or membership in a specified formation. The paper also derives corollaries and then shows that many previously studied embedding notions—such as CAP-subgroups, S-quasinormality, weakly S-permutable subgroups, and related conditions—imply partial Π-property. These connections are presented as structural applications within finite group theory rather than as experimental outcomes.

No human participants, instructional setting, intervention, or outcome evaluation are reported. The paper is purely theoretical and mathematical, with proofs and applications to abstract subgroup properties in finite groups.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This paper is a pure abstract algebra/theory manuscript about subgroup properties in finite groups, not an educational technology study. It contains no empirical educational methodology, no intervention evaluation, and no K-12 outcomes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: There is no evidence of impact on education or learning outcomes because the paper does not study any educational intervention or population. No comparable effect sizes or outcome measures are reported.

paper_profiles.title: Property R∞ for some spherical and affine Artin–Tits groups
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper studies the Reidemeister number problem for automorphisms of certain Artin–Tits groups, asking when every automorphism has infinitely many twisted conjugacy classes, i.e. property R∞. The authors focus on irreducible Artin–Tits groups of spherical types An, Bn, D4, I2(m), their pure subgroups, and affine types \u007eAn−1 and \u007eCn.

The main approach is group-theoretic and geometric: the authors identify suitable central quotients of these groups with finite-index subgroups of extended mapping class groups of punctured surfaces. For an arbitrary automorphism ϕ, they construct an associated extension Gϕ and use its action on the curve complex of the relevant surface. Combining non-elementary hyperbolic actions, Delzant's lemma, and known results on twisted conjugacy in hyperbolic groups, they show that the coset corresponding to ϕ contains infinitely many conjugacy classes, which implies R(ϕ)=∞.

The paper does not involve human participants, classrooms, or an educational intervention; it is a theoretical result in geometric group theory. The main conclusion is that the specified spherical and affine Artin–Tits groups, along with several pure and central quotient variants, all have property R∞. The authors also recover and generalize a recent result for pure braid groups as a special case.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a mathematics research paper on group theory and twisted conjugacy, not an empirical education study. It does not evaluate any instructional technology, AI intervention, or learner outcome.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No educational intervention, comparison group, or K-12 outcome is studied, so there is no measurable educational impact to code.

paper_profiles.title: The group of self-homotopy equivalences of A2n-polyhedra
paper_profiles.extended_summary: This paper addresses a purely algebraic topology question about the group of self-homotopy equivalences of certain CW-complexes called A2n-polyhedra. The authors study the quotient group E(X)/E*(X), where E(X) is the group of self-homotopy equivalences of a space X and E*(X) consists of those inducing the identity on homology. The motivation is a realisability problem: whether arbitrary groups can appear as such self-equivalence groups or quotients.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a theoretical mathematics paper on homotopy equivalence groups of A2_n-polyhedra, with no education technology intervention, no K-12 population, and no empirical study design. It does not present experimental, quasi-experimental, or observational evidence relevant to the requested educational AI taxonomy.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No educational intervention or learner outcome is evaluated, so there is no measurable instructional impact to map. The paper has no demonstrated impact on K-12 science inquiry or learning outcomes.

paper_profiles.title: Lessons Learned and Future Directions of MetaTutor: Leveraging Multichannel Data to Scaffold Self-Regulated Learning With an Intelligent Tutoring System
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper synthesizes more than a decade of research on MetaTutor, a hypermedia-based intelligent tutoring system designed to scaffold self-regulated learning (SRL) while students learn human biology, especially the human circulatory system. The article asks how different scaffolding approaches, learner characteristics, and multimodal data sources contribute to understanding and improving SRL processes such as cognitive strategy use, metacognitive monitoring, motivation, and emotion.

The intervention/approach studied is MetaTutor, which includes adaptive prompts, feedback, embedded pedagogical agents, and an SRL palette that allows learners to initiate or respond to prompts for strategies such as goal setting, note-taking, summarizing, relevance judgments, judgments of learning, and feelings of knowing. The paper reviews findings from many prior experimental studies comparing adaptive scaffolding versus no scaffolding, and it also draws on log files, eye tracking, facial expression analysis, self-reports, and screen recordings to examine how learners interact with the system.

The population discussed across the reviewed studies is predominantly undergraduate college students, often described as predominantly Caucasian female students, learning in laboratory-based studies. The context is advanced learning technology for science learning rather than K-12 schooling. The authors conclude that adaptive scaffolding can improve SRL behaviors and some learning outcomes, that learner prior knowledge strongly shapes how students use cognitive and metacognitive strategies, and that multimodal trace data provide a richer picture of how SRL unfolds over time. They also emphasize open challenges, including how to integrate multiple data channels analytically, how to design better real-time interventions, and how to account for emotion and motivation in future ITS research.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed narrative review/synthesis rather than a single experimental study or meta-analysis. It summarizes many underlying lab studies, but the paper itself does not provide a unified causal estimate and much of the evidence is correlational or study-specific.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reviewed findings suggest meaningful but uneven benefits of adaptive scaffolding for SRL and learning, with effects varying by learner prior knowledge and outcome type. Because no single effect size is established in this paper and the main evidence is from adult learners in a specific STEM domain, the overall impact is modest/unclear for the broader K-12 target area.

interventions.use_case: MetaTutor, a hypermedia-based ITS for scaffolded self-regulated learning while college students study the human circulatory system, using pedagogical agents, prompts, feedback, quizzes, and adaptive scaffolding based on learner interactions.

finding.finding_summary: The review synthesizes multiple experimental studies on MetaTutor and reports that adaptive scaffolding can improve learning outcomes, but results vary by learner prior knowledge, timing, and the specific SRL process measured. For example, collaborative subgoal setting with pedagogical agents was associated with higher proportional learning gains, while some strategies such as shallow note-taking negatively predicted learning.
finding.measure: Posttest learning gains, knowledge tests on circulatory-system content, proportional learning gains

finding.finding_summary: Across the summarized studies, MetaTutor’s prompting and feedback generally supported self-regulated learning behaviors and sometimes reduced negative emotions, but effects depended on condition and learner characteristics. The paper reports that prompt-and-feedback conditions tended to elicit more effective SRL use and fewer negative emotions than prompt-only or no-scaffolding conditions, though some learners still experienced frustration, boredom, or confusion.
finding.measure: Self-regulated learning strategy use, emotion-value self-reports, facial-expression emotion coding

finding.finding_summary: This review primarily focuses on self-regulation, metacognition, monitoring, planning, and strategic learning processes, and it synthesizes evidence that MetaTutor can scaffold these skills. Results across studies show higher frequencies or better use of metacognitive judgments and monitoring behaviors under adaptive scaffolding, but accuracy and benefits were inconsistent across prior knowledge groups and measurement granularity.
finding.measure: JOLs, FOKs, content evaluations, monitoring progress toward goals, strategy-sequence analyses, eye-tracking and log-file indicators of SRL

paper_profiles.title: Lab4CE: a Remote Laboratory for Computer Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses how to improve engagement and learning in remote practical activities for computer science education, with an emphasis on the scaffolding needed around virtual laboratories. The authors argue that virtualization alone is not sufficient for effective learning, and ask how scaffolding, collaboration, awareness, and learning analytics can increase students’ engagement in remote lab work.

To address this problem, they introduce Lab4CE, a remote laboratory for computer education built on a three-layer architecture. The environment includes an experiment authoring tool for instructors, a rich learning interface for students and tutors, instant messaging, artifact-awareness tools showing who is doing what on shared resources, learning analytics timelines, and a management dashboard for tutors. The system supports both individual and collaborative practical sessions over virtual machines and networked resources.

The paper reports an exploratory study with 139 first-year undergraduate computer science students at the University of Toulouse, France, in a face-to-face course on Linux system use. Students could optionally use Lab4CE to practice file, folder, permission, and process management tasks. Results suggest the system had a positive effect on engagement, as many students used the remote lab rather than only practicing on their own computers, and there was a significant positive correlation between activity in the system and achievement on a later academic test. The authors conclude that scaffolding and analytics can support remote computer science practical work, while noting that intelligent tutoring remains a future improvement.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed exploratory correlational study, not an RCT or QED. The evidence is useful but limited by self-selection, missing comparison equivalence, and the fact that the main achievement result is a correlation rather than a causal estimate.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported association between system activity and achievement is moderate in size (r=0.41), which indicates a meaningful positive relationship. However, because the design is observational and the intervention is a broader remote lab environment rather than a tightly controlled treatment, the practical impact is promising but not definitive.

interventions.use_case: remote virtual laboratory for computer science practical work with scaffolding tools, shared control, chat, awareness, analytics, and authoring for Linux/system administration exercises

finding.finding_summary: In an exploratory study with 139 first-year computer science students, the authors report that the Lab4CE remote laboratory appeared to increase engagement in practical learning. Usage data showed that more than 50% of students used a virtual machine in Lab4CE, compared with 25% who installed their own Linux VM, and students opened 477 sessions with a mean duration of 39 minutes.
finding.measure: Engagement / on-task behavior in remote practical activities; system usage logs (sessions, duration, commands)

finding.finding_summary: The study found a significant positive correlation between students’ activity in Lab4CE and their learning achievement on the final test. Using 55 students and 17 test questions after filtering, the authors report Pearson’s r=0.41 (p=.002) between activity level and achievement, suggesting that more active use of the system was associated with better performance.
finding.measure: Final academic achievement test on Linux/system administration topics

paper_profiles.title: A Systematic Review of Robotic Rehabilitation for Cognitive Training
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper reviews recent research on robot-assisted cognitive training and rehabilitation, focusing on how robots have been used to support cognitive, social, and functional outcomes for people with cognitive disabilities. The review asks what applications have been studied, what enabling technologies are being used, and what experimental evidence exists for robot-assisted cognitive training.

The intervention space includes socially assistive robots, companion robots, assistive robots, and service robots used for cognitive training, therapy, and support. The review highlights multimodal sensing and feedback, gamification, virtual/augmented reality, and artificial intelligence as key enabling technologies. Across the included studies, the most common applications were social communication skills, memory, attention, and general cognitive training, with many studies targeting children with ASD and older adults with dementia or cognitive impairment.

The authors synthesized 99 eligible articles and meta-analyzed 53 experimental studies involving primary end users. They conclude that robot-assisted cognitive training shows promise for engagement, communication, attention, memory, and related outcomes, but the field is limited by small samples, inconsistent measures, and uncontrolled factors. They also note that most studies were short, lab-based, and varied widely in design and duration, and they call for more rigorous, personalized, and long-term research.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a systematic review with a meta-analysis component over experimental studies of robot-assisted cognitive training. The evidence synthesis is peer-reviewed and directly aggregates primary studies, giving it strong methodological credibility for taxonomy purposes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The review reports many promising but heterogeneous effects, often qualitative or small-sample, with limited pooled effect sizes and frequent concerns about sample size and measurement consistency. Overall impact appears modest and uneven across populations and outcomes rather than clearly large.

interventions.use_case: systematic review and meta-analysis of robot-assisted cognitive training using social, companion, and assistive robots (e.g., NAO, PARO, Pepper) for training/rehabilitation tasks such as joint attention, imitation, memory, attention, and social communication

finding.finding_summary: The review synthesizes 53 experimental studies and reports many positive social-emotional effects, especially improved communication, interaction, engagement, and reduced distress in some groups. However, findings were inconsistent across studies and outcomes; several studies reported no significant change or mixed results (e.g., engagement and behavior improvements varied by population and robot condition).
finding.measure: observational behavior ratings, engagement/communication scales, mood and distress measures, usability/interview feedback

finding.finding_summary: Across the review, robot-assisted training often improved task-specific cognitive and social learning outcomes such as joint attention, imitation, turn-taking, attention, and memory, with some studies showing transfer to human interaction. The review also notes that several studies found no significant gains or comparable performance to human-led conditions, indicating benefits are task- and context-dependent.
finding.measure: joint attention performance, imitation accuracy, turn-taking, attention tests, memory task performance, cognitive flexibility

finding.finding_summary: The review reports that some robot-assisted interventions reduced caregiver workload and could support therapy delivery with repeatable, fatigue-free assistance. These operational benefits were based on experimental and user-study evidence rather than a single pooled estimate, and the paper emphasizes feasibility and usability improvements alongside human labor savings.
finding.measure: caregiver workload, usability, session feasibility, interaction logs

paper_profiles.title: How Should Intelligent Tutoring Systems Sequence Multiple Graphical Representations of Fractions? A Multi-Methods Study
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how intelligent tutoring systems should sequence multiple graphical representations of fractions to best support learning. The central question is whether representations should be blocked, fully interleaved, moderately interleaved, or increasingly interleaved across problems, and whether any observed advantage is driven mainly by reactivation of prior knowledge or by abstraction across representations.

The authors study the Fractions Tutor, an intelligent tutoring system for 4th- and 5th-grade fractions instruction that uses interactive circle, rectangle, and number line representations. In the main classroom experiment, 230 students from six schools in Western Pennsylvania were randomly assigned to one of four representation-sequencing conditions while keeping task-type sequencing moderately interleaved across all groups. Students completed pretests, immediate posttests, and delayed posttests; outcomes included reproduction with area models, reproduction with number lines, conceptual transfer, and procedural transfer. The paper also includes a small think-aloud study with six 5th-grade students and a log-data analysis using Bayesian knowledge tracing to probe the mechanisms behind any effects.

Overall, students improved from pretest to posttest across conditions, showing that the tutor supported learning. Evidence for an advantage of interleaving graphical representations was qualified but suggestive: the fully interleaved condition performed best on some outcomes, especially delayed conceptual transfer, and interleaving was particularly beneficial for students with low prior knowledge. The think-aloud data suggested that students did not spontaneously make many connections between representations unless prompted, supporting reactivation more than abstraction as the main mechanism. The authors conclude that interleaving representations can improve robust learning in an ITS for fractions, but that the best schedule may depend on learners' prior knowledge and the target knowledge type.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed classroom experiment with random assignment to four conditions and hierarchical linear modeling, so it has substantial credibility. It is not blue because it is not a full meta-analysis and there are some design/interpretation limits, including a modest sample in the final analytic sample and only partial/conditional effects.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The intervention produced modest but meaningful gains on some fraction outcomes, with effect sizes in the small-to-moderate range (e.g., d=0.33 on delayed conceptual transfer and up to d=0.75 on delayed number-line reproduction within the fully interleaved condition). The impact is positive but not uniformly large across all outcomes or schedules.

interventions.use_case: fractions tutoring with step-by-step guidance, hints, and multiple interactive graphical representations (circles, rectangles, number lines) for 4th- and 5th-grade learners; the study manipulates the sequencing of representations within the tutor

finding.finding_summary: In a classroom experiment with 230 4th- and 5th-grade students, all conditions improved from pretest to posttest on several fraction outcomes, including reproduction with area models (e.g., fully interleaved post>pre d=0.45; delayed>pre d=0.38), reproduction with number lines (e.g., fully interleaved post>pre d=0.51; delayed>pre d=0.75), and conceptual transfer (e.g., fully interleaved post>pre d=0.34; delayed>pre d=0.60). However, the advantage of interleaving over blocking was limited and heterogeneous: the fully interleaved condition significantly outperformed the other conditions on delayed conceptual transfer (d=0.33), while the increasingly interleaved condition showed a marginal advantage on reproduction with area models (d=0.30).
finding.measure: Fraction knowledge tests: reproduction with area models, reproduction with number lines, conceptual transfer, and procedural transfer
finding.effect_size: d=0.33 to d=0.75 (depending on condition and outcome)

finding.finding_summary: The paper’s broader instructional focus also included conceptual transfer and robust learning, which are proxies for deeper reasoning and the ability to apply fraction knowledge to novel tasks. The strongest evidence was for delayed conceptual transfer, where the fully interleaved condition significantly outperformed the other schedules (d=0.33), suggesting better long-term application of knowledge rather than only short-term practice performance.
finding.measure: Conceptual transfer items and delayed posttest performance

paper_profiles.title: Circuit Design: An inquiry lab activity at Maui Community College
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper describes the design and classroom implementation of an inquiry-based circuit design lab for first-year community college students in Electrical Engineering Technology. The authors focus on how to adapt a science-inquiry format to an engineering-oriented inquiry activity, using the Wheatstone bridge as the central system for students to explore voltage dividers, Kirchhoff’s voltage law, and resistive network analysis.

The intervention was a hands-on lab in which students first completed “Starters” that exposed them to balanced and unbalanced bridge circuits, thermistors, and variable resistors. Students then generated questions that facilitators sorted into four engineering design goals: building a perfectly balanced bridge, building a bridge that operates in a linear regime, using the bridge as a thermometer, or using it to determine an unknown resistance. Teams selected one challenge, built and tested their own circuits from scratch on breadboards, and concluded by presenting posters and being assessed with a rubric designed for engineering inquiry.

The activity was implemented in Electronics 101 at Maui Community College with twelve primarily first-year undergraduate students. The paper’s main contribution is not an effect evaluation but a description of inquiry design elements, facilitation, and assessment changes needed when shifting from science inquiry to engineering inquiry. The authors conclude that the approach supported learning goals and student engagement, while also noting that the rubric needed improvement for reliability.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a descriptive conference paper about the design and implementation of an inquiry lab, not a controlled evaluation. It includes student work and rubric scores but no comparison group, randomization, or pre/post causal analysis.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests modest benefits for engineering process skills and engagement in a small class, but the evidence is qualitative and lacks effect sizes or a rigorous evaluation design. Any impact is therefore unclear and likely modest.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports an inquiry lab in circuit design with 12 first-year Electrical Engineering Technology students, focused on building and analyzing Wheatstone bridge circuits to meet engineering design goals. Students completed the activity and produced poster presentations, but the summative rubric showed only moderate performance (mean class score 6.2/9) and limited scoring reliability (mean SD=1.2), so evidence of learning gains is suggestive rather than strong.
finding.measure: Summative rubric scores on poster presentations evaluating solution, support/circuit analysis, and reasoning/justification

finding.finding_summary: The inquiry explicitly targeted engineering process skills, including teamwork, problem solving, building from schematics, testing with multimeters, and justifying design choices. The authors report that the activity accomplished many learning goals and that students seemed to enjoy it, but no pre/post or comparison-group effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Observed completion of engineering process tasks; rubric evidence of reasoning/justification and design solution quality; author-reported student enjoyment

finding.finding_summary: Attitudinal goals included teamwork, self-confidence in engineering skills, and motivation via real-world applications. The paper provides qualitative evidence that students enjoyed the inquiry and engaged with the engineering challenges, but it does not report standardized attitude or motivation measures.
finding.measure: Author observations and informal reports of student enjoyment/engagement

paper_profiles.title: Advancing Education through Tutoring Systems: A Systematic Literature Review
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how tutoring systems in education have evolved from early computer-assisted instruction to modern AI-driven intelligent tutoring systems (ITS), robot tutoring systems (RTS), and multimodal hybrids, and what these systems imply for learning, engagement, and ethics. The authors frame the topic around the growing educational challenge of persistent achievement gaps and the promise of AI-supported personalized instruction.

The study is a systematic literature review using PRISMA. It searched multiple databases and included 86 representative studies published from 1972 through 2024. The review analyzes tutoring systems across four dimensions: artificial intelligence, system behavior, engagement, and affordances. It classifies systems into computer-based ITS, verbal robot-based systems, and multimodal systems using latent class analysis.

Across the reviewed literature, the paper concludes that AI techniques such as Bayesian Knowledge Tracing and large language models have improved adaptability, feedback, and personalization, while robots add social and emotional engagement through human-like interaction. However, the review also emphasizes persistent challenges, especially ethics, privacy, scalability, and limitations in robotic cognitive adaptability. The authors argue that future work should integrate the cognitive strengths of ITS with the social strengths of RTS while strengthening responsible AI safeguards.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a systematic literature review using PRISMA and latent class analysis, but it is not itself a primary experimental study or meta-analysis with pooled causal estimates. The paper synthesizes existing evidence qualitatively and therefore provides moderate methodological rigor but limited direct causal credibility.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The review argues for meaningful benefits of tutoring systems, especially for math learning and engagement, but it does not report pooled effect sizes from this paper itself. Because the impact claims are broad and not quantitatively estimated here, the overall impact is best characterized as modest/unclear rather than clearly medium or large.

interventions.use_case: Systematic review of classical and modern AI-driven tutoring systems for K-12 and related educational contexts, including adaptive math tutoring, Bayesian Knowledge Tracing systems, and LLM-enhanced tutors with real-time personalized feedback.

Systematic review of robot tutoring systems and educational robots that tutor children through verbal, gestural, and socially interactive embodied support, including NAO-style and humanoid tutoring robots.
Review of generative-AI and chatbot-based tutoring supports that provide conversational explanations, adaptive responses, and context-aware feedback in tutoring settings.

finding.finding_summary: The review synthesizes prior studies showing that ITS and robot tutor systems can improve math learning outcomes, with software-based ITS particularly strong for adaptive math instruction. It cites middle-school mathematics tutoring work and a 6th-grade math ITS as representative evidence, but the paper itself does not report a pooled effect size; it mainly concludes that learning gains are significant across included studies.
finding.measure: Math learning outcomes / academic performance in mathematics tutoring studies

finding.finding_summary: The review finds that robot-based tutoring systems consistently support motivation, engagement, and social-emotional interaction through gestures, verbal encouragement, and human-like presence. It cites elementary education robot studies and robot-child tutoring trials as evidence, but does not report a meta-analytic effect size; the conclusion is based on qualitative synthesis across 86 reviewed studies.
finding.measure: Student motivation, engagement, and social-emotional engagement measures

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that tutoring systems can support deeper learning behaviors such as problem-solving, attention, and adaptive responding, especially when AI-driven feedback and conversational tutoring are used. However, these claims are synthesized from heterogeneous studies rather than directly pooled, so the evidence is suggestive rather than quantified.
finding.measure: Problem-solving, concentration, and learning-process indicators

finding.finding_summary: Across the review, tutoring systems are described as improving general academic performance and personalized learning in core subjects beyond a single domain. The paper emphasizes gains from adaptive content delivery and real-time feedback, but it does not provide a unified effect size because the evidence is drawn from disparate primary studies.
finding.measure: General academic performance / personalized learning outcomes

finding.finding_summary: The paper identifies important institutional benefits and constraints: tutoring systems are portrayed as scalable and increasingly deployable, but ethics, privacy, bias, and hardware cost limit real-world adoption. The review is qualitative and does not quantify institutional impact, instead arguing that governance and responsible-AI frameworks are needed for effective deployment.
finding.measure: Scalability, deployment feasibility, ethics/governance considerations

paper_profiles.title: Do intelligent tutoring systems benefit K-12 students? A meta-analysis and evaluation of heterogeneity of treatment effects in the U.S.
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether intelligent tutoring systems (ITS) benefit K-12 students in the United States, and whether the effects vary by study design, student characteristics, instructional features, outcome measures, and setting. The authors position ITS as an AI-supported educational technology that can personalize practice, hints, feedback, and instructional support, but note that evidence across prior meta-analyses has been mixed in terms of internal and external validity.

The study is a systematic review and meta-analysis of experimental ITS studies conducted in U.S. K-12 schools from 2011 to 2021. After screening more than 2,000 records, the authors included 18 experimental studies yielding 77 effect sizes across 11 ITS, such as ALEKS, MATHia, Cognitive Tutor Algebra I, SWELL, and the Intelligent Tutoring System for the Structure Strategy. The included studies covered elementary, middle, and some high-school contexts, with many interventions delivered in classrooms, as homework, or as separate activities. Outcomes were primarily academic achievement measures, including mathematics and reading/writing, with both standardized and researcher-developed tests.

Overall, the meta-analysis found a statistically significant positive effect of ITS on learning outcomes (g=0.271). Effects were similar across elementary and middle school, across several student subgroups, and across urban/suburban settings, but were smaller in rural schools. Among the most important moderators were worked-out examples, intervention duration, intervention condition, type of learning outcome, and immediate measurement. The authors conclude that ITS can improve K-12 achievement, especially when they include worked-out examples and are implemented in ways that align with classroom use, but that effect sizes vary meaningfully by context and design.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a meta-analysis of 18 experimental studies with 77 effect sizes, using multilevel meta-regression and robust variance estimation. It directly evaluates causal evidence and moderator heterogeneity in K-12 ITS studies, which fits the highest evidence-quality tier despite some attrition-reporting limitations.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The overall effect is modest but clearly positive (g=0.271), meeting the threshold for medium/large impact in this framework. Effects are also positive across major subgroups and several subject areas, indicating meaningful potential for K-12 implementation.

interventions.use_case: Meta-analysis of classical intelligent tutoring systems used in U.S. K-12 schools, including systems such as ALEKS, Cognitive Tutor Algebra I, MATHia, ASSISTments-like vocabulary tutoring, and related adaptive step-based or hint-based tutors providing feedback, worked examples, and question sequences.

finding.finding_summary: Across 18 experimental studies and 77 effect sizes from 11 ITS, the overall effect on U.S. K-12 learning outcomes was positive and statistically significant (g=0.271, SE=0.011, p=0.001). This supports a modest average benefit of ITS relative to comparison conditions, with the meta-analysis also showing variation by moderators such as duration, measurement timing, and support type.
finding.measure: Student learning outcomes / academic achievement (varied subject-specific tests across studies)

finding.finding_summary: Math-focused ITS studies showed positive effects, including g=0.253 for mathematics outcomes across 22 effect sizes. The paper also reports that math ITS had lower importance than worked-out examples but still contributed positively to achievement, with stronger effects observed for some short-to-medium duration implementations and for immediate posttests.
finding.measure: Mathematics achievement tests

finding.finding_summary: Reading and writing outcomes showed a positive effect of ITS, with g=0.323 across 55 effect sizes and statistically significant results. The MetaForest analysis also ranked reading/writing ITS as having higher effect sizes than math ITS, and immediate post-intervention measures were notably larger than end-of-year measures.
finding.measure: Reading and writing achievement tests

finding.finding_summary: The paper includes motivational support as an ITS feature and notes that support types related to learner regulation and encouragement had positive effects, with motivation support showing g=0.265 across 23 effect sizes. While not the paper's main outcome, this indicates modest gains in engagement-related support within ITS implementations.
finding.measure: Motivation support / engagement-related learning support in ITS

paper_profiles.title: Lens Inquiry: An Astronomy Lab for Non-science Majors at Hartnell Community College
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper describes the design and implementation of a three-hour inquiry-based astronomy lab activity centered on converging lenses and telescopes. The authors focus on replacing a more guided laboratory exercise with an inquiry format in which students generate their own questions, design investigations, discuss observations, and present results to the class. The paper is primarily concerned with instructional design and classroom implementation rather than with testing a specific AI or digital intervention.

The activity was implemented in a semester-long astronomy laboratory course for non-science majors at Hartnell Community College, a Hispanic-serving institution in Salinas, California. Students worked in small groups of 2-4, first exploring lens phenomena through demonstrations and guided question generation, then selecting a question to investigate, making posters, and presenting findings. The lesson concluded with a telescope-building worksheet and synthesis segment connecting lens properties to telescope design.

The authors report that the activity was effective at promoting communication, peer interaction, and engagement with scientific inquiry, but they also note that it was difficult to cover all desired content within the available time. They conclude that the lab would likely work better if split into two sessions and that more facilitation time and tighter limits on materials and possible investigations would improve future implementations. The paper provides formative and summative assessment observations, including a final-exam item on converging lenses, but does not present a controlled comparison study of outcomes.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed conference paper describing a classroom intervention, but it is primarily a qualitative design/implementation report rather than a controlled evaluation. No experimental comparison group, effect size, or rigorous causal design is reported.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests positive classroom engagement and some content understanding, but the evidence is descriptive and based on a small community-college sample rather than a measured medium/large effect. The reported 58% correct on one exam item is informative but not enough to establish strong impact.

finding.finding_summary: The inquiry lab was designed to build scientific process skills, including planning investigations, controlling variables, and communicating findings. The paper reports qualitative success in these areas, but also notes that some groups reached premature conclusions and did not revise them despite contradictory evidence; on a final exam conceptual item about converging lenses, 58% answered correctly, which the authors describe as close to the class average for the lab final.
finding.measure: Observation of inquiry process skills; group poster/presentation rubrics; final exam question on converging lenses

finding.finding_summary: A major goal of the activity was to strengthen communication, collaboration, and confidence through group investigations and short presentations. The authors report that students were generally relaxed during presentations, engaged in active class discussions, and the activity helped students get to know classmates better; these were descriptive findings rather than quantified effects.
finding.measure: Classroom observations; student feedback/comments; presentation participation

finding.finding_summary: The paper focuses on astronomy content learning about converging lenses and simple telescope construction rather than a core K-12 subject area. Students completed a telescope worksheet and a conceptual final-exam item, and the authors report that 58% answered the lens question correctly, suggesting some content uptake despite time constraints.
finding.measure: Telescope worksheet; final exam conceptual question on converging lenses

paper_profiles.title: Personalized Multimodal Feedback Using Multiple External Representations: Strategy Profiles and Learning in High School Physics
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether and how students’ use of elaborated, multimodal feedback is associated with learning in high school physics. The authors focus on a key design question for adaptive instruction and future intelligent tutoring systems: when students can choose between verification feedback alone and optional elaborated feedback, do different patterns of feedback use relate to better post-test performance, and do these patterns depend on students’ initial representational competence?

The intervention context was a computer-based physics practice platform (KI4SCool) that delivered immediate verification feedback after each multiple-choice item and allowed students to open additional elaborated feedback in three multiple external representations: verbal, graphical/pictorial, and mathematical. The study followed 661 10th- and 11th-grade students across 26 schools and 66 classes in Germany over roughly one term (16–24 weeks). Students completed pre- and post-tests on kinematics and worked on optional exercises, while platform logs captured feedback usage, response confidence, and performance.

Analyses showed a small but consistent positive association between elaborated feedback use and post-test scores after adjusting for prior knowledge, platform performance, number of exercises solved, and confidence. The authors also identified distinct feedback-use profiles, including students who rarely opened elaborated feedback, students who frequently opened all three representations, and students who mainly preferred verbal feedback. However, they found no robust evidence that students’ initial representational competencies explained these feedback preferences, and the observed performance differences between feedback strategies were weak. Overall, the findings support the promise of adaptive, multimodal feedback in physics learning, but the observational design prevents causal conclusions.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed observational cohort study with clustering and regression analyses, but it is not randomized and cannot support causal inference. The design has reasonable analytic rigor, yet confounding remains a substantial concern.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The observed learning association is small (β≈0.08-0.13) and correlational, so the practical impact is modest and uncertain. It is promising for adaptive feedback design, but evidence of actual intervention impact on general K-12 outcomes is limited.

interventions.use_case: computer-based physics exercises with immediate verification feedback plus optional elaborated feedback in verbal, graphical, and mathematical representations

finding.finding_summary: Across two observational cohorts of high school physics students (Cohort 1 n=351; Cohort 2 n=310), more frequent use of elaborated feedback was associated with higher post-test physics scores. The association was small but positive in both cohorts, reaching significance in Cohort 1 (standardized β=0.13, 95% CI [0.05, 0.22]) and remaining positive but marginal in Cohort 2 (β=0.08, 95% CI [0.00, 0.16], p=.054).
finding.measure: Physics post-test score (% correct) after kinematics instruction
finding.study_size: n=661 total; n=351 Cohort 1; n=310 Cohort 2

finding.finding_summary: The study suggests that learners’ representational choices reflect differences in strategy use and may relate to underlying representational competence, but the evidence for this is limited and mixed. Initial representational competences did not differ significantly across feedback-strategy clusters (MANOVA Pillai's trace=0.018, F=0.74, p=.67), and the authors found no robust moderation by competence profiles.
finding.measure: Representational competence measures and feedback-selection strategy clusters

paper_profiles.title: Intelligent Tutors Beyond K-12: An Observational Study of Adult Learner Engagement and Academic Impact
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether an intelligent tutoring system designed for college algebra can support adult learners when use is voluntary and supplementary, rather than mandated as in many K-12 studies. The authors focus on both adoption/engagement patterns and whether tutor use is associated with measurable learning outcomes.

The intervention studied is Apprentice Tutors, a novel intelligent tutoring platform for college algebra. It provides adaptive problem selection using Bayesian Knowledge Tracing, real-time correctness feedback, multi-layered hints, and links to supporting resources. The system was deployed through Blackboard and Canvas as an optional resource, letting students decide whether and when to use it.

The study was conducted with adult learners enrolled in College Algebra at a 2-year state technical college in the United States. The authors analyzed tutor interaction logs, grades, and demographic data across a two-year deployment. They report that tutor users were more likely to be female, slightly older, and tended to use the system in the evenings and on Thursdays. Within the tutor, error rates decreased with practice, and tutor use was positively associated with Unit 1 assessment scores. Because the study is observational and voluntary, the authors caution that causality cannot be inferred, but they conclude that intelligent tutors appear to be a viable supplementary learning tool for adult learners.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed observational/quasi-experimental study with real usage and grade data, but without random assignment or a control group. The design supports correlational evidence only, with acknowledged selection effects and limited causal credibility.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The observed relationship is positive but modest: tutor transactions predicted higher grades with a small regression coefficient, and the authors describe the impact as slight. Because the population is adult technical-college learners and the findings are preliminary, the study suggests modest positive impact rather than strong effect.

interventions.use_case: optional supplementary algebra tutoring for adult learners, with adaptive problem selection via Bayesian Knowledge Tracing, real-time correctness feedback, and multi-layer hints

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports within-tutor learning gains for adult learners using Apprentice Tutors in College Algebra. In the tutor learning-curve analysis, error rates decreased significantly with additional practice opportunities (p<0.001); students started at an average error rate of about 65% on first attempts, and performance improved over repeated skills practice. The study is observational (n=3,510 enrolled; 520 tutor users; 214 Unit 1 users), so causality cannot be established.
finding.measure: Tutor-internal error rates / learning curve on algebra knowledge components; Unit 1 assessment grades
finding.study_size: n=3,510 enrolled; n=520 tutor users; n=214 Unit 1 tutor users

finding.finding_summary: Tutor use was associated with slightly higher Unit 1 assessment grades for adult learners. A linear regression using tutor transactions as the sole predictor found a significant positive association (estimate=0.26, SE=0.08, t=3.39, p<0.001), and the authors describe the grade difference as modest; no standardized effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Unit 1 course assessment grades / exam scores
finding.study_size: n=3,510 enrolled; n=520 tutor users; n=214 Unit 1 tutor users

paper_profiles.title: Adaptive-TMLE for the Average Treatment Effect based on Randomized Controlled Trial Augmented with Real-World Data
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the statistical problem of estimating an average treatment effect (ATE) when randomized controlled trial (RCT) data are available together with external real-world data (RWD). The authors argue that directly pooling RCT and external data can increase precision but may also introduce bias because the trial and real-world populations, settings, and measurement processes may differ. To resolve this tension, they develop an adaptive targeted maximum likelihood estimation (A-TMLE) framework that can learn when and how to borrow information from external data while preserving valid inference.

The proposed approach decomposes the desired ATE into two parts: a pooled-ATE estimand that uses both RCT and external data, and a bias estimand that captures the effect of RCT enrollment on outcomes. Separate data-adaptive working models are built for the treatment effect and for the bias component, and the final estimate subtracts the estimated bias from the pooled estimate. The paper develops the theory for the estimators, derives canonical gradients and TMLE updates, and shows that the method can achieve super-efficiency in finite samples when the working models are simple approximations of the truth.

The paper is methodological rather than an education study. Its empirical illustration uses the DEVOTE clinical trial augmented with Optum Clinformatics real-world healthcare data, not K-12 learners or educational interventions. Simulation results suggest the proposed estimator can outperform alternative data-integration methods in mean-squared error and confidence-interval width, while retaining asymptotic normality and valid nonparametric inference. The main conclusion is that adaptive borrowing from external data can improve trial efficiency without sacrificing bias control, especially when the bias structure is learnable with a parsimonious model.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a statistical methods paper about adaptive TMLE for augmenting randomized trials with real-world data, not an educational intervention study. It contains simulations and a medical trial application, but no K-12 educational experiment or learner outcome evaluation.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper has no direct impact evidence for K-12 education or AI-supported science inquiry outcomes. Any contribution is methodological and domain-general, with no reported educational effect sizes or learner outcomes.

paper_profiles.title: Automated Personalized Feedback Improves Learning Gains in an Intelligent Tutoring System
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether automatically generated, data-driven personalized feedback can improve student learning in an intelligent tutoring system (ITS). The authors focus on the challenge of producing useful hints and explanations at scale without relying on hand-authored rules or expert intervention, and they evaluate whether different feedback-generation strategies lead to better learning outcomes.

The intervention is implemented in Korbit, a large-scale dialogue-based ITS that combines machine learning, natural language processing, and reinforcement learning. The system generates multiple forms of feedback, including personalized hints and explanations, Wikipedia-based explanations, and mathematical hints. The study compares baseline, shallow personalization, and deep personalization models for selecting feedback, and also reports analyses of Wikipedia-based explanations and mathematical hints.

The empirical evaluation used 796 annotated student-system interactions from 183 students enrolled in a free machine learning course on the Korbit platform between January and February 2020. The paper reports that deep personalization produced the highest learning gains, with a statistically significant advantage over the baseline in some comparisons, and that students generally rated the generated explanations as helpful. The authors conclude that automated personalized feedback can substantially improve learning gains and appears promising for scalable ITS support.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed empirical system study with annotated interaction data and a comparison between feedback conditions, but it is not a randomized controlled trial and relies on historical/observational interaction data with limited methodological detail. The reported significance test and confidence intervals strengthen credibility, but causal inference remains moderate.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The intervention shows modest-to-strong positive learning gains in a large-scale tutoring platform, with gains of roughly 9-23 percentage points depending on comparison and timing. However, the evidence is from a single platform and domain, and the strongest reported outcome is a process measure rather than a standardized achievement test.

interventions.use_case: large-scale dialogue-based intelligent tutoring system with automated personalized hints, explanations, Wikipedia-based explanations, and mathematical hints for students solving machine learning/data science exercises
machine-learned personalized feedback selection and generation for incorrect student solutions, including hints and explanations tailored to the student's recent interaction history

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports improved student learning gains after receiving automated personalized feedback in Korbit. Across 796 annotated student-system interactions from 183 students, deep personalization achieved 48.53% learning gain for all attempts versus 39.47% for the baseline, and 60.47% versus 37.93% before the second attempt; the latter difference was statistically significant (z-test p=0.03005).
finding.measure: Proportion of instances where a student provided a correct solution after receiving a personalized hint or explanation
finding.confidence_interval: [44.41%, 75.02%] for deep personalization before second attempt; baseline [20.69%, 57.74%]

finding.finding_summary: The paper also found that automatically generated Wikipedia-based explanations produced learning gains comparable to the other feedback conditions. Students rated either or both types of explanations as helpful 83.33% of the time, suggesting the explanations were perceived as useful and supportive of learning.
finding.measure: Learning gain following Wikipedia-based explanations; subjective helpfulness ratings

finding.finding_summary: The feedback intervention appears to support problem-solving and response revision during tutoring, which is a durable-skill-adjacent process, though this was not directly isolated as a separate construct. The paper does not report a dedicated standardized measure of metacognition or critical thinking; evidence is indirect from improved post-feedback correctness rates.
finding.measure: Post-feedback correctness / revised solution success

paper_profiles.title: Iris: An AI-Driven Virtual Tutor For Computer Science Education
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the 2024 Innovation and Technology in Computer Science Education V. 1 (ITiCSE 2024)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the challenge of providing scalable, personalized support for students in large computer science courses. The authors present Iris, a chat-based virtual tutor integrated into the Artemis learning platform, designed to help students with programming exercises through context-aware, calibrated assistance. Rather than giving complete solutions, Iris is prompted to provide subtle hints, counter-questions, and best-practice guidance so that students can continue solving problems independently.

Technically, Iris uses GPT-3.5-Turbo with a structured interaction pipeline: it first assesses whether a question is relevant, then selects likely relevant code files, generates a response using the exercise description, student submission context, automated feedback, and chat history, and finally performs a self-check to reduce responses that violate the tutoring constraints. The study evaluates Iris through an online survey of users in three CS1-level undergraduate courses at the Technical University of Munich. Students who had used Iris at least ten times were retained for analysis, and their perceptions were measured with Likert-scale questions about usefulness, comfort, and reliance.

Results suggest that students generally view Iris positively. Many reported that it understands their questions, provides helpful guidance, increases engagement, and improves understanding of programming concepts. Students also felt very comfortable asking Iris questions they might hesitate to ask human tutors, although they did not view it as a replacement for human support. The authors conclude that Iris is a promising supplementary tool for programming education, but they emphasize that the current evidence is based on subjective perceptions rather than objective learning gains and call for future controlled studies with comparison groups and pre/post testing.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed survey study with a clear methodology, but it is qualitative/correlational and relies on self-reported perceptions rather than experimental comparison or objective learning measures. It does not meet RCT/QED criteria and has selection bias toward heavier users.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports positive perceptions of usefulness and engagement, but no objective learning effect size is provided and the outcomes are subjective. Impact on learning is therefore plausible but unclear, with no demonstrated medium or large effect.

interventions.use_case: chat-based virtual tutor integrated into Artemis for CS1 programming exercises, providing context-aware hints, counter-questions, and guarded responses instead of full solutions

finding.finding_summary: This paper reports students' perceived impact of Iris on programming learning rather than objective achievement. In the survey of students who used Iris at least 10 times (reported analysis sample n=121; 221 total engaged users), 50% agreed that Iris improved their understanding of programming concepts, while 22% disagreed and 28% were neutral. The study did not report test scores, effect sizes, or confidence intervals.
finding.measure: Likert-scale survey item on perceived improvement in understanding of programming concepts
finding.study_size: n=121 analyzed survey respondents; n=221 engaged users

finding.finding_summary: Students reported strong comfort and trust in using Iris: 92% agreed they felt comfortable asking questions without being judged, and 62% felt safe asking questions they would not ask a tutor or professor. Engagement was also perceived positively, with 60% agreeing that interacting with Iris makes the learning process more engaging, though motivation was more mixed (37% agree, 40% neutral, 23% disagree).
finding.measure: Likert-scale survey items on comfort, safety, engagement, and motivation

finding.finding_summary: The study suggests Iris may support independent problem-solving, but only indirectly through subjective perceptions. For reliance, 43% of respondents felt programming exercises would be more challenging without Iris, while 27% felt exam tasks would be difficult without it and 41% disagreed, indicating moderate reliance for routine work but less dependence in exam contexts.
finding.measure: Likert-scale survey items on perceived difficulty solving programming tasks without Iris

paper_profiles.title: Enhancing LLM-Based Feedback: Insights from Intelligent Tutoring Systems and the Learning Sciences
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses how large language models (LLMs) are being used to generate feedback in educational systems, especially intelligent tutoring systems (ITS), and argues that current LLM-based feedback work often lacks the theoretical grounding and empirical rigor that characterized earlier ITS research. Rather than presenting a new experimental intervention, the paper synthesizes prior research on feedback generation from expert-built learner models, data-driven learner models, and recent LLM-based approaches.

The paper organizes its discussion around four stages of LLM-based feedback design: when feedback is triggered, what information is provided to the LLM as input, what content the LLM is asked to produce, and how feedback is delivered. For each stage, it draws on learning sciences frameworks and examples from prior ITS work, including student modeling, prompt design, feedback content selection, and multimodal delivery options such as text, images, audio, and video. The paper also reviews how feedback quality has historically been evaluated, distinguishing system-level evaluation, expert ratings, classroom usage logs, surveys, and controlled experiments.

The authors do not study a specific learner population or school context; instead, they aim to guide researchers and practitioners designing LLM-powered educational feedback systems. Their main conclusion is that LLM-based feedback should be designed and evaluated more carefully using established instructional principles, better student modeling, and stronger experimental evidence, so that generative AI tools support learning rather than simply producing plausible responses.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a conceptual/review paper rather than an empirical study, so it does not present a primary research design, comparison groups, or direct causal evidence. It synthesizes prior work and offers design recommendations for LLM-based feedback.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper has indirect impact by shaping how future educational AI systems may be designed and evaluated, but it reports no direct measured student outcome from the paper itself. Its influence is therefore informative but unproven empirically.

interventions.use_case: The paper reviews and synthesizes classical model-based ITS feedback generation approaches, including production-rule tutors, constraint-based tutors, hint generation, and student-model-driven formative feedback design.
The paper discusses LLM-powered educational feedback generation and conversational tutoring, including prompt-based feedback for students and LLMs acting as tutors, instructors, or peer-like agents.
The paper focuses on AI-generated formative feedback and hint generation for student work, especially in programming and other problem-solving tasks.
The paper cites and discusses LLM feedback and hint generation in a digital learning game context as an example of evaluation and deployment.

paper_profiles.title: Accessible Computer Science for K-12 Students with Hearing Impairments
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the lack of accessible computer science learning resources for Deaf and Hard of Hearing (D/HH) K-12 students, especially those who rely on American Sign Language (ASL) and have limited access to accurate, age-appropriate CS instruction in ASL. The authors argue that captions alone are often insufficient because of language differences, reading-level barriers, and the need for technical vocabulary to be presented in a linguistically and culturally accessible way.

The paper proposes an accessible block-based computer science web application and associated ASL video content that explains core programming concepts such as commands, conditionals, loops, variables, functions, debugging, and object-oriented programming. The approach is designed to support middle-school D/HH learners within a hands-on, block-based coding environment, with additional accessibility features such as visual feedback, adjustable video speed, captions, and ASL tooltips for code blocks. The project also includes a robot platform for programming practice and is intended to be usable by teachers in inclusive or specialized classrooms.

The work is primarily a design and project description rather than an evaluated intervention. The authors outline planned production of ASL videos and future studies with middle-school deaf students to examine the impact of the resources on CS learning. Their main conclusion is that culturally and linguistically appropriate ASL-based instructional supports are needed to make K-12 computer science more accessible and engaging for D/HH students, and that their proposed platform is a promising direction for inclusive computing education.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a project/design paper describing an in-development accessible CS curriculum and planned study, not an empirical evaluation. No comparison condition, outcome data, or effect estimates are reported.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports no measured learner impact yet, so there is no demonstrated effect on academic or social outcomes. Its contribution is conceptual and prospective rather than evidence of impact.

interventions.use_case: accessible block-based coding curriculum for middle school Deaf/Hard of Hearing students, using ASL videos, captions, tooltips, and simulation-based robotics tutorials to teach core CS concepts

paper_profiles.title: A Web-based Adaptive and Intelligent Tutor by Expert Systems
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper proposes a web-based adaptive and intelligent tutoring system built around expert systems, with the goal of making e-learning more dynamic, customized, and efficient. The authors argue that static, one-size-fits-all web instruction is inadequate for diverse learners, and they present an architecture intended to adjust content, pacing, and presentation style to learner characteristics and learning style.

The proposed approach combines learner profiling, a pre-test, adaptive delivery of learning concepts, and a post-test. The system uses a questionnaire to infer learner type, then selects content and teaching methods from a knowledge base and updates the learner model as the learner progresses. The paper frames this as an intelligent tutoring system for web-based learning, with supporting features such as remote access, virtual class functionality, and feedback-driven adaptation.

The paper discusses intended use for learners in intelligent schools and more broadly for remote web-based education, but it does not report an empirical study with participants, comparison groups, or measured learning outcomes. Its main contribution is a conceptual system design and justification for adaptive expert-system-based tutoring, along with examples of related intelligent tutoring systems and a proposed workflow for implementation.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a conceptual/prototype paper describing a proposed system rather than reporting a controlled empirical evaluation. It does not present a study design, comparison group, or analyzed outcome data.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No measurable educational impact is reported. The paper makes qualitative claims about improved efficiency and lower cost, but provides no effect sizes or outcome evidence.

interventions.use_case: web-based adaptive intelligent tutoring that models learner style/knowledge, delivers a pre-test, personalized concept instruction, and a post-test using an expert system and learner model
personalized web-based learning platform that adapts content sequence, pace, and presentation style to learner characteristics and learning style
web-delivered instructional software with quizzes, multimedia, FAQs, and remote access for individualized study

paper_profiles.title: Fitted avatars: automatic skeleton adjustment for self-avatars in virtual reality
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of accurately fitting a self-avatar to a user's body dimensions in virtual reality, so that inverse-kinematics animation produces more realistic body posture and less visible misalignment. The authors argue that common low-cost VR setups often rely on uniform avatar scaling from height alone, which can leave the avatar's limbs, shoulders, and joints mismatched to the user and reduce embodiment.

They propose an automatic avatar-fitting framework that uses an HTC Vive HMD, two hand controllers, and three trackers on the waist and feet. Through a short sequence of guided exercises, the system estimates shoulder and neck joint locations as well as limb lengths, then performs two-pass adjustment: uniform scaling followed by skeleton tuning of the arm, leg, and spine chains. A final walk-in-avatar step lets the user align themselves to compute exact tracker-to-joint offsets for animation.

The evaluation used 27 adult participants drawn from one academic institution, including faculty/staff and master's/Ph.D. students, in an immersive VR setup.
