finding.finding_summary: The benchmark evaluation found that Chinese-dominant LLMs generally outperformed English-dominant models on Chinese K-12 subject knowledge, with Qwen-72B-Chat achieving the highest average accuracy at 88.8% and ERNIE-Bot 4.0 close behind at 85.5%. However, performance varied widely by subject and grade, with arts subjects consistently easier than science and no clear advantage at the primary level; this paper is a benchmark paper rather than an intervention efficacy study.
finding.measure: Accuracy on Chinese K-12 multiple-choice benchmark across 23 subjects and 3 grade bands

paper_profiles.title: Environmental large language model Evaluation (ELLE) dataset: A Benchmark for Evaluating Generative AI applications in Eco-environment Domain
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the lack of a standardized and reliable evaluation framework for generative AI and large language models (LLMs) in the ecological and environmental domain. The authors argue that existing evaluations do not sufficiently measure domain professionalism, clarity, feasibility, or applicability for specialized eco-environment tasks, limiting trustworthy comparison of models and their derivatives such as fine-tuned models and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems.

To address this gap, the paper introduces the ELLE-QA Benchmark, a question-answer dataset designed specifically for evaluating LLMs in ecological and environmental sciences. The benchmark contains 1,130 QA pairs covering 16 environmental subjects, with items sourced from expert questionnaires and open-source authoritative materials. The dataset is annotated by content domain, difficulty, and question type (knowledge, calculation, reasoning), and the authors describe a cross-screening and expert validation process to improve quality and reliability.

The benchmark is intended for use as a standardized evaluation tool rather than as an intervention with human participants. It is positioned to support consistent, objective comparisons of AI models in environmental contexts and to promote more robust development of AI technologies for ecological and environmental applications. The paper concludes that the ELLE-QA Benchmark can help advance the standardization of AI assessment in this domain and provide a foundation for ongoing model evaluation.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed benchmark/dataset paper with a clear methodology for constructing and validating QA items, but it does not evaluate an educational intervention or causal effect on learner outcomes. Evidence credibility is moderate for benchmark construction, not for impact on students.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports no K-12 learning or implementation outcomes; it introduces a dataset to assess model proficiency in environmental QA. There is no demonstrated impact on student achievement, engagement, or classroom practice.

interventions.use_case: Benchmarking generative AI / LLM systems and retrieval-augmented generation for answering ecological and environmental science questions, including domain-specific QA and reasoning tasks.

paper_profiles.title: PB-LLM: Partially Binarized Large Language Models
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of compressing large language models to extremely low bit-widths while preserving their reasoning and language capabilities. The authors argue that existing binarization methods, when directly applied to LLMs, collapse performance and can even perform worse than random guessing on common-sense reasoning tasks. The core question is how to binarize LLM weights without destroying model utility.

The proposed approach is Partially-Binarized LLM (PB-LLM), which keeps a small subset of salient weights in higher precision and binarizes the rest. The paper investigates different criteria for selecting salient weights (magnitude vs. Hessian) and different granularities (element-wise vs. column-wise), then extends the method to both post-training quantization and quantization-aware training. It also derives an optimal scaling factor for binary weights and shows that freezing salient weights during training improves convergence.

The experiments are conducted on pretrained OPT-1.3B and LLaMA-7B models using language modeling and common-sense reasoning benchmarks such as BoolQ, PIQA, HellaSwag, WinoGrande, ARC-Easy, ARC-Challenge, OBQA, WikiText2, and C4. The results show that existing binarization methods fail badly on LLMs, while PB-LLM can preserve substantially more performance, especially when a modest fraction of weights remains unbinarized. The paper concludes that partial binarization is a promising route toward extreme LLM compression, although very aggressive binarization still causes notable degradation.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a model-compression / machine learning methods paper, not an educational intervention study. It does not evaluate K-12 learning outcomes, classroom use, or any student-facing AI support, so it provides no direct evidence for the requested education topic.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No educational impact is measured or implied. The reported results concern LLM binarization performance on language/reasoning benchmarks and perplexity, which are not K-12 learner outcomes or evidence of positive/negative classroom effects.

paper_profiles.title: Integration of AI in STEM Education – Addressing Ethical Challenges in K-12 Settings
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the ethical, pedagogical, and equity challenges of integrating artificial intelligence into K-12 STEM education. Rather than testing a specific AI tool, it reviews recent scholarship on AI-powered educational applications such as intelligent tutoring systems, automated assessment, predictive analytics, and surveillance technologies, with attention to their potential benefits and risks. The authors argue that while AI can provide personalization, real-time feedback, and scalability, it can also amplify bias, privacy violations, opaque decision-making, and inequitable access.

The paper proposes a responsible integration framework for K-12 STEM that combines a three-phased implementation roadmap with a four-phase professional development model for educators. The roadmap moves from short-term pilot AI literacy units, to medium-term teacher certification and capacity building, to long-term policy alignment, ethics audits, and student data governance. The professional development model is grounded in TPACK and critical algorithmic literacy and is designed to help teachers understand AI, adapt STEM lessons, and critically evaluate AI systems with students. The paper also emphasizes low-resource and culturally responsive implementation strategies for underfunded or diverse school contexts.

The population context is K-12 schools broadly, especially STEM classrooms and educators responsible for integrating AI into instruction. The paper does not report an empirical participant sample or a specific country-based study; instead, it synthesizes literature from education, AI ethics, and policy sources. The main conclusion is that AI in K-12 STEM should be introduced cautiously and intentionally, with human oversight, equity-centered design, teacher preparation, and governance structures to prevent harmful overreliance and ensure AI supports rather than undermines learning.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This paper is a critical conceptual review and synthesis, not an empirical study. It does not present original data, experimental design, or a systematic review with quantified pooled effects.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper has potentially meaningful institutional relevance because it proposes a concrete roadmap for AI integration, ethics, and professional development in K-12 STEM. However, it provides no direct evidence of impact on student outcomes or implementation effectiveness.

interventions.use_case: critical conceptual review and proposed framework for responsible AI integration in K-12 STEM education, including AI literacy, ethics instruction, and educator professional development

finding.finding_summary: This is a conceptual review, not an empirical intervention study, but it argues that AI in K-12 STEM can improve access and efficiency while also creating risks related to bias, privacy, and inequity. The paper proposes a three-phased implementation roadmap and tiered professional development model, citing prior work rather than generating new outcome data (n=not_reported; effect sizes=not_reported).
finding.measure: narrative synthesis of prior literature; proposed policy/implementation framework

paper_profiles.title: Disagreement as a way to study misinformation and its effects
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a conceptual problem in misinformation research: the prevailing definition of misinformation is often too narrow to explain the broader social, political, and psychological harms commonly attributed to it, such as polarization, distrust, vaccine hesitancy, and rumors. The authors argue that these outcomes are better understood as effects of disagreement—conflicting attitudes and beliefs—rather than as direct effects of false or misleading information alone.

The paper proposes disagreement as an alternative analytic framework and compares it with the misinformation framework across several dimensions, including explanation, intervention design, and measurement. Rather than studying whether information is true or false, the disagreement approach focuses on the social dynamics between communities, the normative and epistemic factors that shape conflict, and the strength of disagreement as a risk indicator for harmful outcomes. The authors also review nine common misinformation interventions and reinterpret them through the disagreement lens.

Although the paper is primarily theoretical, it includes a quantitative demonstration using text data from letters to the editor of The New York Times from 1950 to 2022, plus a comparison with vaccine-related tweets. These analyses suggest that disagreement can be measured automatically and that disagreement has increased since 2006, offering preliminary evidence consistent with claims about a post-truth era. The authors conclude that disagreement may provide a more useful framework for studying, measuring, and mitigating misinformation effects, especially in longitudinal, cross-topic, and automated analyses.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a conceptual/theoretical paper rather than an empirical study of an educational technology intervention. It does not evaluate a K-12 AI tool, and the quantitative text analysis is used to illustrate a misinformation framework, not to estimate an educational effect.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No direct educational or K-12 intervention impact is measured. The paper's implications concern misinformation research and measurement in general, so it provides no evidence of positive or negative impact on learner outcomes.

paper_profiles.title: PaperTrail: A Claim-Evidence Interface for Grounding Provenance in LLM-based Scholarly Q&A
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the 2026 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI ’26)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a reliability and trust calibration problem in LLM-based scholarly question-answering systems. The authors argue that existing provenance cues, such as coarse source citations, are insufficient for detecting subtle model errors like unsupported claims, omissions, and hallucinated or misleading evidence in academic contexts.

To address this, they introduce PaperTrail, an interface that decomposes both source papers and LLM answers into discrete claims and evidence, then matches them to reveal which answer claims are supported, unsupported, or omitted from the source literature. The system uses a three-stage backend: offline claim/evidence extraction from papers, real-time extraction from generated answers, and real-time claim-evidence matching to produce provenance indicators. The interface presents these matches through a multi-panel layout with claim coverage indicators and claim-level highlights.

The empirical evaluation is a within-subjects user study with 26 researchers working in a research organization. Participants completed two scholarly editing tasks: a multi-paper synthesis task and a devil’s-advocate review task, using PaperTrail and a citation-based baseline. Results show that PaperTrail lowered participants’ trust in LLM outputs compared with the baseline, indicating that granular provenance cues can make users more cautious. However, this reduced trust did not translate into meaningful behavioral changes in reliance: participants still tended to use the LLM-generated text because of time pressure and the cognitive burden of verification.

Overall, the paper concludes that claim-evidence provenance can improve trust calibration in scholarly AI settings, but trust reduction alone is not enough to change reliance behavior. The authors argue that interface design must also reduce cognitive load and better fit researchers’ workflows if provenance tools are to meaningfully affect how people use LLM-generated scholarly outputs.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed within-subjects HCI study with a modest sample (n=26), but it is not an RCT in an educational setting and the population is adult researchers rather than K-12 learners. The evidence is useful for understanding trust/reliance effects, but direct educational relevance and causal strength are limited.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The intervention reduced trust but did not change reliance behavior, and the study does not report a positive learning or efficiency effect of meaningful magnitude. Overall impact is unclear and, for the requested K-12 science-inquiry context, the findings are indirect and modest at best.

interventions.use_case: LLM-based scholarly question-answering that answers user queries over source papers and generates/editable draft text, with claim-evidence provenance annotations and citation-style comparison baseline

finding.finding_summary: In a within-subjects study with n=26 researchers, the PaperTrail interface significantly lowered participants’ trust in LLM outputs compared with a baseline citation interface. However, this caution did not produce a corresponding behavioral change in reliance: participants still relied on LLM-generated scholarly edits to avoid the cognitively burdensome editing task.
finding.measure: Subjective trust ratings; behavioral reliance quantified via normalized Levenshtein edit distance between original LLM text and participant edits

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that granular claim-evidence provenance increased cognitive burden and cluttered the interface, reducing usability under time constraints. Although it improved caution and visibility into unsupported claims, participants did not translate that into more efficient verification behavior or meaningful changes in editing workflow.
finding.measure: Usability feedback; task performance and interaction burden during scholarly editing and QA

paper_profiles.title: VLM@school – Evaluation of AI image understanding on German middle school knowledge
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper presents VLM@school, a new benchmark for evaluating vision-language models on German middle-school subject matter. The authors argue that existing multimodal benchmarks are often English-only, overly multiple-choice oriented, and not well aligned with real-world reasoning tasks, so they create a dataset of open-ended questions grounded in real curriculum materials and images.

The benchmark contains 486 images and 2,038 questions spanning nine domains: arts, biology, geography, history, math, music, physics, religion, and sports. The questions were drawn from German school textbooks for grades 8–10 and supplemented with author-created items and some internet images. The dataset also includes adversarial questions that are intentionally misleading and cannot be answered from the image, to test whether models can appropriately refuse uncertain answers.

The study evaluates 13 open-weight VLMs, using LLM-as-a-judge and a jury-style aggregation of multiple judge models for scoring open-ended responses. The main conclusion is that current VLMs struggle substantially with these middle-school-level tasks: even the best model scores under 45% overall, and performance drops sharply on adversarial questions. The authors conclude that German, curriculum-grounded, open-ended multimodal benchmarks expose important weaknesses not captured by popular public benchmarks, especially for contextual reasoning and saying “no” when the image does not support an answer.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a benchmark/evaluation paper, not a study of an educational intervention in K-12 classrooms. It uses a constructed dataset and model benchmarking methodology, but does not test a pedagogical AI tool with student outcomes, so the evidence framework criteria for intervention research are not met.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper has no direct educational impact estimate because it does not measure learner outcomes or operational change in schools. Its contribution is methodological and diagnostic for VLM evaluation, not an intervention effect on K-12 education.

paper_profiles.title: Democratizing Foundations of Problem-Solving with AI: A Breadth-First Search Curriculum for Middle School Students
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses how to broaden access to AI education in K–12 by embedding AI problem-solving into regular subject-area instruction rather than offering AI as a standalone enrichment activity. Specifically, it asks whether middle school students can learn the foundations of AI search and reasoning through a curriculum built around Breadth-First Search (BFS), and whether the curriculum fits well within a science classroom setting.

The intervention was a co-designed, seven-day module implemented in a rural public middle school health science class. Students used the i-SAIL Snap!-based learning environment for four guided BFS simulation activities, then reinforced learning through unplugged tracing exercises, contact-tracing and virus-transmission science activities, and a final simulation linking BFS reasoning to hypotheses about virus spread. The study used pre/post BFS knowledge assessments, student work artifacts, and a post-implementation teacher interview to evaluate learning and classroom fit.

The sample included six classrooms across grades 6–8 in one school, with analysis focused on students who had consent and matched data. Results showed significant gains in BFS understanding from pre to post, and many students could correctly identify shortest paths on a paper worksheet, though procedural tracing was often incomplete. Teacher feedback indicated the module fit well within the science curriculum, helped students see the relevance of BFS to health science, and supported both AI and science learning outcomes. The teacher also suggested clearer vocabulary supports and more frequent knowledge checks. Overall, the paper concludes that interactive, contextualized AI curriculum can make algorithmic reasoning accessible to middle school students without prior computing experience.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a classroom implementation study with pre/post assessment and qualitative interview data, but not a randomized design and without a comparison group. Evidence is therefore credible but primarily correlational/qualitative rather than high-causal-inference.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The main learning gain was moderate (Cohen’s dz=0.453), which clears the threshold for a modest-to-meaningful effect. However, the study is small and context-specific, so the broader impact is promising but limited.

interventions.use_case: interactive Snap!-based BFS learning environment (I-SAIL) with map-based graph tracing, queue/frontier manipulation, and step-by-step shortest-path problem solving for middle school science-integrated instruction

finding.finding_summary: Students improved their understanding of BFS/problem-solving after the seven-day curriculum. On the matched pre/post assessment (n=41), mean score increased from 0.683 to 0.790, with a statistically significant paired t-test result (t(40)=2.90, p=.006) and a moderate within-subject effect size (Cohen’s dz=0.453).
finding.measure: 5-item BFS knowledge assessment (proportion correct)

finding.finding_summary: The curriculum was designed to support science learning by embedding BFS in virus transmission and contact-tracing contexts, and the teacher reported that it fit well within the health science unit and supported intended science outcomes. This evidence is qualitative rather than a direct science achievement test, so the finding is best interpreted as supportive but not rigorously quantified.
finding.measure: Teacher interview about curriculum fit and support for science learning

finding.finding_summary: Students were able to trace BFS procedures and many could identify the shortest path on an unplugged worksheet, suggesting developing procedural reasoning and algorithmic thinking. However, written work often omitted intermediate steps and ordering details, indicating partial rather than fully stable procedural mastery.
finding.measure: BFS tracing worksheet accuracy and completeness of step-by-step records

finding.finding_summary: The teacher reported that the interactive and movement-based activities supported engagement and retention, noting that students on active days were more likely to understand and recall the material. No formal engagement scale was reported, so this is a qualitative indication of positive engagement rather than a quantified effect.
finding.measure: Teacher interview on engagement, motivation, and recall

paper_profiles.title: Learning Factors in AI-Augmented Education: A Comparative Study of Middle and High School Students
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how students’ perceptions of AI-mediated learning are structured across developmental stages, asking whether four learning factors—experience, clarity, comfort, and motivation—relate to one another in the same way for middle school and high school students. The authors frame the work around concerns that most prior AI-in-education research has focused on higher education, leaving K-12 understudied, especially with respect to how students evaluate AI tools and whether those evaluations vary by age.

The study was conducted in extracurricular computer science courses in Italy, where students used AI tools during programming-related activities. High school students worked with large language models such as Gemini and Claude for vibe coding and prompting, while middle school students used Teachable Machine and chatbot interaction in an introductory AI course. Data came from a 17-item questionnaire with Likert-scale and open-ended items, and the authors analyzed responses using correlation analysis, Mann-Whitney U tests, and text mining of student reflections.

Participants included 25 middle school students and 28 high school students. The main finding is that both groups reported generally positive experiences with AI, but the structure of their perceptions differed sharply: middle school students showed strong, positive intercorrelations across learning dimensions, suggesting a holistic evaluation pattern, whereas high school students showed weaker or near-zero correlations between several dimensions, indicating a more differentiated appraisal of usability, clarity, motivation, and comfort. The authors conclude that AI-supported educational design should be developmentally sensitive, emphasizing clarity and scaffolding for younger learners and more targeted support for older learners’ more critical and independent judgments.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a cross-sectional survey with correlation analysis and text mining, not an experimental or longitudinal causal design. It provides useful descriptive evidence on K-12 AI use, but credibility is limited for causal inference and relies on self-report measures from a small convenience sample.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The study suggests positive but modest perceived benefits of AI-supported programming activities, with no direct achievement effect sizes or outcome gains reported. Its main contribution is developmental insight into student perceptions rather than demonstrated instructional impact.

interventions.use_case: AI-mediated programming learning activities in middle and high school, including use of Gemini and Claude for vibe coding, prompting, code explanation, and chatbot-style interaction; middle school also used Teachable Machine with chatbot interaction as part of an introductory AI course.
Structured AI-related classroom learning activities in extracurricular computer science courses, where AI tools were embedded as instructional support rather than as a standalone tutor.

finding.finding_summary: Students reported generally positive attitudes toward the AI tools, with higher ratings for overall experience, ease of use, comfort, and motivation across both groups. However, the study is primarily correlational rather than causal; the strongest statistically significant group difference was for ease of use (Mann-Whitney U=192.00, p=0.0013), with high school students reporting greater usability (67.9% 'very much' easy) than middle school students (24.0%).
finding.measure: Likert-scale ratings of experience, ease of use, comfort, motivation, and willingness to use AI in other courses
finding.std_deviation: 0.85 overall experience SD in middle school; 0.65 in high school for Q1

finding.finding_summary: The paper found that AI-supported programming activities were associated with clearer, more differentiated student evaluations of usability, clarity, and learning support, especially in high school students. Middle school students showed strong positive coupling across dimensions (e.g., Experience-Clarity ρ=0.79; Clarity-Motivation ρ=0.60), whereas high school students showed weaker or near-zero links for several pairs (e.g., Experience-Motivation ρ=0.02; Experience-Comfort ρ=0.16), suggesting more critical appraisal and metacognitive differentiation rather than uniformly positive reactions.
finding.measure: Spearman correlations among survey dimensions and text-mined reflections on learning influence

finding.finding_summary: Students generally perceived the AI tools as helping them understand course content and support coding-related tasks. Open-ended responses emphasized learning support for middle schoolers ('learn', 'understand', 'helped') and more analytical support for high schoolers ('explanation', 'code', 'think'), but the paper does not report achievement test gains or learning performance effects.
finding.measure: Self-reported perceived learning support and text-mined reflections on AI influence on learning

paper_profiles.title: Designing AI Peers for Collaborative Mathematical Problem Solving with Middle School Students: A Participatory Design Study
paper_profiles.venue: CHI '26 / Proceedings of the 2026 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how middle school students perceive an AI peer in collaborative mathematics problem solving, and what features, behaviors, and controls they want from such a system. The motivation is that while generative AI tools are increasingly used for tutoring and feedback, much less is known about how they should function as peers inside small-group classroom collaboration rather than as expert instructors.

The authors ran a five-day participatory design summer camp with 24 rising grades 6-8 students in the United States. Students worked on grade-aligned middle-school mathematics CPS tasks in human-only groups and in AI-supported settings using a web-based technology probe with two AI peers (Alice and Bob) built on GPT-4o. The study combined paper surveys, workload and group-climate measures, audio-recorded reflections and interviews, and analysis of student design artifacts. Students then co-designed their ideal AI peer personas, behaviors, and controls.

Findings show that students preferred an AI peer that was scaffold-first, giving hints, checks, concept refreshers, and follow-up practice rather than full answers. They wanted the AI to be deferential, controllable, and socially attuned: it should ask questions, listen, avoid repetitive or domineering turns, and support emotional as well as cognitive needs. The paper concludes that AI peers for middle-school CPS should prioritize co-agency, adjustable help delivery, and a peer-like but expert tone, while minimizing overly scripted or teacher-like behavior.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed participatory design and comparative user study, but not a randomized trial and not designed to estimate causal learning effects. The evidence is informative but primarily qualitative plus small-sample within-subject survey comparisons, so it fits a lower-credibility tier.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper shows mixed but meaningful effects on workflow and collaboration perceptions, including a large reduction in temporal demand (d=1.15) alongside sizable downsides in physical demand and cohesion. Because the study does not measure learning gains and is based on a small camp sample, the overall impact on student outcomes remains unclear.

interventions.use_case: AI peer technology probe using GPT-4o to simulate two text-based conversational AI classmates (Alice and Bob) that support middle-school collaborative mathematics problem solving with hints, checks, explanations, and turn-taking dialogue.

finding.finding_summary: In a participatory design study with 24 middle-school students (paired survey analyses on n=22), students reported that the AI peers could speed up problem solving and provide mathematical scaffolds, but they did not evaluate learning gains on standardized mathematics tests. Qualitatively, students preferred hinting, error detection, and concept refreshers over direct answers, and they found conflicting solution paths distracting when not clearly scaffolded.
finding.measure: NASA-TLX temporal demand/physical demand during math CPS; GEQ task coordination during math CPS; interviews and design artifacts about math help preferences
finding.effect_size: d=1.15 (temporal demand reduction with AI peers); d=1.14 (physical demand increase); d=0.81 (lower group integration-task); d=0.94 (lower attractions to group-social)
finding.std_deviation: Temporal demand SD=4.38 vs 4.13; Physical demand SD=4.65 vs 2.41; ATGS SD=1.81 vs 2.05; GIT SD=1.58 vs 1.52

finding.finding_summary: Students reported that the AI peers often failed to recognize frustration, hesitation, or uncertainty, which weakened trust and sometimes redirected frustration inward toward self-blame. The qualitative findings indicate that emotionally unresponsive AI support was experienced as less supportive than human peers, even when the AI’s mathematical explanations were correct.
finding.measure: Interviews, whole-class reflections, and participatory design artifacts about emotional responsiveness and trust

finding.finding_summary: The study found that AI peers created a tradeoff for collaboration: they reduced temporal pressure but increased operational burden and lowered perceptions of group cohesion and coordination. Quantitatively, temporal demand decreased substantially (d=1.15), while physical demand increased (d=1.14) and GEQ group integration-task and attractions-to-group-social decreased (d=0.81 and d=0.94, respectively) in the AI condition versus human-only CPS.
finding.measure: NASA-TLX; Group Environment Questionnaire (GEQ); interviews about co-agency, listening, and collaboration norms
finding.study_size: n=22 for paired survey comparisons; n=24 in the camp overall

finding.finding_summary: Compared with human-only CPS, the AI peer condition significantly lowered perceived temporal demand, suggesting faster task progression and reduced time pressure during collaborative math work. This came with higher physical demand from the text-based interface, so the efficiency gain was real but not cost-free.
finding.measure: NASA-TLX temporal demand and physical demand subscales
finding.std_deviation: Temporal demand SD=4.38 vs 4.13; Physical demand SD=4.65 vs 2.41

paper_profiles.title: The Illusion of Understanding: How Middle-Schoolers Fail to Regulate Inquiry with ChatGPT in a Science Task
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether middle school students can regulate inquiry effectively when using ChatGPT for science investigation tasks. The authors focus on three aspects of interaction quality: discriminating between efficient and inefficient prompts, evaluating the usefulness of AI-generated answers, and deciding whether to continue asking follow-up questions or terminate the inquiry cycle. The broader motivation is to understand over-reliance, poor epistemic vigilance, and the potential for AI to create an “illusion of understanding” in K-12 learners.

The study involved 63 French middle school students aged 14–15 from four schools in the Nouvelle-Aquitaine region. Students completed questionnaires on AI attitudes and metacognition, then worked through six science inquiry tasks during a one-hour session with unrestricted access to ChatGPT 3.5. For each task, they judged a suggested prompt as efficient or inefficient, interacted with ChatGPT, rated every answer they received, and submitted a final written explanation in their own words. Researchers analyzed logs, ratings, and final responses, comparing student judgments with expert-coded answer quality.

Results showed that students were generally unable to reliably distinguish efficient from inefficient prompts and were similarly poor at evaluating whether AI responses were informative. Follow-up questioning was rare, indicating weak regulation of the inquiry cycle, and task success was only moderate. Positive attitudes toward AI and higher confidence in prior domain knowledge were associated with worse calibration, while metacognitive regulation and more critical views of AI predicted better interaction quality. The authors conclude that students need explicit AI literacy instruction focused on metacognitive regulation and critical evaluation, not just technical familiarity with generative AI.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical observational study with quantitative analyses, but it is not an experiment or randomized comparison, and the authors themselves note limitations such as small sample size and reliance on correlational/path analyses. It provides useful evidence, but internal validity is limited for causal claims.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The study suggests meaningful negative effects of unscaffolded ChatGPT use on K-12 inquiry quality, overreliance, and conceptual understanding, but the observed academic impact is modest-to-unclear overall (e.g., success rate 0.51) and based on a small sample. It is important for priority populations, but the direct effect size evidence is not strong enough for a higher impact tier.

interventions.use_case: Middle-school students used ChatGPT 3.5 as a conversational science inquiry support for unrestricted question-asking, prompt selection, answer evaluation, and follow-up questioning across six science investigation tasks.

finding.finding_summary: Students using ChatGPT for science inquiry showed only moderate task success, with an average correct solution rate of Msuccess=0.51 (SD=0.25) across six problems (n=63). Although high-level AI answers were associated with better outcomes, students’ inability to reliably discriminate prompt quality (Md′=0.19, t=1.77, p=0.08) and answer quality (Md′=0.07, t=-0.45, p=0.65) limited their ability to build accurate conceptual explanations.
finding.measure: Binary-coded written science explanations judged as deep, clear, explicitly addressing the problem, and accurate (success rate across six tasks)

finding.finding_summary: The study found strong evidence of weak metacognitive regulation during LLM-supported inquiry: prompt discrimination was at chance (Md′=0.19, SD=0.8; t=1.77, p=0.08), answer discrimination was also at chance (Md′=0.07, SD=1.2; t=-0.45, p=0.65), and only 14 of 63 students asked any follow-up questions. Positive AI attitudes and prior domain knowledge were associated with worse sensitivity to prompt or answer quality, indicating overreliance and poor epistemic vigilance.
finding.measure: Signal detection sensitivity to prompt quality and answer quality; follow-up-question frequency; correlations/regressions with metacognition and AI attitudes
finding.effect_size: Md′=0.19 for prompt discrimination; Md′=0.07 for answer discrimination; β values reported for predictors (e.g., β=-.39, β=-.35, β=.3)
finding.std_deviation: SD=0.8 for prompt d′; SD=1.2 for answer d′

finding.finding_summary: The interaction patterns suggest over-reliance and premature termination of inquiry rather than sustained engagement. Only 14 students generated follow-up questions (22 total across six tasks), and students often accepted or reused prompts they had judged inefficient, indicating low persistence in the QA cycle despite unrestricted access to ChatGPT.
finding.measure: Follow-up-question frequency; prompt acceptance/termination behavior; task completion patterns

paper_profiles.title: Elementary School Students’ and Teachers’ Perceptions Towards Creative Mathematical Writing with Generative AI
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how elementary school students and teachers perceived a generative AI-powered tool designed to support creative mathematical writing. The authors were interested in both the benefits and the challenges of using GenAI in a math learning activity where students create and revise math stories rather than only solve conventional problems.

The intervention, called [ANONYMOUS] in the paper, follows a three-step process: Ask, Represent, and Transform. Students first read and unpack math stories, then visually represent their thinking, and finally use GenAI (GPT-4 and DALL·E 3) to generate and revise culturally relevant math stories from their own inputs. The system also asked students to evaluate AI-generated stories using a checklist. The study used classroom implementation, semi-structured interviews, open-ended student survey responses, and observation notes, with thematic analysis of data from 79 fifth-grade students and six elementary teachers in two U.S. schools.

The main findings were that students and teachers saw several benefits: increased creativity, improved mathematical understanding, better AI literacy, and more interest, curiosity, and ownership in learning. At the same time, they identified important challenges, including students’ weak critical evaluation of AI output, difficulty generating coherent stories, the AI being perceived as “too perfect,” limited pedagogical feedback, reduced autonomy, weak social connection features, and lack of multiple communication modes. The paper concludes that GenAI can support mathematical creative writing, but its educational value depends on careful instructional and interface design that preserves room for student thinking, feedback, interaction, and accessibility.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative classroom study using thematic analysis of interviews, open-ended survey responses, and observations. It provides rich evidence about perceptions and design issues, but it does not test causal effects or report quantitative outcomes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests meaningful but unquantified benefits and barriers for a small sample of 5th-grade students and teachers. Because no effect sizes or achievement gains are reported, the overall impact is promising but unclear.

interventions.use_case: GenAI-powered creative mathematical writing support for elementary students, using GPT-4 to generate and revise math story drafts from student prompts and DALL·E 3 to generate matching images.

finding.finding_summary: The study reports perceived gains in mathematical understanding, including better problem comprehension, mathematical knowledge representation, and uncovering misconceptions during story creation. Evidence comes from qualitative interviews, open-ended survey responses, and classroom observations with 79 fifth-grade students and 6 teachers; no effect size was reported because the study did not measure achievement quantitatively.
finding.measure: Perceived mathematical understanding, problem comprehension, representation of mathematical ideas, and identification of misconceptions

finding.finding_summary: The intervention was perceived to support creative mathematical writing, including divergent thinking, convergent thinking, originality, and flexible thinking in math story creation. The paper is qualitative and reports thematic findings from 79 fifth-grade students and 6 teachers, so no quantitative effect size is available.
finding.measure: Perceived creativity in mathematical writing and story generation

finding.finding_summary: Students and teachers perceived the GenAI-supported activity as increasing interest, curiosity, enjoyment, and ownership of learning. These outcomes were derived from thematic analysis of interviews, surveys, and observations in six classrooms (79 fifth-grade students, 6 teachers), with no quantitative effect size reported.
finding.measure: Perceived interest, curiosity, enjoyment, and ownership in learning

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that students developed prompt-engineering awareness and a better sense of AI strengths and weaknesses, indicating gains in AI literacy and metacognitive evaluation of AI outputs. Findings are qualitative from 79 fifth-grade students and 6 teachers, so no effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Perceived AI literacy, prompt engineering use, and critical evaluation of AI capabilities

finding.finding_summary: The system appeared to support some durable skills such as evaluating AI outputs and reflecting on math ideas, but it also revealed barriers including weak critical evaluation of AI-generated content and difficulty generating coherent original stories. The evidence is qualitative and based on classroom implementation with 79 students and 6 teachers.
finding.measure: Critical evaluation of AI output, original idea generation, and coherent story formulation

paper_profiles.title: Children’s Overtrust and Shifting Perspectives of Generative AI
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates how middle school girls understand and evaluate generative AI, especially ChatGPT, and how exposure to mistakes or biased outputs changes their perceptions. The authors were motivated by concerns that genAI can produce misinformation and bias, and by the need to understand how children may overtrust these systems in school-related contexts.

The study used an IRB-approved educational workshop format with 26 middle school girls from two outreach programs at a university in a mid-sized East Coast U.S. city. The workshop included four activities: an introduction to genAI and bias, a guessing game exposing participants to incorrect ChatGPT outputs, a future-uses ideation activity, and a discussion of school and payment policies for genAI. Data came from session notes, participant artifacts, and some recorded one-on-one conversations, and were analyzed thematically.

Findings show that participants initially overtrusted ChatGPT and often treated it as similar to search engines, voice assistants, or calculators. Many judged incorrect outputs as correct based on superficial cues such as polished formatting or apparent reasoning, though some became more skeptical when they checked answers themselves. After seeing erroneous examples, their trust shifted toward disillusionment and a more realistic understanding of genAI’s limits, while they still remained optimistic about future applications. The paper concludes that deliberate exposure to erroneous outputs can support genAI literacy, and that educators should explicitly teach how genAI differs from conventional AI and other tools.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed qualitative workshop study with a small, self-selected sample and no control group or causal estimation. It provides useful exploratory evidence about children’s trust and reasoning, but not high-credibility intervention impact evidence.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests potentially important effects on trust calibration and policy thinking, but the evidence is qualitative and the observed change is not quantified as an outcome effect size. Its impact is therefore promising but unclear for general K-12 populations.

interventions.use_case: ChatGPT used in a middle school girls workshop to explore how a generative AI chatbot answers factual, procedural, and school-related questions, including deliberate exposure to incorrect outputs and bias examples to study trust and reasoning about the system.

finding.finding_summary: The workshop found that middle school girls initially overtrusted ChatGPT’s answers, with 59% of assessments for the incorrect outputs in Q2-Q4 labeling them as correct. After exposure to deliberate errors and bias examples, participants became more skeptical and better able to question the system’s limitations, indicating improved critical reasoning and metacognitive reflection rather than direct academic performance gains.
finding.measure: Qualitative thematic analysis of workshop discussions, plus proportions of incorrect ChatGPT outputs judged correct in a guessing game

finding.finding_summary: Students discussed school policies, fairness, and access issues around ChatGPT, including bans, cheating concerns, and the fairness of paid access. Their views were nuanced: some supported restrictions to prevent misuse, while others argued ChatGPT can help learning and that free access would be more equitable.
finding.measure: Qualitative thematic analysis of policy and fairness discussions about school use and paid access to ChatGPT

paper_profiles.title: AI-Fuzzy Markup Language with Computational Intelligence for High-School Student Learning
paper_profiles.venue: 2021 IEEE CIS Summer School on Computational Intelligence for High-School Student Learning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper reports on the 2021 IEEE CIS Summer School on Computational Intelligence for High-School Student Learning, with a focus on an AI-FML (AI-Fuzzy Markup Language) and AIoT workshop intended to introduce students to computational intelligence concepts. The work addresses the educational goal of making fuzzy logic, neural networks, and evolutionary computation understandable and engaging for younger learners through lectures, demonstrations, and hands-on co-learning with AIoT devices and robots.

The intervention combined recorded lectures, live tutorials, AI-FML learning platforms, and workshops using devices such as Kebbi Air, AIoT-FML-LT, and MoonCar. Participants included high school students as the primary target group, but the event also involved elementary school students, university students, graduate students, and teachers from Taiwan, Japan, Indonesia, and a few other countries. Students worked in small groups, often with tutors, to explore fuzzy-system parameters, design robot expressions, and interact with the learning tools through Zoom breakout rooms and physical/virtual activities.

The paper concludes that participants quickly understood the basic principles of computational intelligence and that the summer school successfully supported early exposure to AI/CI topics. Feedback and short reports suggested positive reception and a perceived educational benefit, especially for introducing students to rapidly evolving AI fields and fostering interest in future research. The authors also note that grouping by background knowledge is important for making such outreach events effective.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a descriptive outreach/report paper with qualitative feedback and attendance counts, not a controlled study. It provides some evidence of implementation and perceived understanding, but lacks pre/post measures, comparison groups, or causal identification.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests modest positive educational impact for participating students, but the evidence is anecdotal and non-quantitative. No effect sizes or formal outcome gains are reported, so the broader impact is unclear.

interventions.use_case: AI-FML robot Kebbi Air used in a high-school summer-school AIoT workshop for co-learning, interaction, and simulating perception/cognition during CI activities
AI-FML learning platform and AI-FML Lab used to teach computational intelligence basics, fuzzy inference, and AIoT concepts through guided hands-on instruction
AI-FML learning platform with AI-FML Blockly, ANFIS/PFML-based knowledge/rule-base training, and parameter exploration for student-directed learning

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that workshop participants 'quickly understood the principles of CI, FL, NN, and EC' after the 2021 summer school and AIoT workshop. This is based on short reports and feedback from attendees (n=80 submitted reports; n=77 feedback surveys), but no formal pre/post test scores or effect sizes are provided.
finding.measure: Participant short reports and feedback surveys about understanding of computational intelligence concepts

finding.finding_summary: Authors state that the event stimulated students to engage with rapidly evolving fields and fostered interest in future research adventures, suggesting positive motivation/engagement effects. Evidence is qualitative and anecdotal, drawn from participant and teacher remarks rather than standardized engagement measures.
finding.measure: Participant/teacher feedback on motivation and interest

finding.finding_summary: The workshop required students to examine fuzzy-system parameters, design robot expressions, and present short reports, indicating practice with problem solving, collaboration, and applied reasoning. The paper describes these tasks and reports that students gained experience with real-world applications, but no quantitative skill outcomes are reported.
finding.measure: Workshop task completion, group work, and student reports on applied problem solving/collaboration

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues the summer school supports broader institutional goals for STEM outreach and computational thinking education across Taiwan and Japan. This is an implementation/reporting paper, not an evaluation of policy impact, so findings are descriptive rather than causal.
finding.measure: Program participation, certificate completion, and outreach coverage
finding.study_size: n=214 registered; n=78 attended at least two-thirds of lectures/workshops

paper_profiles.title: Students' Perceived Roles, Opportunities, and Challenges of a Generative AI-powered Teachable Agent: A Case of Middle School Math Class
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how middle school students perceive the roles, benefits, and challenges of a generative AI-powered teachable agent (TA) in mathematics learning. The authors are interested in whether GenAI can strengthen the long-standing learning-by-teaching approach by making the TA more interactive, personalized, and conversational, while also introducing new problems such as confusion, weak feedback, or usability issues.

The intervention was a chatbot-like GenAI-powered TA built for middle school math, powered by GPT-4-Turbo and augmented with a knowledge graph, retrieval-augmented generation, personalization features, gamification, and scenario-based math problems. Students interacted with the TA by solving rate-and-ratio problems, explaining their reasoning, and helping the agent “learn” from them. The study was conducted in a public laboratory research middle school in the southeastern United States with 108 sixth-grade students across six classes. Data came from classroom observation, focus-group interviews, and open-ended survey responses.

Findings show that students saw the TA as a learning companion, learning facilitator, and collaborative problem-solver. They reported benefits including a more student-centered learning climate, greater autonomy, improved cognitive/social/emotional capacities, stronger math understanding, more positive attitudes toward AI, and interdisciplinary learning. At the same time, students identified important barriers: the TA’s weak problem presentation, overly surface-level questions, poor accommodation of learning styles, disorganized problem sequencing, limited social-emotional skill, technical glitches, interface issues, students’ own lack of domain and pedagogical knowledge, and the need for teacher facilitation. Overall, the paper concludes that GenAI can meaningfully extend teachable agents in K-12, but effective classroom use depends on stronger pedagogical design, better multimodal interaction, and continued human teacher support.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative exploratory classroom study using observations, focus groups, and open-ended surveys rather than a controlled impact evaluation. It is peer-reviewed and methodologically systematic, but it does not provide causal evidence of learning effects.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests potentially meaningful benefits for middle school math learning and engagement, but the evidence is perception-based and not quantified with effect sizes. Impact is therefore promising but unclear rather than demonstrated.

interventions.use_case: A generative AI-powered teachable agent for middle school math that simulates a less-knowledgeable peer in text-based dialogue, asks students to explain and fix math solutions, and uses GPT-4 Turbo with retrieval-augmented generation for personalized conversational support.

finding.finding_summary: Students reported that interacting with the GenAI-powered teachable agent improved their understanding of rate and ratio concepts and helped them apply knowledge to new contexts. This was a qualitative classroom study with n=108 sixth-grade students; no effect size was reported because outcomes were perceptions rather than standardized achievement measures.
finding.measure: Student perceptions of math understanding, conceptual clarity, and application of rate/ratio knowledge from interviews, open-ended surveys, and classroom observations

finding.finding_summary: Students perceived gains in enjoyment of math, self-efficacy, intrinsic motivation, and emotional resilience while working with the GenAI-powered TA. The study used qualitative data from n=108 sixth graders and found students described the experience as fun, confidence-building, and encouraging persistence, but it did not report quantitative effect sizes.
finding.measure: Student perceptions of enjoyment, self-efficacy, intrinsic motivation, and resilience

finding.finding_summary: Students perceived the TA as fostering cognitive, social, and collaborative skills, including elaboration, perspective-taking, communication, and problem-solving. In this qualitative study of n=108 sixth graders, students repeatedly described being pushed to explain reasoning, think from the agent’s perspective, and solve problems collaboratively; no quantitative effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Student perceptions of cognitive capacity, social capacity, collaboration, and metacognitive elaboration

finding.finding_summary: The system was seen as helpful for structuring interaction, but students also reported multiple usability and technical barriers, including glitches, slow loading, non-intuitive interface design, lack of multimodal input, and poor interoperability. This was based on qualitative feedback from n=108 sixth graders and 14 interviewees; no effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Student-reported usability, technical reliability, and interface/interaction barriers

paper_profiles.title: “How can we learn and use AI at the same time?”: Participatory Design of GenAI with High School Students
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates how high school students think generative AI should be designed and governed for educational use. The authors focus on a central tension raised by GenAI in schools: it can support learning and productivity, but it also introduces risks such as misinformation, bias, cheating, false accusations, and over-reliance. Rather than studying a fixed intervention, the paper asks how student perspectives can inform more actionable GenAI design guidance for education.

The study uses a participatory design workshop with 17 high school students in the United States. Students brainstormed concerns about GenAI, designed hypothetical GenAI tools, and created school policies to address the harms they identified. Workshop activities included discussing GenAI concepts, identifying problem spaces, sketching tool features, role-playing tool use, and reflecting on tradeoffs in classroom deployment. The context was high school education, with participants drawn from public and private schools and with prior experience using tools such as ChatGPT.

The main findings show that students preferred system-level safeguards over user-only education. They wanted GenAI tools to cite sources, use high-quality and diverse training data, improve accessibility across devices, and support learning through hints and feedback rather than direct answers. They were also concerned about teachers relying on unreliable AI detectors and spreading AI-generated misinformation, and they emphasized the need for transparent, consent-based data practices and stronger regulation. The paper concludes with design guidelines for GenAI in high school EdTech, arguing that student voices should be included in both tool development and school AI policy making.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative participatory design study with a small convenience sample of 17 high school students and no experimental comparison or causal inference. It is peer-reviewed and methodologically explicit, but it provides stakeholder perspectives rather than efficacy evidence.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper has clear relevance to K-12 GenAI governance and design, especially around misinformation, overreliance, and academic integrity, but it does not test an intervention or demonstrate measurable student impact. Its practical impact is therefore important but indirect and still uncertain.

interventions.use_case: participatory design of generative AI tools and school policies for high school education, including chatbot-style educational assistants that provide sources, personalized hints, and regulated student support

finding.finding_summary: This was a qualitative participatory design study with 17 high school students (n=17), not an effectiveness trial. The paper found students strongly preferred system-facing safeguards and policy changes—such as citations, consent-based data practices, teacher oversight, and regulation—over relying only on user education, indicating a positive institutional design contribution but no measured causal impact.
finding.measure: student workshop discussions, design artifacts, and post-workshop survey responses about AI policy/design preferences

finding.finding_summary: Students expressed concern that GenAI could erode critical thinking and other foundational skills through over-reliance, but they also valued tools that preserve learning via hints and reflection rather than direct answers. The workshop did not measure skill outcomes directly; instead, it surfaced student-designed approaches intended to balance AI use with the maintenance of critical thinking and self-accountability.
finding.measure: student-reported concerns and design ideas about critical thinking, independence, and learning balance

finding.finding_summary: Students reported that heavy workloads and pressure made them more likely to rely on AI as a 'last resort,' but they also felt the workshop increased confidence and knowledge about GenAI use in schools. Post-survey results showed 13/17 students (76.5%) felt the workshop improved understanding of GenAI tools, and 11/17 (64.7%) reported shifted views, but these are perception outcomes rather than direct measures of engagement or well-being.
finding.measure: post-workshop survey items on understanding, confidence, and feelings about GenAI in schools

finding.finding_summary: Students believed GenAI could support schoolwork, but they were concerned about hallucinations, cheating, and unreliable detectors, especially in writing and research tasks. The paper reports no academic achievement data; findings are qualitative and focused on how students want GenAI to support legitimate school use without replacing student research and writing.
finding.measure: student discussion of homework/classwork/testing, source citation, and academic integrity

paper_profiles.title: High School Science Profile Predicts Adults’ Views on the Future of AI and STS
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether students’ high school science profiles are associated with their later use of artificial intelligence (AI) and their perceptions of AI and science–technology–society (STS) issues in adulthood. The motivation is the growing concern that science education should prepare students to engage responsibly with AI, including understanding both its benefits and risks such as misinformation, privacy loss, labor displacement, and social consequences.

The study uses longitudinal panel data from the Korea Employment Education Panel (KEEP) II, tracking a cohort of Korean general high school students from 2016 to 2023. The analysis focused on 2,348 respondents who had complete data across waves. High school science interest and science achievement were measured during secondary school, and adult outcomes at age 24 included AI use, positive perceptions of AI, negative perceptions of AI, and three STS viewpoints related to human–AI relations, future quality of life, and monopoly of science/technology benefits. Structural equation modeling was used to examine direct and indirect paths among these variables.

The findings show that science achievement in high school, but not science interest directly, predicted later AI use. AI use in adulthood was associated with both more positive and more negative perceptions of AI. Those perceptions, together with AI use, shaped adults’ STS views: both positive and negative AI perceptions predicted attitudes about human–AI relations and quality of life, while negative perceptions were especially important for beliefs about technological monopolization. Overall, the study concludes that secondary science education may have long-term influence on how people later engage with AI and interpret its societal implications, though the relationships are indirect and mediated by achievement and AI use.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed longitudinal correlational SEM study using panel data, but it is not experimental and relies on observational associations with model modification. It provides useful evidence about relationships over time, but not causal evidence.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper’s findings are informative but indirect for K-12 intervention evidence: it does not test an educational tool or classroom intervention, and the outcomes are adult perceptions rather than immediate student learning. The observed effects are modest and primarily attitudinal/system-level rather than direct educational impacts.

finding.finding_summary: This longitudinal correlational study (n=2,348) found that high school science achievement positively predicted later AI use in adulthood (β=.18, p<.001), while science interest did not directly predict AI use (p>.05). AI use then related to both positive and negative perceptions of AI (β=.412 and β=.295, respectively), and these perceptions shaped broader STS views; the strongest path was from negative AI perception to beliefs about science and technology monopolization (β=.474, p<.001).
finding.measure: Structural equation model paths linking high school science profile, adult AI use/perceptions, and STS attitudes
finding.effect_size: β=.18 for science achievement→AI use; β=.412 and β=.295 for AI use→positive/negative AI perception; β=.474 for negative AI perception→STS monopoly

paper_profiles.title: Peak into the Past: An Archaeo-Astronomy Summer School
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper describes the design, delivery, and perceived impact of an archaeo-astronomy summer school intended to support transition from primary to secondary school and to enrich STEM learning through outdoor, interdisciplinary activities. The authors aim to show how local heritage sites can be used as outdoor classrooms to engage pupils with astronomy, archaeology, ecology, citizenship, and related science and mathematics concepts.

The intervention was a five-day summer school in 2009 run with The Meden School and Technology College in Worksop. Twenty-seven gifted and talented pupils from Years 5-8 participated. Activities were split between school-based preparation, field visits to two Peak District monuments (Arbor Low and Nine Ladies), analysis workshops at Nottingham Trent University, and a final presentation day for parents. Students conducted practical investigations such as surveying, sampling ecology, estimating construction effort, using planetarium software, and learning archaeological interpretation.

The paper reports mainly descriptive evidence of impact: student presentations, reflections, and follow-up activities suggested increased confidence, retention of knowledge, stronger subject understanding, and successful engagement with interdisciplinary content. The authors conclude that archaeo-astronomy can be integrated into the curriculum and that outdoor learning with local heritage sites can support both student learning and teacher development.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a descriptive practitioner article in a school science magazine, not a controlled study. It reports outcomes anecdotally and does not provide a formal evaluation design, comparison group, or statistical analysis.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The program appears beneficial for the participating gifted and talented students, but the evidence is qualitative and lacks quantified effect sizes. Impact is promising but unclear for general K-12 populations, so it fits a yellow tier.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that the archaeo-astronomy summer school improved students’ ability to apply scientific ideas in context, including using Stellarium, compasses, sampling, and measurement to test hypotheses about monument alignment and site ecology. The evidence is descriptive and qualitative rather than experimental, with the authors stating that pupils achieved all predefined outcomes and demonstrated better understanding of misconceptions such as the Sun’s rising/setting positions.
finding.measure: Student presentations, fieldwork products, and teacher/researcher observation of conceptual understanding and application of astronomy/ecology methods

finding.finding_summary: The summer school had positive impacts on interdisciplinary subject learning in archaeology, astronomy, ecology, and citizenship-related content. The authors report that student presentations on the final day showed coverage of all targeted topics and appropriate use of key vocabulary, with some evidence of retained knowledge during a follow-up museum visit more than a year later.
finding.measure: Final-day student presentations, follow-up museum visit observations, and use of topic-specific vocabulary/knowledge

finding.finding_summary: The paper describes improved self-confidence, motivation, and enjoyment among participants, especially in the initial focus group and during presentation activities. The evidence is qualitative: students were described as becoming more confident, more engaged, and better able to reflect on their work through the wiki and public presentations.
finding.measure: Observed student confidence, engagement, and willingness to present/reflection activities

finding.finding_summary: The project appears to strengthen collaboration, communication, and presentation skills through group fieldwork, creative displays, poetry, theatre, and PowerPoint presentations. The authors explicitly note improvements in social skills and individual growth, and the follow-up wiki work supported reflection and communication over time.
finding.measure: Student collaboration, presentations, reflective wiki use, and teacher/researcher observations

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that the wiki and supporting resources made it easier for teachers to maintain contact, monitor progress, and run follow-up work without requiring repeated specialist visits. This is presented as a practical benefit for delivery and sustainability of the enrichment program rather than as a measured workload outcome.
finding.measure: Described teacher coordination/support needs and sustainability of follow-up activities via wiki

paper_profiles.title: DMP_AI: An AI-Aided K-12 System for Teaching and Learning in Diverse Schools
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the challenge of applying AI effectively in K-12 education across diverse primary and secondary school settings. The authors argue that, although AI has promise for personalization, prediction, and decision support, real-world K-12 deployment remains limited and complicated by privacy concerns, heterogeneous school data, and uneven user understanding of AI.

To address these issues, the paper presents DMP_AI (Data Management Platform_Artificial Intelligence), an AI-aided educational system that integrates data mining, natural language processing, machine learning, learning analytics, and federated learning. The system includes five modules: student academic performance prediction and intervention, an early warning system, individualized education plan (IEP) analytics, talented student prediction and identification, and cross-school personalized electives recommendation. The paper describes the design of these modules and the privacy-preserving, cross-school data infrastructure supporting them.

The system was piloted in eight local Hong Kong schools, including three primary schools and five secondary schools, with feedback collected from 33 users via a 10-item survey. Results were generally positive: users rated the interface and usefulness favorably, and they expressed interest in continued use. However, respondents reported weaker gains in understanding AI, and the talented-student module received comparatively lower ratings, likely due to unfamiliarity with AI-based identification and heterogeneous data across schools. The authors conclude that DMP_AI is feasible and promising, but that continued training, explanation, and ethical attention to bias and transparency are needed for sustainable adoption.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed implementation/pilot study with survey-based feedback and descriptive reporting, but not a controlled design. Evidence is largely qualitative/correlational and focused on feasibility and user perceptions rather than causal outcome effects.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests modest positive institutional impact through successful deployment and acceptable user experience, but it does not provide strong evidence of learning gains or large-scale effects. Reported benefits are mainly feasibility and usability, with unresolved implementation challenges limiting impact strength.

interventions.use_case: AI-aided K-12 data management platform for student academic performance prediction, behavior prediction, early warning alerts, talented-student identification, IEP analytics, and cross-school elective recommendation

finding.finding_summary: The system was piloted in eight local schools (n=33 survey respondents) and users reported generally positive perceptions of usability, helpfulness, and willingness to continue using it. Average ratings were above 3.0 on a 5-point scale for most items, including overall satisfaction with module performance (3.03 overall), perceived helpfulness (3.54 overall), and intent to continue using the module (3.51 overall).
finding.measure: User experience survey ratings on 10 Likert-scale items covering performance, interface, usability, helpfulness, and future use

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports successful real-world implementation of an AI-aided K-12 platform across eight schools, indicating institutional feasibility and strong user acceptability. However, it also identifies persistent implementation challenges, especially heterogeneity of school data, privacy constraints, and the need for ongoing training to improve users' understanding of AI (mean 2.89/5 on understanding AI).
finding.measure: Cross-school deployment feasibility, user experience survey, and qualitative implementation reflections

paper_profiles.title: A Benchmark for Math Misconceptions: Bridging Gaps in Middle School Algebra with AI-Supported Instruction
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of helping AI systems and educators identify students’ algebra misconceptions and common errors more accurately. The authors argue that existing educational AI tools often lack grounding in real classroom misconceptions and that better benchmarks are needed to support diagnosis and targeted instruction. To address this, they build a benchmark of 55 algebra misconceptions/common errors with 220 diagnostic examples drawn from 145 peer-reviewed sources.

The study evaluates the benchmark with GPT-4-turbo using in-context learning. Two experiments were run: one with randomly sampled misconceptions across the whole dataset and one constrained within topic, showing better performance under topic-constrained testing. The authors also conducted a small educator survey and structured interviews with five middle school algebra teachers, four of whom participated in interviews, to assess clarity, classroom relevance, and potential AI uses. Teachers generally recognized the misconceptions as real classroom phenomena and expressed interest in using the dataset with AI for diagnosis and teacher support.

The population context is middle school algebra, especially grades 6–8, although the benchmark itself includes misconceptions relevant to 4th–8th grade algebra-related learning. The educators worked in U.S. public schools, including schools serving underserved populations and one youth correctional facility. The main conclusion is that GPT-4-turbo can identify misconceptions moderately well, especially when constrained by topic and supplemented by educator feedback, but performance varies substantially by topic and is weakest for ratios and proportional thinking. The paper concludes that topic-aware benchmarks, multimodal inputs, and human expertise are important for practical AI-supported misconception diagnosis.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed-style empirical benchmark/evaluation study, but it is not a controlled student learning trial and does not test causal impact on learner outcomes. Evidence is based on model classification performance plus small educator feedback, so it meets only limited credibility criteria for educational effectiveness evidence.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests potentially useful AI support for diagnosing algebra misconceptions, but it does not measure student learning gains or classroom impact. The reported gains are on model diagnostic accuracy rather than direct K-12 educational outcomes, so real-world impact remains unclear.

interventions.use_case: Using GPT-4-turbo as an AI-supported diagnostic assistant to identify middle school algebra misconceptions from student question/answer pairs, with topic-constrained prompting and educator feedback.

finding.finding_summary: The paper evaluates GPT-4-turbo on diagnosing 55 algebra misconceptions across 220 diagnostic examples. In repeated subsampling, performance was 0.526 precision / 0.529 recall when testing across the full dataset, improving to 0.753 precision / 0.748 recall when train/test examples were constrained by topic; with expert relabeling, topic-constrained accuracy reached 83.91% (1,100 iterations).
finding.measure: Precision, recall, and expert-reviewed classification accuracy for misconception diagnosis

paper_profiles.title: Personalized Multimodal Feedback Using Multiple External Representations: Strategy Profiles and Learning in High School Physics
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether and how students’ voluntary use of elaborated feedback in an online physics learning platform relates to later learning outcomes. The authors are motivated by the design problem of adaptive feedback systems: when learners are given both simple verification feedback and richer, multimodal explanations, which feedback formats do they choose, and do those choices associate with better performance? The study is also positioned as relevant to emerging AI-enabled tutoring systems and multimodal large language models, because it informs how feedback could be tailored across verbal, graphical, and mathematical representations.

The intervention/approach was a computer-based platform (KI4SCool) that delivered immediate verification feedback after multiple-choice kinematics questions and optional elaborated feedback in three external representations: verbal, graphical/pictorial, and mathematical. Students could open any combination of these representations, and the researchers logged their feedback-selection behavior. The study used a prospective observational cohort design rather than random assignment. Participants were high school students in grades 10–11 at schools across Germany, split into two cohorts with slightly different pre/post-test designs, and data were collected over approximately one term (16–24 weeks). In total, 661 students who completed both pre- and post-tests and answered at least one exercise were analyzed.

The main findings were that greater use of elaborated feedback was associated with higher post-test scores, even after controlling for prior knowledge, platform performance, exercise count, and confidence. However, the authors stress that this is correlational and cannot establish causality. Clustering analyses suggested four broad feedback-use groups, including students who never opened elaborated feedback, those who frequently used all three formats, those who favored verbal feedback, and those who used a more balanced mix. Time-resolved sequences did not reveal meaningful temporal strategy differences beyond frequency of feedback use.
